title: Best wet season in decades gives life to living medicine cabinet
content:
Best wet season in decades gives life to Barkindji people's living medicine cabinet
In short:
A new community-made field guide shares cultural knowledge utilised by Barkindji people for thousands of years.
The Barkindji Edible and Medicinal Plants book share uses of locally-found native plants throughout Menindee, Wilcannia and Broken Hill, in New South Wales' far west.
What's next?
Barkindji and Malyangapa tour guide and co-creator of the book, Dave Doyle, hopes it will inspire young people to spend more time in nature and to also protect it.
To most travellers passing through Menindee, the bushland along the Darling-Baaka River is a striking outback landscape, abundant with wildflowers and greenery.
But where others see a stretch of native scrub, Barkindji and Malyangapa man Dave Doyle sees something more valuable — a living medicine cabinet, teeming with plants whose healing properties have been used by his family for generations.
There's emu bush, which can help with wounds and headaches; native lemongrass to soothe a sore throat, and river mint, which makes for a soothing tea and helps with digestion.
A particularly wet season in Far West New South Wales has seen flora in the region flourish in numbers not seen for decades, according to Mr Doyle.
"It was probably the 90s or maybe early 2000s last time we had a season like this," Mr Doyle explains to tour guests who admire the flowers from the back seat of his ute, which he occasionally pulls over to take a closer look.
Mr Doyle's cultural tours depart from Broken Hill and traverse the Darling-Baaka River and Menindee Lakes, sharing cultural knowledge of medicinal and edible plants that Barkindji people have utilised for thousands of years.
The recently released field guide, Barkindji Edible & Medicinal Plants, a collaboration between Barkindji community members and friends, encourages young people to get out into nature and learn more about the plants around them.
"I think the more that we see the environment as something valuable, the more we'll look after it," Mr Doyle says.
On a recent tour, the guide demonstrated the kind of knowledge he is trying to pass on to younger generations.
"We actually wrote it for people of teenage years to be able to understand, rather than something a little bit more technical, hoping that kids will have a look at it and get interested in plants," he says.
Thousands of years sustained by natives
Along Menindee Road, he pulls over to the road's shoulder, climbing out into a field of lilac Darling peas that have sprouted in the red dirt, seemingly from nowhere.
While hunting was a big part of Barkindji culture, Mr Doyle says that plants were often more vital to Aboriginal diets throughout history.
"For us along the river, plants, vegetables that we collect, are probably like a main staple, more so than proteins that people tend to associate with Aboriginal people: kangaroos, emus, goannas, that kind of thing," he says.
"It was the plants that sustained us, gave us energy, gave us the vitamins and minerals to be able to absorb the nutrients and proteins out of those bigger animals as well, to give us the energy to continue to do our day-to-day work.
"There's so many uses like medicines, and a lot of the plants also are fibrous, so making string for twine nets, fishing lines."
Mr Doyle first became interested in learning about native medicinal and edible plants during COVID, when supermarkets often ran out of fresh produce.
"Through COVID, people were having trouble sourcing food a lot of time, and we actually have a lot around us, but we forget it's there or don't know what's edible and what's not," he says.
His interest in native plants has since extended beyond cultural tours and he also runs a catering business focused on native plants and traditional bush tucker.
In Kinchega National Park, along the Darling-Baaka River, he hosts a morning tea for tour guests featuring locally-sourced native plants.
The menu includes quandong and finger lime tarts and river mint tea — the latter picked on a walk along the river while the kettle boils.
He picks Warrigal greens, handing the leaves around the group for tasting.
"A lot of these plants have more nutrition than things we buy in the shops," he says.
"Warrigal greens are actually comparable to English spinach, and we don't have to pay for it, we just go and collect it off the edge of the river."
A garden medicine cabinet
Mr Doyle, also hopes the field guide will inspire people to plant native species in their own gardens.
"So if we need them, they're actually right there for us to use, as well as they look really beautiful," he says.
"I reckon every time a house is built, we should be putting natives in there, especially for Aboriginal people.
"We should be putting things like emu bush [in the garden], that is one of the most important bush medicines we have out here.
"And we should be planting things that don't need much water, they don't need any fertilisers or insecticides.
"It would be great if you've got a rash or a sore and you can just go out in the backyard, pick it and use it."

title: A Father’s Unfinished Dream Is Now Giving Hundreds of Seniors the Courage to Travel
content: “I couldn’t fulfil my father’s dream for him. But I could build something that would help hundreds of others fulfil theirs,” says Saakshi. For Saakshi Maheshwari (38), that thought became the beginning of something she had never planned to build. A travel writer and content creator for more than a decade, she had spent years helping others find places. But after losing her father in 2023, travel began to mean something different. It became a way of giving senior citizens the freedom to experience the journeys they had spent years postponing. Today, she runs ‘The Original Travel Company’ with her husband, Rajat Arora, taking small groups of seniors across India and overseas. Since launching the senior travel initiative in June 2023, she says she has travelled with approximately 350 senior citizens across more than 40 domestic and international journeys. But the story began with a man who believed retirement should not mean giving up on life. The man behind the idea Her father, Dr S K Maheshwari, was an army doctor who served for five years, including a posting in Tawang. Today, Saakshi runs ‘The Original Travel Company’ with her husband, Rajat Arora, taking small groups of seniors across India and overseas. He later worked with organisations including WHO and UNICEF on India’s polio eradication programme and with the Uttar Pradesh government on leprosy eradication and grassroots healthcare. Even during the COVID-19 pandemic, when most people were afraid to step outside, he travelled to villages around Agra to help people who had contracted the virus. “He was a doctor by profession, but service was at the core of everything he did. He believed that medicine was a way of serving people, and that compassion was as important as treatment,” she tells The Better India. He also had a particular concern for senior citizens. He wanted to spend more time visiting old age homes and using his medical experience to help elderly people. But work and family responsibilities kept pushing that dream into the future. He was also an enthusiastic traveller. He loved long drives, wanted to explore Kerala, and hoped to return to Tawang. He often spoke about travelling through the Northeast. Then, in January 2023, he was diagnosed with stage IV liver cancer. Two months later, at just 64, he died. One last holiday Just months before the diagnosis, Saakshi had travelled with her father to Kerala in October 2022. She remembers him dancing beside the sea, laughing whenever the waves touched his feet. “I didn’t know then that it would be one of our last trips together,” she says. His death made her question something many families take for granted. Time. “Like many families, we had assumed there would always be ‘later’,” she says. “Later to travel, later to slow down, later to fulfil dreams. His diagnosis, and then his death, taught me that later is never guaranteed.” She had already spent much of her adult life around travel. Born and raised in Meerut, she completed her BTech in Greater Noida between 2004 and 2008. She then worked with Accenture from 2008 to 2011 before pursuing an MBA in Mumbai from 2011 to 2013. She returned to the corporate world, working with companies and startups until late 2015. But travel had always been an itch she could not ignore. Around 2015, she began travel writing and content creation while still working. She later left the corporate world and spent more than 10 years travelling, writing for publications including AirAsia’s in-flight magazine and working with tourism boards such as Assam Tourism, Madhya Pradesh Tourism and Malaysia Tourism. “Travel taught me empathy, openness, and perspective. It was never just about seeing the world, but about understanding people, cultures and, ultimately, understanding myself,” she says. After her father died, she knew where she wanted to take that experience. In June 2023, she launched her senior travel initiative. In January 2026, she gave the venture a name of its own, The Original Travel Company. What was missing Before starting, she noticed that senior citizens were occasionally the focus of mainstream travel planning. The itineraries were mostly designed around speed. Wake up early, board the bus, visit several attractions, climb stairs, move to the next destination, and return late. That might work for younger travellers. For many seniors, it can turn a holiday into an exhausting exercise. “Most of them had not stopped dreaming about travel,” she says. “What had changed was their confidence, and the support available to them.” Companionship was another major barrier. Some had lost their spouses, while their children lived in other cities or countries, and friends who once travelled with them had stopped doing so, leaving many hesitant to join large groups of strangers. The founder felt the problem was not where seniors travelled, but how they were expected to travel. The founder felt the problem was not where seniors travelled, but how they were expected to travel. “What they needed was a slower, more thoughtful experience, one that put their comfort, confidence and wellbeing before ticking places off a list,” she says. That philosophy now decides every trip. It starts with a recce The couple does not take senior travellers to a destination until they have personally studied and experienced the route themselves. First, they research the destination. Then they travel there themselves, checking routes, hotels, attractions, and transport. They ask themselves one question. “If I were travelling with my own parents, what would I want them to experience?” They check hotels for accessibility, comfort, and location, and even ask hotel staff to show them the rooms and facilities over video calls when needed. In Japan, for instance, repeated visits taught them that hotel size matters because rooms can be considerably smaller than those in other countries. They also consider the number of stairs at sightseeing spots, the distance between attractions, the availability of lifts and the location of healthcare facilities. A first aid kit accompanies the group everywhere, even during short stops. “Health planning can never be an afterthought,” she says. The pace is deliberately slower, with breaks built in. Meals include a combination of Indian and local cuisine, while dietary requirements are considered individually. Every itinerary goes through multiple revisions. “The objective is not to maximise sightseeing. It is to maximise relaxation and enjoyment,” she says. Nothing is left to chance The attention to detail continues once the group begins travelling. The team tracks visa requirements, flight schedules, weather conditions and health advisories, particularly for international destinations. Before a recent Sri Lanka trip, they learnt about a dengue outbreak around Colombo. Travellers were informed and asked to carry full-sleeved clothing, while the co-founders carried anti-mosquito sprays. Even hotel check-ins are planned in advance. “We like to call the hotel two hours before we are about to reach there with the group to make sure that the rooms are ready, the ACs are turned on, the welcome drinks are ready,” she says. The goal is that seniors should never have to arrive after a long journey and wait at reception. Their groups are also capped at 12 to 14 people. Saakshi and Rajat personally accompany every group, meaning they know the travellers, their needs and their concerns. “We want to return as a family,” she says. The holiday is only part of it For many travellers, the friendships become just as important as the destination. They celebrate birthdays, remember anniversaries, and frequently see travellers who arrive alone leave with new friends and a WhatsApp group they are reluctant to close. Leena Menon, a retired children’s librarian who spent more than 20 years working with Auckland Libraries in New Zealand, travelled to Bhutan with the company. She was looking for something different from a conventional package tour. “The focus was not just on covering destinations but on creating memorable experiences,” she says. During the trip, the team surprised Leena and her husband with an anniversary celebration. “It made us feel that we were travelling with friends rather than a tour company,” she says. For 76-year-old Ahmedabad resident Mrs Pervin Phiroze Guard, the biggest concern was safety. After losing her partner, she was living alone and worried about travelling without a companion. Her daughter found the company on Instagram in April or May 2024. She was initially sceptical. The team answered her questions and even shared contact details of previous travellers so she could speak to them. Her first trip was a mother-daughter holiday to Goa in June 2024. “What touched me the most was Saakshi’s genuine care; she constantly checked on everyone’s comfort and made sure every senior traveller felt included, valued and cared for,” Pervin says. The experience changed her outlook. “The trip reminded me that age is just a number,” she says. The couple does not take senior travellers to a destination until they have personally studied and experienced the route themselves. Then there is 68-year-old Ranjana Dixit from Satna, who retired from Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board in 2020. Work, family responsibilities and health problems, including a knee replacement, had kept her from travelling as much as she wanted. She first heard about the initiative through her daughter in May 2024. Since then, she has travelled to Kashmir, Bhutan and Rajasthan with the company and celebrated her birthday on trips in 2024 and 2025. “Fulfilling my dreams has raised my confidence and made me want to travel even more,” she says. Even after undergoing another knee replacement in April 2026, she already has two trips lined up for October and November. She wants other seniors to remember one thing, “If your trip is led by Saakshi or Rajat, then you can keep your worries at home and enjoy the trip to the fullest.” 350 stories and counting So far, the founder says approximately 350 senior citizens have travelled with her across more than 40 domestic and international trips. Their destinations have included Japan, South Korea, Turkey, Bali, Bhutan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Dubai and Abu Dhabi, as well as Kashmir, Ladakh, Meghalaya, Rajasthan, the Andamans, Sikkim, Varanasi, Ayodhya, Madhya Pradesh, Assam and the Rann of Kutch. Around 40 percent of travellers return for another journey. But the number that matters most is not 350. It is the person boarding an international flight alone for the first time at 68. It is the widow taking her first holiday after losing her husband. It is someone seeing the ocean for the first time at 70. And it is the children who call afterwards to say they have seen their parents happier than they have been in years. “We are a source to give them the confidence to step out, experience new places, and bring more joy and happiness into their lives,” the founder says. A legacy in motion The company remains intentionally small, with four core members. The couple works alongside a social media executive and an operations executive, supported by trusted local partners. Rajat left his corporate career of more than 15 years to join the venture full-time. There is no strict division of responsibilities between the couple. “From social media to marketing, from operations, from booking flight tickets to doing every little thing that needs to be done for a business, both of us are all hands on deck,” Saakshi says. For her, the company has become more than work. “I have to say that I wouldn’t have survived these three years if not for the senior travel company that I have built,” she says. “That kept me going.” The work has changed how she thinks about ageing too. “I have met people in their seventies who are more adventurous, more inquisitive, and more open to new experiences than people half their age,” she says. Her biggest lesson has been not to postpone life. “I have always believed in putting relationships before business, because when you invest in genuine relationships, the business naturally follows,” she says. The Original Travel Company’s next plans include destinations across Central Asia, Europe and Africa. But she wants growth without losing the personal care that brought the company this far. They check hotels for accessibility, comfort, and location, and even ask hotel staff to show them the rooms and facilities over video calls when needed. Her goal is not to become the biggest senior travel company. She wants to become the most trusted. She hopes families will stop seeing travel as a luxury for their ageing parents and begin seeing it as an investment in their happiness and wellbeing. And if her father could see what his daughter has built, she believes he would not care about the number of destinations or travellers. “He’d simply look at the seniors laughing together, and say, ‘This is exactly what I hoped for,’” she says. Her father spent his life helping people live healthier lives. Saakshi hopes she is helping them live happier ones. All pictures courtesy Saakshi Maheshwari.

title: Treat education as infrastructure during wartime, say researchers in Ukraine
content:
War destroys laboratories and instruments. It also severs the human networks through which science reproduces itself. It disrupts mentorship, collaborations and informal ties that turn students into researchers.
In a new Comment in Nature Genetics, an international team including Centre for Genomic Regulation (CRG) researcher Roderic Guigó argues that protecting science under the systemic stress of wartime means treating education and training itself as infrastructure rather than as a series of one-off events.
The authors draw on the experience of running the Ukrainian Biological Data Science Summer School (UBDS3), held in person at Uzhhorod National University in western Ukraine since 2023, which is in session again this month from July 11 to 25, 2026.
Because martial law prevents most male students and early-career researchers from leaving the country, any model that depends on traveling abroad excludes them entirely. BDS³ inverts this by bringing world-class researchers into Ukraine, giving participants a point of contact with the international scientific community they would otherwise have no easy way to directly interact with.
What started as a two-week pilot that drew more than 100 students to Uzhhorod, Ukraine's westernmost city, has run every summer since. UBDS3 is offered free of charge, with travel, room and board covered, and taught bilingually in Ukrainian and English by faculty from leading research institutions across Europe, North America and Asia, including the CRG.
The school is one half of a larger effort centered on Uzhhorod. A new genomics research facility at the city's university has already begun to deliver clinical dividends, including corrected diagnoses for patients with a rare, treatable form of diabetes, a reminder that research depends entirely on the trained people the school exists to produce.
"Biological data science did not exist as an organized field in Ukraine before this initiative. My objective is to bring as much expertise to Uzhhorod as I can in whatever time I have left and turn it into the Cambridge of Ukraine," says Taras Oleksyk, corresponding author from Uzhhorod National University and Oakland University in the United States and one of the main instigators of the school.
From this experience, the authors set out three design principles for resilient scientific capacity. The first is decentralized, cloud-based computing that does not depend on any single facility. Research institutes face infrastructure damage, energy instability and power cuts, so decentralized workflows can keep running even when local conditions are disrupted by events like air raids.
The second is a "train-the-trainer" structure in which former students return as instructors. Alumni now regularly return to teach the next cohort of BDS³, a self-renewing pipeline that has turned a series of courses into lasting institutional memory.
"It is an irreplaceable experience for the trainers. It is a sobering reminder of both how privileged we are and how fragile the stability of the world we live in is," Guigó says.
Finally, the authors call for a non-extractive type of international collaboration, in which partners contribute expertise and access without recruiting participants permanently away so that internationalization strengthens local science rather than draining it.
The school's scientific leadership also includes CRG alumnus Fyodor Kondrashov, a former group leader now at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology, where he directs the School of Molecular and Theoretical Biology. Working with Oleksyk and with support from the Zimin Foundation and the European Molecular Biology Organization (EMBO), he has helped establish the school. The CRG's Guigó has also helped organize BDS³ and has taught at past editions in person.
The lesson, the authors argue, is not confined to Ukraine. Climate disasters, energy failures, cyberattacks and funding shocks increasingly disrupt research systems everywhere, and the same distributed, people-centered model applies wherever infrastructure or mobility cannot be taken for granted.
Five early-career researchers from Barcelona's community took part in this year's edition, all connected to the school through the CRG's networks: Julia Rühle and Iseult Leahy, both at the CRG; Max Ticó, of the University of Barcelona; Guillem Guigó-Corominas, of the University of Girona and the University of Vic; and Helena Crowell, of CNAG. Many other CRG researchers have participated in previous editions.

title: He spent years reconciling his identity. Now he’s the first Arab bishop in Episcopal history.
content:
He spent years reconciling his identity. Now he’s the first Arab bishop in Episcopal history.
Get RNS’ thoughtful, essential religion reporting every morning. Sign up for free!
BROOKVILLE, N.Y. (RNS) — When Adam J. Shoemaker became the first bishop of Arab and North African descent in the Episcopal Church’s 237-year history this past weekend, many of his colleagues saw it as a glass-ceiling smashing.
Donning vestments with a Turkish blue tulip and North African pattern, Shoemaker greeted families, clergy and laypeople alike after his ordination and consecration as the ninth bishop of the Episcopal Diocese of Long Island on Saturday (Sept. 19). Nearly 2,000 people attended the ceremony at Tilles Center for the Performing Arts in Brookville, New York. The line to meet him stretched for more than 90 minutes.
“He embodies what it means to be the church in the world, and in particular, in New York City and the suburbs,” said the Rev. Lindsay Lunnum, rector of Zion Episcopal Church in Queens, which is part of Shoemaker’s diocese alongside Brooklyn.
Shoemaker, 47, told RNS he sees himself as an “imperfect vessel” for serving the church. But his background is almost tailor-made for leading one of the Episcopal Church’s most ethnically diverse dioceses: he was baptized in the diocese; he’s lived in Latin America and speaks advanced Portuguese and basic Spanish; and he is the son of a Muslim Egyptian and a New Yorker with Jewish roots. His background covers the trifecta of the Abrahamic faiths.
But accepting his heritage hasn’t always come easily for him, he said.
Prior to his election as bishop in April, Shoemaker served as rector of St. Stephen’s Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, for nine years. His ministry assignments have also taken him to North Carolina, Massachusetts and Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. He holds degrees from the General Theological Seminary in New York City, Harvard Divinity School, Boston University and a Doctor of Ministry from Duke Divinity School.
“The first time someone breaks that glass ceiling is really meaningful and really powerful, to be able to see yourself represented in the positions of high power in the church that you have served,” said the Rev. Leyla King, canon for Mission in Small Congregations in the Episcopal Diocese of West Texas and co-founder of Palestinian Anglicans and Clergy Allies. His ordination means a great deal to her and other Southwest Asia and North Africa (SWANA) Episcopalians and clergy from other traditions, particularly in an era of increasing anti-Arab and anti-Muslim rhetoric, she noted.
Shoemaker, born Adam James Haggagi, was raised in New York, where his parents moved just before he was born. They had met at a train station in Luxor, Egypt, while his mother — a New York native, secular Jew and Egyptologist — was on vacation. His father struck up a conversation, and romance ensued. His mother didn’t come back from that vacation until just before he was born, he said.
While he was still a young child, his parents separated, and his father returned to Egypt. Shoemaker would see him only periodically when he had business trips to New York. Upon advice from the State Department, his mother never allowed him to travel to Egypt to visit his father’s family.
Eventually, his mother remarried, and he was enrolled in school with his stepfather’s name, Shoemaker.
Without much contact with other Arabs, Shoemaker described internalizing a sense of racism around his heritage growing up.
“There were times in my life when I would blame everything I didn’t like about myself on my Arabness,” he said. “It had a really corrosive effect on my personhood.”
By the time he was 18, he legally changed his name to Shoemaker. He estranged himself from his father after his mother died a few years later, he said.
The 9/11 terrorist attacks, which happened during his senior year of college, began to change things for him, however. “I remember 9/12, 9/13, 9/14 very differently because of my background,” he said.
While he said he was largely shielded from racism because of his lighter skin tone, he saw the accelerating racism toward Southwest Asian and North African Americans and Muslims in the U.S. He remembered seeing Arabs and Muslims pinning American flags to their clothes, in efforts to shield themselves from a pervasive feeling of retribution.
Between seeking therapy and serving as a missionary in his early 20s in Brazil — where his mixed ethnic background was both normal and celebrated — he began learning to cherish his ethnic identity, he said. At the same time, he had begun discerning a call to the priesthood in the Episcopal Church, in which he was raised.
He was ordained as a deacon in 2007, and as a priest in 2008.
Around that time, in his mid to late 20s, he reconciled with his father in Egypt. When he visited in 2020, just before the COVID-19 pandemic, he wasn’t sure if his Muslim family would accept their half-American relative who was a Christian priest.
But when one of his aunts saw him for the first time, she approached him with tears in her eyes and immediately embraced him “the way you hug something that’s been lost for so long, and you’ve found it,” he recalled. His father drove him around Luxor honking and exclaiming to neighbors that his long lost son had returned. It was a deeply meaningful experience for the bishop.
“The journey that I’ve been on my whole life to reconcile the disparate parts of my personhood and certainly my Arabness … it’s been liberating,” he said. “It’s helped me to become more fully the beloved child of God that I believe I’ve been called to be, and the priest and hopefully the bishop that I’ve been called to be.”
He hopes to use his new role to help elevate the voices and experiences of SWANA peoples within the Episcopal Church, he added.
The Rev. Julie Hoplamazian, the Armenian-American rector of St. Michael’s Episcopal Church on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, said Shoemaker is the perfect person to help bring that perspective.
“The perspective of folks who live in that region of the world is a perspective that the church has conventionally tried to colonize,” she said. “And now we have a person from that part of the world who is a voice and a leader in the church to remind us and be a voice for the people who are the original Christians, the oldest Christians.”
The Rev. Halim Shukair, a Lebanese Episcopal priest who serves as priest-in-charge of Christ Episcopal Church and Mother of the Savior, an Arabic-speaking Episcopal-Lutheran mission congregation in Dearborn, Michigan, said the lack of awareness of SWANA peoples and cultures has led to frustrating, and at times, comical experiences in the church. While at Virginia Theological Seminary, he said he was regularly asked when he converted to Christianity, before reminding his classmates that Christianity, in fact, started in the Middle East.
But for King, the challenges go beyond ignorance. She pointed to a failed Episcopal House of Bishops resolution to acknowledge Palestinians as “among the indigenous people of the lands of Palestine and Israel lying between the Mediterranean Sea and the Jordan River.” Shoemaker’s election demonstrates the possibility of change, she said.
“There’s far more to come, and it doesn’t erase the hurt and sense of betrayal … but there is hope,” she said. “Adam is representative of that hope.”
Shoemaker also said he sees his leadership as an opportunity for change within the church, including in its relationship to the realities of violence in Israel and the Palestinian territories.
“I would hope to find ways to share my (Arab-American) perspective in Christian love, not only as bishop of the diocese, but as a bishop writ large in the wider church, and to be compassionate for the suffering that goes on in Gaza, in the West Bank,” he said.
As bishop, he believes part of his job is to serve as a public theologian. This compels him “to speak for fundamental Christian values, baptismal covenant values — dignity, respect, the inherent dignity and worth of all,” he said.
A large contingent from South Carolina, where he previously served, attended the ceremony on Saturday.
“I think the people of Long Island will not only embrace him, but be energized by the passion which he speaks to the issues that are so prevalent in our society today,” said Michael Shaffer, rector of St. Mark’s Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, and a former colleague of Shoemaker.
Donna Landers-George, a parishioner at Church of the Advent, an Episcopal church in Westbury, New York, said the overwhelming feeling across the diocese is one of excitement. “He’s the bishop for what is yet to come, a bishop for the future,” she said.

title: Educación, clave para la justicia social: ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil
content:
Rachel Barros de Oliveira resaltó en conferencia magistral el papel central de las acciones afirmativas
Miércoles 2 de septiembre de 2026, p. 12
La ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil, Rachel Barros de Oliveira, enfatizó el papel primordial de las acciones afirmativas para alcanzar la igualdad y la justicia social. Al dictar una conferencia magistral, en el contexto de su participación en la convención internacional A 25 años de Durban, destacó que brindar oportunidades educativas a las juventudes negras, indígenas y afrodescendientes es central para consolidar la democracia, la justicia y la igualdad en nuestras sociedades.
Ante la presencia de estudiantes de licenciatura y posgrado, especialistas, docentes y activistas reunidos en el auditorio Benito Juárez de la Facultad de Derecho de la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM), recordó que Brasil fue el último país en América Latina en abolir la esclavitud, el 13 de mayo de 1888. Sin embargo, pasarían 100 años más antes de que se incluyera en su Constitución el reconocimiento a la dignidad y plenos derechos de la población negra y afrodescendiente.
Destacó que fue en los años 90 del siglo pasado cuando los movimientos por la defensa de los derechos de los pueblos negros en Brasil elaboraron un pliego de demandas centrales que entregaron al Estado, las cuales se verán reflejadas en la propia agenda del encuentro mundial de Naciones Unidas para combatir el racismo, la discriminación racial, la xenofobia y toda forma de intolerancia, celebrado en Durban, Sudáfrica, en 2001, que daría como resultado la Declaración y el Programa de Acción de Durban.
Reconocimiento
Barros de Oliveira recibió un reconocimiento por el programa Caminos Amefricanos, que promueve la formación e intercambio de conocimientos entre Brasil y los países de África, América Latina y el Caribe.
Con este esfuerzo, señaló, son seleccionados profesores de enseñanza básica, estudiantes y otros profesionales de la educación para participar en experiencias de formación e intercambio internacional mediante estancias cortas, y que el año próximo incluirá a México.
Destacó las acciones afirmativas en pro de los grupos más vulnerables, como el programa de cuotas para el ingreso de jóvenes negros y afrodescendientes a las universidades públicas, con las que se logró matricular a más de 4 millones de estudiantes; el Plan Juventud Negra Viva para el derecho a una vida digna; el programa de impulso a las mujeres negras en la ciencia, y la aprobación de una ley que indica la enseñanza de la historia y la cultura afrobrasileñas y africanas en los niveles de educación básica y media superior.
La ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil subrayó el papel central de la educación como vía para fortalecer la justicia social, pero también el ejercicio pleno de otros derechos para la población negra, afrodescendiente e indígena de nuestra región, así como para reconocer su aportación cultural, social y de conocimientos en América Latina y el mundo.

title: Indigenous fisherwoman finds ‘lost’ spinach pipefish, not seen by science in 40 years
content:
Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.
On the final day of a two-week expedition, where researchers were searching for a “lost” species along Papua New Guinea’s Sepik River, Helen Asu arrived with two small, greenish-brown fish. She had caught them while fishing for prawns with an umben, a traditional hand net, near Imbando village in East Sepik province.
They were spinach pipefish (Microphis spinachioides), a species known only from the Sepik and not recorded by scientists since 1985, reports Mongabay’s Spoorthy Raman.
“It was honestly an incredible moment,” said Jerrica Agebigo, a researcher at the Papua New Guinea University of Technology and the New Guinea Binatang Research Centre, who led the expedition. “When Helen showed the fish to us, I immediately realized that we had found something very special.”
The spinach pipefish is a freshwater relative of seahorses and seadragons. It grows to about 15 centimeters (6 inches) and uses its elongated snout to catch small prey. Its coloring helps conceal it among water lilies and other plants along the banks of the Sepik, Papua New Guinea’s longest river.
Almost everything else about it remains uncertain. The specimen used to describe the species was held at Hamburg’s natural history museum, but was destroyed during the second world war. When the fish was last assessed for the IUCN Red List in 2016, it was classified as data deficient. It later became one of the 10 most sought-after species on the “Lost Fishes” list, compiled by SHOAL, Re:wild and the IUCN Freshwater Fish Specialist Group. The wider list includes more than 300 freshwater fishes missing to science.
Agebigo’s team, made up of local scientists and community members, set out in June to learn whether the pipefish still survived and, if so, what threats it faced. Along the Sepik river they showed pictures to residents and asked fishers whether they recognized it. On June 18, Asu supplied the answer.
The rediscovery will allow scientists to begin filling gaps in knowledge left by four decades without a confirmed record of the fish.
“The fact that a species could go without a confirmed record for around four decades — and then be found through the daily activities of a local fisher — is a powerful reminder of the importance of local ecological knowledge,” Agebigo said. “Without Helen’s knowledge, experience and willingness to help us, we may not have found the species.”

title: Sites of memory in Western Azerbaijan: History of Abilkend village
content:
Sites of memory in Western Azerbaijan: History of Abilkend village
- 24 September, 2026
- 14:40
Western Azerbaijan is a geographical region where hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis historically lived. Despite attempts to erase the traces of compatriots in these territories today, it is considered a duty to remember their ancient places of residence in Western Azerbaijan and to stay informed about them.
The purpose of the Sites of Memory of Western Azerbaijan project is precisely to convey information to the younger generation about the native lands of compatriots expelled from their historical homeland.
Sites of Memory of Western Azerbaijan is a joint project by AZfront and a Ukrainian historian working under the pseudonym Kuzari. The project is based on the historical research titled "The Perished Civilization."
During field research conducted between 2021 and 2024 on the territory of modern Armenia, photo and video materials were collected about nearly 600 villages where the ancestors of modern Azerbaijanis originally lived. Information regarding the history of these settlements, their population, and surviving objects of Turkic cultural and historical heritage - such as cemeteries, shrines, mosques, and other monuments - has been systematized.
As part of the project, video materials in Azerbaijani, Russian, and English have been prepared for each village, along with a separate text based on historical sources. The materials will be presented in stages for each settlement.
The authors of the project first presented the history of the Azerbaijani village of Sheki (now Shaki), located in the territory of Armenia.
The new episode recounts the history of the Azerbaijani village of Abilkend (now Noramarg) in Armenia, whose population was subjected to expulsion and deportation on three occasions.
In documents of the Russian Empire and other written sources from the 19th century through the first third of the 20th century, the ancestors of present-day Azerbaijanis were referred to as "Tatars," "Caucasian Tatars," "Tiurks," or "Muslims," Report informs.
Some of the sources referenced in this project also use the terms "Turks," "Tiurko-Tatars," "Islams," or "Myugammedans." Hereafter, "ancestors of the Azerbaijanis" will be used when referring to the period before 1920, while "Azerbaijanis" will be used for the subsequent period.
The names of Abilkend in historical documents:
● during the Tsarist period – Abil-kend, Abul-kend, Abyul-kend
● during the Soviet period – Abilkend, Ablkend, Bulakhly, Bulagli, Bulakhlar, Kalinin Settlement, Kalinin.
In Russian imperial-era sources, the village appeared under the name Abilkend. It was renamed Bulakhly in April 1946 and Kalinin Settlement in the early 1960s. In April 1991, the village was renamed Noramarg as part of a policy of Armenianization and the erasure of Azerbaijani heritage in Armenia.
Since 1995, the village has been part of the Ararat Province of the Republic of Armenia.
From the mid-18th century until the Russian conquest, the territory of the village formed part of the Zangibasar mahal of the Iravan Khanate.
Russia occupied the territory of the Iravan Khanate in 1827, and its incorporation into the Russian Empire was formalized by the 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay. During the Tsarist period, the village formed part of the Erivan Uyezd of the Erivan Governorate.
Historical population statistics
Between 1829 and 1832, an administrative census of the territories of the former Iravan and Nakhchivan khanates was conducted at the direction of the Russian authorities. According to the census, Abilkend had 85 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Tsarist-era statistical records, also cited in Armenian sources, indicate that at various times before 1914 the village was inhabited exclusively or predominantly by ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
According to the collection of Information about the Caucasus, in 1873, the village had 183 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis. Also, according to the Summary of Statistical Data on the Population of the Transcaucasian Krai, Extracted from the 1886 Family Lists, in 1886, the village had 222 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Z. Korkotyan, in his book "The Population of Soviet Armenia over the Last Hundred Years (1831–1931)," writes that in 1897, the village had 234 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Caucasian Calendar for 1909 says that in 1906, the village had 256 inhabitants, who were predominantly ancestors of the Azerbaijanis. Memorial Book of the Erivan Governorate for 1908 says that in 1908, the village had 256 inhabitants, all of whom were ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Caucasian Calendar for 1912 notes that in 1911, the village had 272 inhabitants, who were predominantly ancestors of the Azerbaijanis. Caucasian Calendar for 1915 says that in 1914, the village had 376 inhabitants, who were predominantly ancestors of the Azerbaijanis.
Events of 1918
On May 29, 1918, the government of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic (ADR) ceded Erivan, present-day Yerevan, and several surrounding territories to the Armenians. The First Republic of Armenia was thereby established on territory that had historically been inhabited by ancestors of present-day Azerbaijanis. Within the first few months of its existence, it began to make territorial claims against its neighbors: Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Türkiye (the Ottoman Empire at the time).
Between 1918 and 1920, Dashnaktsutyun, the nationalist party that held power in the Republic of Armenia, carried out ethnic cleansing of the Turkic population in the Erivan Governorate and in other areas, particularly in Zangezur, Karabakh, and Nakhchivan.
On October 20, 1919, the residents of Abilkend appealed to the government of the ADR in a letter in which they reported atrocities committed by the Dashnaks against the Muslim population and asked the government to take them under its protection and accept them as its subjects.
The consequences of the ethnic cleansing are reflected in the 1922 Soviet Armenian census, which recorded the village as destroyed.
Following the proclamation of Soviet rule in Armenia in late 1920, the communist regime fully consolidated its power over the country in 1921. The Azerbaijani population then began returning to the village.
During different periods, the village formed part of the Gamarli and Zangibasar districts (later the Artashat and Masis districts, respectively). During the Soviet period, the territories of the abolished Azerbaijani villages of Reyhanli, Seyidkend, and Gulujan were incorporated into Abilkend.
Azerbaijanis continued to live in Abilkend during the Soviet period as well.
Armenian sources indicate that Azerbaijanis inhabited the village until the late 1980s.
Z. Korkotyan, in his book "The Population of Soviet Armenia over the Last Hundred Years (1831–1931)," writes that in 1926, the village had 40 inhabitants, 36 of whom were Azerbaijanis.
In 1931, the village had 75 inhabitants, all of whom were Azerbaijanis.
Between 1948 and 1953, the Soviet authorities carried out the deportation of Azerbaijanis from the Armenian SSR to the Azerbaijan SSR. As a result, part of Abilkend's population was forcibly resettled to the territory of Azerbaijan.
A. P. Manvelyan and G. M. Martirosyan, in their book "Settlements and Population of the Armenian SSR over the Period 1831–1959," note that in 1959, the village had 413 inhabitants, who were predominantly Azerbaijanis.
T. Kh. Hakobyan, St. T. Melik-Bakhshyan and H. Kh. Barsegyan, in their "Dictionary of Toponymy of Armenia and Adjacent Territories," say that in 1970, the settlement had 741 inhabitants. In 1979, the settlement had 1690 inhabitants.
During the Soviet period, the organized resettlement of Armenians from abroad to Armenia took place. This is also confirmed by former residents of the village.
Sulduz Khalilov, who was born in Abilkend in 1965 and lived there until November 1988, recalls: "Armenians accounted for 38 percent of the population of Masis, and the rest were Azerbaijanis. At the time, we were told that the law required the secretary to be Azerbaijani. Later, Armenians from Lebanon and elsewhere were brought to Masis … in 1982–1983 so that they would make up the majority."
In the late 1980s, as a result of Armenian territorial claims to Karabakh and escalating tensions between the two republics, Azerbaijanis were permanently driven out of the territory of the Armenian SSR.
Sulduz Khalilov: "Thus, in 1988, we were all driven out… We were openly told to leave. During the last two months [September–October 1988], the village was subjected to nighttime raids. No one was specifically responsible for protecting us. The troops had either been disbanded, or something else had happened, but it went as far as armed raids."
Between 2021 and 2024, extensive fieldwork was conducted across the territory of Armenia, including in remote mountainous regions. The research was undertaken in preparation for the book The Perished Civilization and focused on identifying and documenting surviving Azerbaijani heritage sites. During the fieldwork, an Azerbaijani cemetery containing several dozen damaged tombstones was discovered in Abilkend.

title: Daughter of ‘pakcik air balang’ carries on her father’s legacy
content:
Ah Yauddin Ahmad died just a month ago, but his youngest daughter does not want the business that supported their family to simply end with him.
She hopes to continue the legacy of her father, better known as “pakcik air balang”, while preserving the recipes and way of doing business she learnt from him growing up.
“I still want to continue because I enjoy it. I want to keep the recipes and the way my father taught me,” the 22-year-old told FMT at her home in Pangsapuri Meru Ehsan here.
Ah Yauddin died on July 18 at age 64 after suffering a lung infection. He became widely known after a video showing him running his stall while caring for his wife at the night market went viral on social media.
Their story touched many hearts. His wife, Roslina Yusuf, had suffered complications from a stroke and diabetes that led to the amputation of her left leg. Yet Ah Yauddin continued to bring her along while he worked.
Roslina died last October after nearly five years of health problems. The couple had been married for almost 40 years.
Now, Nur Aliah is finding the strength to return to the business and expects to reopen her father’s drinks stall next month.
His trading spot at the Taman Datuk Bandar Meru night market has been retained, with payments to the local authority continuing so the business licence remains valid.
Still, Nur Aliah admits the transition will not be easy: her father had previously handled much of the practical side of the business.
“My father used to help with so much. Now I have to learn to do things on my own, including handling the supplies and transport,” she said.
To make this possible, she is working towards getting her driving licence before applying for one that will allow her to drive a van.
For now, she earns some money helping her aunt sell food at night markets around Meru three times a week. Although the income is irregular, she can occasionally earn around RM250 depending on sales.
She also attended courses in kuih-making and baking at GiatMara Klang after receiving an offer from Majlis Amanah Rakyat (Mara).
Even as she prepares to continue her father’s business, Nur Aliah has not given up on another dream: pursuing further studies in early childhood education. She had put her education on hold to care for her parents.
“I still want to continue studying – maybe not now because I still miss my father, but I plan to enter university next year,” she shared.
Looking back on life after losing both parents, Nur Aliah said she had once felt directionless because she had depended so much on her father.
But support from her aunt, her friends and other relatives has helped her find the strength to move forward.
Nur Aliah said she has not received any specific assistance following her father’s death, apart from zakat support that will continue until December.
She hopes to receive educational assistance if she resumes her studies, so she will be able to cover tuition fees and daily living expenses.

title: Baboon skin worn as cultural totem sparks uproar
content:
When Rhiba Kgawu draped himself in a baboon skin during a march in Bredasdorp in the Western Cape, he saw it as an expression of his cultural identity and connection to his clan totem. But the garment has now placed him at the centre of a dispute over culture, conservation and the laws governing the possession of wildlife products.
CapeNature told the Sunday Times this week that an inquiry docket was opened at Bredasdorp police station on Wednesday after complaints about the baboon skin worn by Kgawu, one of the leaders of the March and March movement.
CapeNature spokesperson Luke Folb said they were awaiting the transfer of the docket to the Swellendam endangered species and stock theft unit, which investigates environmental crimes.
Kgawu insists he has done nothing wrong and said he was unaware that complaints had been lodged against him.
“Don’t they know these skins are sold? My clan name is Mfene, so wearing baboon skin is part of my culture. Even at my place there is a baboon made of clay which sits on top of my roof,” he said.
We have Khoisan people who wear springbok skins; who threatens them with court? This is not about the baboon skin. It is their way of fighting the March and March movement. You can go to Bellville and you will find shops that sell animal skins
— Rhiba Kgawu
Kgawu said he bought the skin and had it sewn into a cloak.
“We have Khoisan people who wear springbok skins; who threatens them with court? This is not about the baboon skin. It is their way of fighting the March and March movement. You can go to Bellville and you will find shops that sell animal skins,” he said.
The Bredasdorp Animal Anti-Cruelty League (AACL) said it had received several complaints from members of the public on the morning of the march.
The organisation’s Tina du Plessis said complainants were concerned about how the baboon had died as well as whether the skin had been legally acquired and possessed.
“The public was primarily concerned about the circumstances surrounding the death of the animal, but also about the legality of the acquisition and ownership of a protected species skin by the wearer,” Du Plessis said.
She said the AACL’s mandate under the Animals Protection Act was primarily to prevent cruelty and establish whether the animal had suffered.
“This instance relates to cultural use of animal products, which does not automatically make the possession legal, as the owner would still need to comply with any laws surrounding the possession and use of a protected species skin,” she said.
Folb said legislation requires a person wanting to keep the carcass of a wild animal to obtain a possession permit. An applicant must provide proof of legal origin showing that the animal was acquired lawfully and that the necessary permits and authorisations were in place.
He said CapeNature’s 2026 annual hunting notice lists a daily bag limit of one chacma baboon (Papio ursinus) “outside the Cape Peninsula”. A permit is required.
“With an annual hunting licence and in line with the annual hunting notice and the Nature Conservation Ordinance, you may possess the carcass, skin, meat [or] trophy of an animal that you have legally hunted,” Folb said.
The investigation has reignited a broader debate about the cultural use of animal skins and how traditional practices intersect with conservation laws.
It is annoying that we have to account to elements of settler communities about the animals that we lived with, lived off, healed ourselves from and from which we acquired our totems and elements of our identity.
— Chief Jongisilo Pokwana ka Menziwa
Chief Jongisilo Pokwana ka Menziwa, a traditional leader, oral historian and researcher, said indigenous communities should not be made to feel that their cultural practices were inherently criminal.
“It is annoying that we have to account to elements of settler communities about the animals that we lived with, lived off, healed ourselves from and from which we acquired our totems and elements of our identity,” he said.
Pokwana argued that wearing animal skins had long formed part of traditional regalia and should be distinguished from the illegal killing of protected wildlife.
“There is no law that prevents the wearing of animal skins; otherwise, we would all be arrested. In all my traditional regalia, I wear my leopard skin. I have one that I wear on my head, one around my wrist and a full skin that I wear at traditional events,” he said.
However, he acknowledged that the origin of an animal skin could become a legal issue.
“If you are caught and there is sufficient evidence that you killed this protected animal, then you will have to prove where you got it,” he said.
Pokwana pointed to markets such as Kwa Mai Mai in Johannesburg and traders in Durban where various animal skins are sold, saying their availability demonstrated how widespread the cultural and commercial use of skins remained.
Gcobani Ndzongana, chief leader of the Land Party, said his party would provide Kgawu with legal representation should the CapeNature investigation result in criminal charges.
“We can’t sit around when people are made victims,” Ndzongana said.

title: Mario Delgado destaca avances clave y becas universales en la política educativa nacional
content:
Mario Delgado destaca avances clave y becas universales en la política educativa nacional
Subrayó que los proyectos desplegados en educación básica, media superior y superior consolidan el derecho constitucional a las aulas.
En el marco de la gira institucional "Honestidad y resultados", encabezada por la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo, el secretario de Educación Pública, Mario Delgado Carrillo, presentó una amplia evaluación de la política educativa nacional. El funcionario subrayó que los proyectos desplegados en Educación Básica, Media Superior y Superior consolidan el derecho constitucional a las aulas, con el objetivo firme de evitar la deserción escolar por limitaciones económicas.
Mario Delgado enfatizó que la Beca Universal de Educación Básica "Rita Cetina" se ha constituido como una pilar central de justicia social. La estrategia ejerció un presupuesto de 87 mil 393 millones de pesos, beneficiando directamente a 15 millones de alumnas y alumnos de niveles inicial, preescolar, primaria y secundaria, con una cobertura que alcanzó a 11.1 millones de familias en el territorio nacional.
En materia de infraestructura escolar, el titular de la SEP resaltó las aportaciones directas otorgadas a través del programa "La Escuela es Nuestra". Tan sólo en el primer semestre de 2026, la iniciativa canalizó 18 mil 406.1 millones de pesos a 65 mil 745 comunidades de educación básica. Paralelamente, en el nivel medio superior se asignaron 4 mil 288.8 millones de pesos para beneficiar a 5 mil 737 planteles.
El funcionario federal puso especial énfasis en la revalorización del magisterio. Delgado Carrillo informó que más de 23 mil docentes de educación básica accedieron al programa de promoción horizontal durante el ciclo 2025-2026, obteniendo incentivos salariales directos. Asimismo, detalló que el gobierno avanza hacia la edificación de un nuevo sistema transparente de admisión, promoción y cambios de adscripción que sustituirá de manera definitiva a la Usicamm, erradicando prácticas de corrupción.
Respecto a la expansión de la matrícula pública en Educación Superior, el secretario anunció la apertura de 13 nuevas sedes de la Universidad Nacional Rosario Castellanos con capacidad para 119 mil 280 estudiantes, así como el crecimiento de las Universidades para el Bienestar Benito Juárez García, que alcanzarán 239 sedes. Estos esfuerzos permitirán integrar a cerca de un cuarto de millón de jóvenes que anteriormente no encontraban opciones en el sistema universitario público.
Finalmente, el titular de la Secretaría de Educación Pública abordó las políticas de salud integral en el entorno escolar. Destacó el impacto del programa "Vive saludable, vive feliz", mediante el cual se evaluó el estado físico, bucal y visual de 10.9 millones de estudiantes de primaria, logrando además erradicar la venta de comida chatarra en más del 86 por ciento de las escuelas públicas.
En el ámbito normativo, Delgado reveló que 17 entidades federativas ya han promulgado leyes para regular el uso de dispositivos móviles y teléfonos inteligentes dentro de las aulas de clase.

title: A Queen Ruled Warangal As A King. Centuries Later, Her Kakatiya Legacy Lives On In Telangana’s Flower Festival
content: Every year, as the monsoon retreats from Telangana's parched plains, women wake before sunrise to gather wildflowers that bloom nowhere else in quite the same way, stacking them into towers shaped like temple gopurams. The ritual is called Bathukamma, and while it now draws crowds from Los Angeles to London, its earliest echoes lead back roughly 800 years, to the fort city of Warangal and a queen who governed disguised as a king. A queen's devotion becomes a kingdom's memory The Kakatiya dynasty ruled large parts of present-day Telangana through the 12th and 13th centuries, with their capital at Orugallu, known today as Warangal. Their reign left behind some of the Deccan's finest architecture, including the Thousand Pillar Temple, built in 1163 under King Rudradeva, and the Ramappa Temple, completed in 1213 and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It was Rudradeva's descendant, Rani Rudramadevi, who became part of one of the enduring stories associated with Bathukamma. Ganapatideva, her father, had no son, so he formally designated her as his male heir through the putrika ceremony and gave her the name Rudradeva. She took the throne around 1262, ruled in male attire, put down rebellions from nobles who resisted a woman's authority, and strengthened the Warangal Fort her father had begun. Historical tradition credits her with promoting the worship of Kakatamma, a regional mother goddess, particularly around Mogilicharla, where grand processions were held on Durga Ashtami, complete with music, dance, and the ceremonial immersion of the deity in nearby water. Wildflowers including tangedu and gunuka form the vibrant base of Telangana's annual Bathukamma celebrations. Photograph: (The Hindu) That closing ritual has often been cited as one thread in the long history of Bathukamma: flowers offered to water and a prayer for their return the following year echo the symbolism of what is now Saddula Bathukamma, the grand finale of the nine-day festival. But Rudramadevi's story is not an uncontested founding account of Bathukamma. Historians and scholars have also traced the festival to older local agricultural, seasonal and feminine fertility traditions, some of which may predate the Kakatiyas. The Kakatiya-Rudramadevi connection is therefore one of the historical memories woven into the festival's story, rather than a definitive origin. Historians admit the precise origin remains genuinely contested, but the Kakatiya connection is the version sung most often in Bathukamma's own folk songs. It is this layered history that leads many in Telangana to call Warangal the symbolic birthplace of Bathukamma, even as other folk traditions, including stories involving a Chola king's daughter and goddess Parvati, circulate alongside it. Flowers that follow the rains Whatever its exact origin, Bathukamma is unmistakably a festival of the land. It begins on ‘Mahalaya Amavasya’ and runs for nine days until Durga Ashtami, tracking the seasonal shift from Varsha Ruthu, the monsoon, to Sharad Ruthu, autumn. Bathukamma's flower towers are traditionally built in concentric layers, often resembling the shape of a temple gopuram. Photograph: (The Hindu) As the rains recede, wild and largely medicinal flowers bloom across Telangana's uncultivated plains, chiefly gunuka and tangedu, alongside banti and chamanti. Men and boys gather these blooms each morning, and women arrange them into seven concentric layers resembling a temple gopuram, crowned with a small turmeric idol called Gauramma. Each of the nine days carries its own food offering, from sesame and rice on the first day to a rich, sweetened rice preparation on the last, and every evening the flower stack is carried in procession, sung to in call-and-response folk verses, and finally immersed in a pond or lake. This closing act depends entirely on Telangana's older water culture: the region's dense network of tanks and lakes was originally built to trap monsoon runoff for farming, a legacy so tied to local memory that a lake in Hyderabad's Amberpet still carries the festival's name. Many of these water bodies, strained by decades of urban growth, are now being nursed back to life by community-led efforts that echo the same ecological instinct Bathukamma has carried for centuries: give back to the water what it once gave you. From village courtyards to a state's identity When Telangana became India's 29th state in 2014, its government declared Bathukamma, alongside Bonalu, an official state festival on 26 June, 2014. Since then, the state has funded free sarees and large public celebrations, and Bathukamma has grown into an emblem of Telangana identity celebrated well beyond its borders, among diaspora communities in Dubai, Qatar, the United Kingdom, the United States and Australia. That instinct to keep an old practice alive through new hands runs through much of Telangana's culture. In Cheriyal, a handful of Nakashi artist families still hand-paint the scroll paintings that once accompanied travelling storytellers narrating exactly the kind of oral folklore Bathukamma's songs preserve. From village courtyards to celebrations around the world, Bathukamma has become a vibrant symbol of Telangana's cultural identity. Photograph: (Dakshinapatha) Around Pochampally, weavers whose craft was transformed by the Laxmi Asu Machine, invented by a school dropout to spare his mother's aching joints, show how tradition survives by adapting rather than standing still. And as concerns grow nationally over flowers dumped into rivers after festivals, entrepreneurs elsewhere are already turning discarded blooms into incense and dye rather than letting them pollute the water, a shift Bathukamma's own communities are beginning to consider for their post-immersion flowers too. This year, Bathukamma runs from 11 October to 18 October. As it has for generations, the festival will unfold as women's private history made public: songs never written down, carried instead from mother to daughter, filling Telangana's streets, courtyards and lakesides with colour that, if the Kakatiya-era memory holds, has been blooming there for the better part of a millennium. Sources 'Historical traditions link Bathukamma to Kakatiya-era worship of goddess Kakatamma at Mogilicharla': Orugallu Andhalu, Published 18 March, 2026 'About Bathukamma': Government of Telangana, Official Bathukamma portal 'How Bonalu festival has become an empowering space for trans women in Telangana’: Written by Jagadish Babu for The News Minute, on Bonalu and Bathukamma being awarded state festival status on 26 June, 2014

title: 13 Contestants of the 2026 Hiri Hanenamo are preparing for the official crowning
content:
As the Boge-Bada reached the shores of Era Kone(Ela Beach), the voices of the Hiri Hanenamos shouting the famous ‘Hedi-horo Boge-bada’ echoed along the shoreline of Era Kone.
The 13 contestants are participating in the Hiri Hanenamo Quest, which is the prestigious cultural pageant held during the annual Hiri Moale Festival in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The 13 contestants, after their official registration had participated in different judging categories, lead-up events and community engagement within their communities, have now reached the peak of the quest, which is the crowning, that will be staged tomorrow, September 13, 2026, at the Sir Herbert Murray Stadium after the last sway (Koea).
Unlike a conventional pageant, the Hiri Hanenamo focuses rigorously on cultural literacy, community leadership, and the preservation of the historic Hiri trade legacy.
These exemplary young women have been formally nominated by their respective local leaders to serve as cultural ambassadors, representing the identity, oral history, and traditional values of their respective Motu and Koitabu villages.
The annual event is organised by the Motu Koita Assembly, in collaboration with the National Capital District Commission and the Hiri Moale Festival Committee.
