title: The Prime Minister’s Literary Award winners include a collective Yolŋu novel – and a murder trial
content:
This year’s winners of the Prime Minister’s Literary Awards query the instability of Australian identity. And the winners of the fiction and nonfiction prizes both point to the cruel legacy of European invasion and colonialism.
A brave and moving historical Yolŋu novel, A Piece of Red Cloth, has won the fiction prize. It was collectively authored by Yolŋu knowledge holders Merrkiyawuy Ganambar-Stubbs, Djawa Burarrwanga and Djawundil Maymuru, and novelist Leonie Norrington.
A pioneering collaboration between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal writers that honours Yolŋu ancestors through the eyes of their descendants, it represents a healing opportunity for Australian culture. As Norrington says, “Aboriginal people, since the first invaders came, have been trying to say, ‘Look, we have a really wonderful way of understanding the world, and you can learn from it.’”
Described by the judges as “a profound work of remembrance, fusing oral history, novelistic technique and deep cultural knowledge”, this innovative book also received this year’s Australian Book Industry Award for Social Impact Book of the Year. It has been shortlisted for multiple prizes.
The nonfiction prize winner, Walkley Award-winning journalist Kate Wild’s The Red House, is a gripping exposé of race and power within contemporary Australia – explored through the tragic killing of Kumanjayi Walker in 2019, and the subsequent murder trial of Constable Zachary Rolfe. It’s also no stranger to literary prizes, having won this year’s Age Non-fiction Book of the Year.
Play, emotion and imagination
Turkish–Australian Ender Başkan’s playful and expansive Two Hundred Million Musketeers has won the poetry prize. Rohan Howitt’s consideration of Australia’s claims to the Antarctic, The Southern Frontier, was awarded the Australian history prize.
Both prizes for younger readers went to verse novels. Drift by Pip Harry, which follows two 14-year-olds as they navigate fitting in and deal with anxiety (and bees), won for young adult literature. And Song of a Thousand Seas by Zana Fraillon, which looks at friendship and different brains through the eyes of an octopus, won for children’s literature.
These are stories about kin, culture and belonging, migration, settlement and territorial rights. They pick at the loose threads of psychological and physical definitions of what it means to be Australian. Their fresh perspectives explore and interrogate ideas of home and nationhood, ownership and entitlement – with imagination, rigour and heartfelt emotion.
The awards, delivered by Creative Australia, boast the biggest prize pool in the country. The winners of each category receive A$80,000, with A$5,000 each for shortlisted writers.
‘True history’ as fiction
A Piece of Red Cloth, set in the 1600s, tells the story of Batjani, a Yolŋu elder trying to protect her beloved granddaughter, Garritji, from Makassan trepang fishermen on the coast of Arnhem Land. The story opens up a complex and unfamiliar chapter of pre-colonial Australian history.
For hundreds of years, trading between Yolŋu and seafarers from the port of Makassar, now eastern Indonesia, took place without issue. But when European merchants claimed the region as the Dutch East Indies, a new chapter of brutality was introduced.
The Makassan traders adopted the cruel tactics of their colonisers, and began plying Yolŋu men with opium and alcohol. In exchange, they claimed the young women and children, and took them for sex-trafficking, until the the elder Yolŋu women rose up in protest.
The novel reimagines these facts as Batjani does her best to protect Garritji, who is approaching womanhood, from the fishermen. “It’s a true history,” says Ganambarr-Stubbs, whose own grandmother was snatched in a similar scenario. “Wider Australia should learn more about the history – all the histories – because that’s how all of us came to be here now.”
Nonfiction: ongoing race inequity
The Red House highlights the ongoing inequities of race in Australia. In her investigation of the legacy of Australia’s colonial past, journalist Kate Wild seeks ways to break the cycle of dehumanisation and state violence that continues to plague this country.
With precision and care, she recounts the confrontation between Walker and Rolfe in an isolated desert community, and tracks the aftermath of Rolfe’s high-profile, emotionally charged court case. Her report reveals the depth of Australia’s damaged and unresolved relationship with its First Nations peoples.
An outsider, she nevertheless finds ways to integrate Warlpiri and Luritj perspectives with care and respect, laying down a challenge to those involved in the work of communicating First Nations stories.
Her book was praised by the judges as a work “of great listening” that “embeds the reader in a supratemporal zone beyond Western ideas of time, history and narrative in order to trace repeating patterns of violence, rhetoric, pain and anger”. It represents a nuanced, compassionate contribution to a critical ongoing national conversation about race, culture, history and entitlement.
A story of transgenerational trauma, difficult questions and unfinished business, Wild’s work takes on issues that many Australians still prefer to avoid or deny. It presses for an end to a situation that appears to have no resolution.
Poetry: fatherhood in an uncertain world
With his debut poetry collection, Two Hundred Million Musketeers, Ender Başkan captures the intensity of parenting young children within an increasingly uncertain world.
Fatherhood impacts his work, friendships and creative practice in inner-city Melbourne. It alters his awareness of social and political concerns, and shifts his attention from the past and the present into the future.
Dealing in connection and bustling with life, Başkan’s poems reflect on his childhood, his grandparents’ exile from Türkiye (where Başkan returns, with his young family), and on being Turkish. He explores his responsibilities to child-rearing and housekeeping, the need to earn a living and to care for older generations.
Başkan has been critically hailed as a writer whose “main point is that poetry can and should be fun”. He won the 2021 Overland Judith Wright Poetry Prize, and the 2025 Anne Elder Award.
His work continues the legacy of migrant poets that included his close friend and mentor, the late Ania Walwicz. According to the judges, Başkan offers “an invitation to explore what might be possible if a line were to stretch between one person and another”.

title: Redfern Reckoning: Lily Shearer on Subverting the Colonial Gaze for the Stage
content: Redfern Reckoning: Lily Shearer on Subverting the Colonial Gaze for the Stage Country Australia agnes Thu, 09/10/2026 - 09:27 Issues Languages and Cultures Program 5 Main Image By Cristina Verán The word Moogahlin, in the Yuin and Bundjalung languages, means “to play” or “to fool around”. This spirited term—and the living philosophy behind it—expands through the work of the renowned Moogahlin Performing Arts, one of the most vital and culturally grounding forces in contemporary Australian performance today. Indigenous theater veterans Lily Shearer (Murrawarri/Ngemba), Fred Copperwaite (Bunuba), and Dr. Liza-Mare Syron (Biripi) co-founded the company in the deeply entrenched Aboriginal community of Sydney’s Redfern district, deliberately rejecting the standard western structures and strictures of theater to instead honor millennia of First Nations storytelling. Over the past decade and a half, Moogahlin has evolved from a grassroots, artist-run setup into a major force on the international stage; one that maintains a deep commitment to the community from which it sprang. Through landmark productions like Jane Harrison’s “The Visitors”—a touring work that inverts the colonial gaze to depict the arrival of the British First Fleet through the eyes of the land’s Original Peoples—and flagship platforms like the Yellamundie Festival, the company continuously champions independent First Nations creators and reclaims historical narratives. Beyond decolonizing performance spaces and redefining what theater can be, Moogahlin broadens its mission to include environmental and cultural advocacy through its biennial Baiame's Ngunnhu Festival, held alongside the ancient Brewarrina Fish Traps. Cristina Verán spoke with Moogahlin Performing Arts Co-founder and Artistic Director Lily Shearer about the political and social histories that shape their work, and how Indigenous storytelling remains essential to the larger projects of community healing and cultural survival. Lily Shearer and Natano Fa'anana (Samoan), Moogahlin's Executive Producer, en route to pitch a new play at the 2025 ISPA Conference (International Society for the Performing Arts) in New York. Cristina Verán: Tell us a bit about the beginnings of Moogahlin Performing Arts and the community it calls home. Lily Shearer: We, the company’s co-founders, started talking about forming something like this back in November 2007, following the passing of Uncle Kevin Smith (Walbung-Murramarang), a deeply respected actor and Aboriginal activist from Redfern, in Sydney. He’d been trying to establish a local Indigenous theater company, and his family asked if we’d pick up the baton and build something proper and lasting for the community. We officially incorporated on May 19, 2009. CV: While it’s become known for performances that can be defined as “theater,” Moogahlin doesn’t refer to itself as a "theater company,” as such. Why is that? LS: That was dead intentional. Western concepts of theater want to put artists in this box, requiring script-bound works and proscenium arches, whereas our mob has been telling stories for tens of thousands of years, across interconnected forms that combine dance, music, visual art, oral yaans, and songlines. Written scripts, in the Western sense, are a form First Peoples here have only really been using for about 50 years. Naming ourselves Moogahlin Performing Arts meant no one could lock us into a single Western performance genre, leaving us free to tell stories our way. CV: What was it like during those early years in terms of size, scale, resources, and before Moogahlin had a permanent home? LS: We started out as a grassroots, purely artist-run setup, working on a project-by-project basis. Each of us, the founders, kept outside jobs to pay the bills and keep roofs over our heads. For years, our office consisted of a single black filing cabinet that held all our documentation, dragged from place to place, wherever I was working. Though we lacked a fixed venue, we had strong relationships with the local Redfern community. CV: What makes Redfern so significant, symbolically and historically? LS: It’s universally recognized as the "Blak Capital" of Australia as well as the geographic and political beating heart of the modern First Peoples movement—where everything from the Aboriginal Legal Services to Koori Radio to the original National Black Theatre were born. Back in the late 1960s and ‘70s, our Indigenous civil rights activists here were exchanging ideas directly with members of the Black Panther movement in the United States. The central block of the neighborhood—known simply as "The Block"—is Aboriginal-owned land handed over under the Gough Whitlam-led federal government in 1972 after community members squatted in tents, right there on country, to demand land rights. This history also ties directly to the closing down of state and church-run missions from the late 1930s to the late 1960s. [Note: In Australia, the terms Blak and Blakfullas are used to refer to Indigenous Australians, not to people of African descent.] CV: What were the social dynamics like at the time, in terms of where people came from and what they were facing? LS: Those missions I noted were run like reservations, or residential schools, with the aim of total control, strict assimilation, and the cultural erasure of our People. When they eventually shut down, generations of displaced mob—many of whom had been stripped from their families under the country’s shameful Stolen Generation policies—had nowhere to go. They started coming to Redfern and setting up camp on The Block because nearby factories offered manual-labor jobs to people who’d been trained on the missions. Sadly, by the early 2000s, the accumulation of intergenerational trauma, poverty, and forced displacement led to serious issues for many residents with drug misuse, domestic violence, alcoholism, and crime. It also became a highly policed neighborhood. CV: Did these folks come primarily from Indigenous communities around Sydney, or from further afield as well? LS: Our people came from all over the nation after the missions were closed. First Peoples from as far as the Northern Territory were taken to Milleewas Half-caste home, Mulgoa NSW, in Western Sydney. Our people on the Mission in my hometown of Brewarrina came from QLD, VIC, and communities close by, but it was a handful of those communities all mixed up on the Mission, so they didn’t speak the same language and have the same ceremonies, they didn’t even have the same diets. When the missions closed, they came to Redfern looking for work, as they were trained as domestic servants and/or laborers. However, most importantly, they came in search of their families, to find out where they belonged. I was involved in a door-to-door survey taken in Western Sydney during the 1990s. There were mobs representing 63 different First Nations tribes and/or language groups living in the Blacktown LGA. Most of our people living in Western Sydney were relocated from Redfern as they were redeveloping The Block. CV: What were you engaged in at that time, and how did it relate to the movements you’ve mentioned? LS: Between 2005 and 2007, while working in Redfern for a mainstream company, Performance Space, I got involved at the Redfern Community Centre (RCC), and I helped launch “Gathering Ground,” a Community Cultural Development project, alongside Pact Youth Theatre. I then became the Cultural Development Officer at RCC, and Frederick Copperwaite stepped in to direct “Gathering Ground” (2008, 2010), while I acted as cultural advisor, to ensure 100% Indigenous creative leadership. Our focus was telling authentic stories through our own lens, as well as using that storytelling to process intergenerational trauma—which we did while also bringing in over 3,000 audience members a night. CV: How did urban development pressures in Sydney begin to impact this community? LS: Gentrification was forced upon it by the state government’s Redfern Waterloo Authority. Homes on The Block were knocked down, and families who’d lived there were forcibly relocated, again. The Aboriginal Housing Company was staunch in holding onto The Block, and began fundraising and working with University of Sydney design students to reimagine its future. CV: The advent of new arts spaces, and arts programming in general, seems to too-often herald and further encourage more gentrification, serving its newly anointed beneficiaries rather than the People already living there in community. How has that played out in Redfern? LS: Well, when Carriageworks Performing Arts Centre opened down the road in 2007, community mistrust around it was huge. People reckoned it’d be yet another elitist venue—like, for example, the Sydney Opera House—that would basically lock locals out. It took years of deliberate, unrushed relationship-building to bridge the Centre’s divide between itself and the local Aboriginal community, ensuring the People would be empowered to tell their own stories through its space and resources. CV: How did Moogahlin transition into a fully funded resident company there? LS: The major shift came in 2014 when the CEO of Carriageworks formally invited us to apply for residency, despite our lack of capital at the time. This provided our first actual office space, and partnering with them on grant applications gave us the organizational weight needed for multi-year operational funding. We secured our first four-year grant from the Australia Council for the Arts (now Creative Australia) for 2017–2021, and are currently in our third consecutive cycle with them, through 2028, matched by multi-year operational funding from Arts New South Wales (now Create NSW) since 2021. That baseline financial stability allowed us to stop surviving hand-to-mouth on project grants and actually engage in long-term strategic planning. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: Now let’s get to “The Visitors,” which has been touring across Australia and internationally in the past couple of years—including here at New York’s prestigious Perelman Arts Center (PACNYC). Tell us how this work came to Moogahlin and what its mission has become now that it is part of it. LS: It was written by playwright Jane Harrison (Muruwari), the author of Stolen, who had pitched the script originally under the title “First Contact” at Moogahlin’s National flagship platform, Yellamundie Festival, in our inaugural year (2013). Following seven years of dramaturgical development and community consultation around it, to ensure authenticity, it premiered at Carriageworks (directed by Fred Copperwaite and produced by Liza-Mare Syron) during the 2020 Sydney Festival. In 2023, “The Visitors” was re-staged under the directorship, Wesley Enoch (Quandamooka) and in partnership with Sydney Theatre Company, premiering at Sydney Opera House as part of their 50th Anniversary program. The play employs a kind of symbolic inversion of all the histories Australians are taught in school that are, in fact, contrary to our own Indigenous stories. Those British colonizers who recorded meticulous entries in their logs about us had operated under the assumption that First Peoples would never read them. But Jane went and found these documents, including many wherein British officers described Aboriginal People as, for example, "brutes" with "narrow heads, stocky bodies, short limbs, fish-like lips, and protruding eyes." Non-Indigenous audiences are often shocked to learn that some offensive language used in the play is, in fact, quoted verbatim from the official British records. She wanted to invert that colonial gaze. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: What should we know about the historical event around which the story is centered? LS: Set in 1788, “The Visitors” depicts six senior [Aboriginal] Law Men & Women, and one new initiate, from surrounding clans, convening in council at what is now known as Sydney Cove to discuss what they saw making its way toward them on the horizon: the British fleet. They begin to debate, per their own diplomatic protocols, whether to welcome, ignore, or resist the newcomers. Events in the play [such as a public hanging witnessed offshore] are drawn directly from colonial logs now reinterpreted through an Indigenous lens. CV: How has Moogahlin managed to design and adapt the staging for “The Visitors,” thus enabling the play to travel beyond major mainstage theaters and work well in different and smaller spaces? LS: We created three distinct production models. Version A is our mainstage configuration, built for major venues like the Sydney Opera House or the Public Theater in New York, and featuring a massive sandstone set piece we’ve nicknamed “Bertha.” Version B is a much more compact, flexible touring setup for use in regional theaters across Australia. And Version C, still being developed, will be further stripped back, ideal for performances on missions, reservations, and in community halls. It requires just the seven actors in business suits around a boardroom table, under basic lighting. When we were in New York earlier this year, to perform this at the Perelman Arts Center (PACNYC) in Manhattan, the cast even considered taking this version to a rock in Central Park to perform it right there. Scene from "The Visitors" at the Perelman Arts Center in New York City. Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: How have Indigenous Australian audiences been responding to it? LS: Mainstage venues often feel alienating to our mob, due to historical barriers we’ve experienced from such spaces. But during our 2024 national tour, regional venues reported record attendance for local First Nations community members—some venues, in fact, saying it brought out the most Blackfullas they’d ever hosted! They come to “The Visitors” because we’ve built real relationships with local communities, presenting a powerful narrative that had never been presented on stage through an Indigenous lens before. CV: I understand that some conversations that came out of the 2010 National Indigenous Theatre Forum led to the launch of your flagship platform, Yellamundie Festival. LS: Between 2008 and 2010, Wesley Enoch (Quandamooka), now chairperson of Creative Australia, had been in discussions with federal Arts Minister Peter Garrett about allocating $2 million toward a new National Black Theatre for Australia. We argued that funds should go directly to artists, script development, and commissions—not more “bricks and mortar.” In response, Wesley and Lea-Anne Buckskin (Narungga, Kaurna, Wirangu, and Wotjobaluk) convened the inaugural National Indigenous Theatre Forum you mentioned, in Cairns, so that First Nations practitioners from across the country could gather to map out sector priorities. When the number one of these policies was identified by a vote: reviving the National Aboriginal Playwrights Conference (which had been defunct for 17 years due to both drops in funding and a generational gap in the sector), Wesley looked out at all the attendees and asked: “Who will take on the responsibility?” The room went dead silent, because no company had either spare cash or extra staff to offer. Liza-Mare Syron and I looked at each other, though, and thought, “OK, we will!”—and thus committed Moogahlin to leading it (despite having bugger-all in our bank account). Creative Australia then backed us with $50,000 in seed funding and paired us with producer Wendy Blacklock at Performing Lines to help build and strengthen our own producing capacity. Moogahlin Performing Arts co-founders Dr. Liza-Mare Syron, Frederick Copperwhite, and Lily Shearer. CV: How did that commitment lead to producing festivals as part of its work of decolonizing performance spaces, and how has Moogahlin’s vision evolved over time? LS: We launched Yellamundie Festival—from the Dharug word for "storyteller"—in 2013, as a biennial national showcase dedicated exclusively to independent First Nations artists (We do not accept proposals for this from established companies). From the 50 to 60 applications we receive from around the country each time, we select six works for intensive workshop development, and showcase the works to the public and sector over 3 nights and 2 days. Under Fred Copperwaite’s direction from 2013 to 2019, the festival focused on script-based plays. When I became Artistic Director in 2020, I expanded the format to include two play scripts, two dance/movement works, and two music/composition pieces, returning us to traditional storytelling methods that treated movement and composition as equal to texts. Across its seven editions so far, Yellamundie Festival has developed 51 original works—21 of which have gone on to full mainstage productions with major companies nationwide. Moogahlin itself also commits to fully producing at least one work from each cohort. CV: Please describe what the broader landscape of Indigenous theater in Australia, especially Indigenous-led theater companies, looks like today, and what particular challenges are still being faced. LS: The sector remains relatively tiny, with just three dedicated Black companies nationwide: Ilbijerri Theatre Company in Melbourne, Yirra Yaakin Theatre Company in Perth, and Moogahlin in Sydney (a fourth company, Kooemba Jdarra in Brisbane, closed around 2008 due to funding and operational pressures). We do have several specialized dance and physical theater organizations to add to the list, including Bangarra Dance Theatre, Marrugeku, and BlakDance. Recognizing also our only national First Peoples-led training institution, the National Aboriginal & Islander Skills Development Association (NAISDA) Dance College. As to the challenges, we as First Peoples entities have to respond to demands that mainstream organizations rarely face, with our teams constantly balancing creative development with support for community needs—including the ongoing work of reconnecting families split by the country’s Stolen Generations policies. We’re also navigating the dynamics around what’s being called a “lost generation”: people who’d previously hidden their Indigenous identity due to systemic racism and discrimination, but now, without having grown up in community, proudly claim this heritage. Cast and crew of "The Visitors." Photo by Maria Baranova. CV: How did the familial and perhaps generational experiences of yourself and your Moogahlin counterparts shape your respective interests in and commitment to reclaiming historical narratives? LS: My generation grew up under Australia’s assimilation policies. First Peoples here were not granted full voting rights until 1967, and our equal access to education was only mandated around 1972. I remember well that, as a student in the mid-1970s, in a Catholic secondary school run by Good Samaritan nuns, we were taught that Captain Cook "discovered" Australia (and therefore us). I dared to challenge my history teacher on this point, insisting that, according to my father and grandfather, that man didn't discover us—our people discovered him when he arrived on our shores. For this, the teacher called me a "brazen toad" and threw me out of her class—permanently. My co-founders, who are also Indigenous, had quite different upbringings. Meanwhile, Liza-Mare Syron grew up away from community in the Sydney suburb of Balmain, while Fred Copperwaite grew up on the other side of the country in Fremantle, near Perth, with his white father’s family. It was at age 30 that he was finally able to connect with his (maternal side) Aboriginal family. CV: Moogahlin now also produces another festival, which connects culturally centered storytelling with environmental advocacy. Tell us about this, especially the significance of the place for its setting. LS: Baiame Ngunnhu Festival, established in 2015, uses performance and community gathering to fight for environmental justice. It takes place along the Ba-Wun (Barwon) River in my home community of Brewarrina (in New South Wales). The site features our traditional Fish Traps—called Ngunnhu—which comprise an ancient stone-pen system and represent the oldest human-made structures on Earth, predating the Egyptian Pyramids and Stonehenge. Despite its immense historical significance, unfortunately, the Australian government provides bugger-all protection or funding compared to those places it sees as global heritage sites. CV: And for the record, what are the most pressing issues for this community right now? LS: The river system has been severely degraded by imported cattle breaking down its banks, invasive European carp displacing native fish, and introduced weeds choking the water channels. Most damaging of all are commercial cotton farms—many owned by foreign corporate interests in America and China—that extract massive volumes of water from our river network, on the driest inhabited continent on Earth. The core message at Baiame’s Ngunnhu Festival is straightforward: if the natural country provided by the Creator is unhealthy, the people who rely on that land cannot be healthy either. Thus, we are able to link our cultural survival directly to environmental survival and, ultimately, to the survival of all our First Nations Peoples. --Cristina Verán is an international Indigenous Peoples-focused researcher, educator, advocacy strategist, network weaver, curator, and mediamaker. She was a founding member of the United Nations Indigenous Media Network and the UN Indigenous Language Caucus. As Adjunct Faculty at New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts and Affiliate Faculty of the NYU Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, she brings emphasis to the global histories, expressions, and socio-political impacts of Indigenous contemporary visual and performing arts, design, tech, media, and popular culture(s). Cast members featured in these images from "The Visitors" America Season, at PAC NYC in New York, include: Najwa Adams-Ebel, Beau Dean, Riley Smith, Sean Dow, Kyle Morrison, Guy Simons, James Slee, and Zoe Walters. (Additional members feature in the Australian and New Zealand Season productions.)

title: I had to move to Rūātoki to learn te reo Māori. Our tamariki shouldn’t have to
content: Growing up unable to understand her own whānau, Rawinia Higgins went home to Rūātoki and discovered a place where te reo Māori wasn’t simply taught – it was the language of everyday life. Thinking about te reo towns, the theme for Te Wiki o te Reo Māori 2026, my mind goes to Rūātoki – a small town just south of Whakatāne where I learnt to speak Māori. I grew up in an English-speaking home in Wellington. When my native reo Māori-speaking mother and family would get together, they would all be speaking Māori, laughing and sharing stories. I would feel left out because I couldn’t understand and take part in what was being said. When I was around 11 years old, I asked my parents if I could move to Rūātoki – where my mum was from – and attend Rūātoki School. The school was the first officially recognised bilingual school, back in 1978, and was well established by the time I got there in 1985. It was the result of a community where te reo Māori was the norm, staffed by Tūhoe relatives of mine including Koro Whitu McGarvey – who was my teacher – and Tāwhiri and Kaa Williams, among others. It was in this small-town community I learnt te reo Māori – where I was finally able to access the richness of the world that I had been missing. A baptism of fire I won’t romanticise it – learning the language was a baptism by fire. I started out, much to the teasing of my cousins, in the remedial class. I had known of remedial classes at my school in Wellington, but that was for English. At Rūātoki though, the remedial class was for te reo Māori. I still chuckle thinking about it today – it was like living in a parallel universe. What was special about Rūātoki was that it was not only a place where te reo Māori was taught, but also lived in the hearts and homes of the locals every day. That’s the idea behind the te reo towns theme for te wiki this year: to pay homage to those communities who helped create the conditions where te reo Māori could continue to be spoken, learned and lived. They built kōhanga and kura, strengthened whānau and community use of the language, and helped ensure future generations would have access to te reo Māori as a normal part of everyday life. March during Māori Language Week, to demand that the Māori language have equal status with English on August 1, 1980, Wellington. (Photo: Alexander Turnbull Library) It wasn’t consciously political for them and yet it was one of the most politically active decisions they could make. It was about ensuring their children would never have to feel the detachment from culture and community the adults had seen among Māori living in cities. It was about making te reo Māori a normal and natural part of life for younger generations. More than a matter of ‘choice’ It’s important not to simplify this story too much. Rūātoki and other similar communities showed remarkable commitment to te reo Māori, but they were also shaped by circumstance. Around the world, indigenous languages have often remained strongest in communities where people had greater opportunity to live, work and socialise in their own language. Larger towns and cities brought different pressures, with English becoming the dominant language of education, employment, media and public life. This was not a matter of some communities valuing their language more than others or willingly giving it up. Given the choice, most indigenous communities would have wanted to see their language flourish from one generation to the next. The differing fortunes of te reo Māori reflects the uneven impacts of colonisation, urbanisation and social change on people’s ability to use and pass on the language. The lesson is not to romanticise isolation, but to understand the conditions that allow a language to thrive and to recreate those conditions wherever Māori live today. Te reo Māori has come a long way since I went to kura in Rūātoki. It’s now on bilingual signage, in official place names, on our screens, in cafés and restaurants, sports commentary, workplaces and across the public life of this country. Statistics support this, with the 2023 Census recording 213,849 people who could hold an everyday conversation in te reo Māori, up from 185,955 in 2018. That is an increase of 27,894 speakers in five years, and something every New Zealander can take heart in. This growth in visibility is worth celebrating. But visibility is not the same as vitality. A language doesn’t just thrive because it appears on signs, screens or posters. It thrives when people have places to use it, people to use it with, and the words they need for everyday life. Rūātoki, Ōtaki, Matawaia and other te reo towns have always understood this. Te reo Māori grows through whanaungatanga, shared purpose, and communities that make the language normal in the ordinary places where life happens. The gift that Rūātoki gave me Rūātoki didn’t give me just lessons, but a living network of language. The kura mattered deeply, but it was part of something bigger: whānau who spoke, kaumātua who carried the dialect, teachers who believed in the kaupapa, homes where Māori was ordinary, and a community that had decided its children would inherit more than a memory of te reo Māori. There are many te reo towns across the motu, each with their own story, dialect, champions and sacrifices. Rūātoki is just one of them. Ngā Tamatoa and supporters protest at St Kevin’s Arcade, Auckland, 1972 (Photo: John Miller) Te reo towns are not an invention; they are a recognition of communities that have already shown the way. They represent the courage, discipline and love of communities that chose, and had the circumstances, geographical or otherwise, to keep te reo Māori alive in homes, schools, marae and public life. Before there were national strategies and policies, there were communities already doing the quiet, determined work of language revitalisation. They built kōhanga and kura, held hui, corrected and encouraged each other, laughed with each other and kept speaking. They made decisions in kitchens, staffrooms, vans, sports clubs and on marae that would later become a part of a national movement. The challenge now is to keep building the conditions where te reo Māori can live beyond the classroom, ceremony and te wiki. If a language is to thrive, it must have places where it is not only heard but used; not only respected, but shared; not only learned, but lived. I had to go home to find my te reo town. The challenge now is to ensure our tamariki and mokopuna do not have to go searching for theirs. If we keep building the conditions for te reo Māori to thrive, then every town, suburb and community can become a place where the language is not only visible, but ordinary. More Reading

title: Good News in History, September 4
content:
Happy 64th Birthday to the Japanese Nobel laureate, Sinya Yamanaka, whose pioneering work in the science of stem cells led him to identify the “Yamanaka Factors”— 4 different genetic transcription factors that he used to turn any adult human cell into a stem cell. He shared the prize jointly with Sir John Gordon of England, and his discovery was described as world-changing. READ a bit more about his work… (1962)
The discovery that mature, fully-formed cells from the skin or elsewhere could be reprogrammed to turn themselves back into pluripotent stem cells meant that stem cell research could not only be conducted without relying on fetal tissues from the placenta or umbilical cord, but also with the patient’s own genetic material. These two realities which arose in the wake of Yamanaka’s experiment changed the field of what stem cells do.
One of the most cutting-edge is cell replacement therapy. Stem cells can replace diseased or lost cells in degenerative disorders like ALS or Parkinson’s, and they are less prone to immune rejection. However, there is a danger that it may introduce mutations or other genomic abnormalities that render it unsuitable for cell therapy. Yamanaka’s research in this area is ongoing.
MORE Good News on this Day:
- George Eastman registered the trademark Kodak, and received a patent for his camera which used rolled film (1888)
- The important Wolfenden Report in Britain suggested that consenting sex between homosexual adults “in private” should no longer be a criminal offense (1957)
- Mark Spitz won his seventh swimming gold medal at the Summer Olympics in Munich, becoming the first Olympian to win seven gold medals, swimming in only seven events and setting world records in each one (1972)
- Google was founded by Larry Page and Sergey Brin, who adopted the unofficial slogan, “Don’t be evil,” while they were Ph.D. students at Stanford (1998)
54 years ago today, the first episode of The Price is Right premiered on CBS. It would go on to become the country’s longest-running television game show, with its combination of endless surprises in terms of prizes, and unique retail-price guessing challenges. Bob Barker became an iconic game show host after debuting alongside the show, and hosting it until retirement in 2007.
In 2019 there were 9,000 episodes recorded. Prizes are donated by companies in exchange for the unique advertising opportunity. In the book Come On Down!: Behind the Big Doors at “The Price Is Right” staffer Stan Blits says the prizes require acres of warehouse space to store.
The Price is Right is often called the greatest game show in TV history, and by 2009, it had given away more than $250 million in cash and prizes. In 2007, Drew Carey took over role as host of the show. (1972)
And, 245 years ago today, Los Angeles was founded by Spanish settlers.
12 diverse working families settled in El Pueblo de la Reina de Los Angeles (The Town of the Queen of the Angels). Eight of the 23 adults arriving from the Mexican town of Álamos—held by Spain at the time—were Indians, ten were of African descent. They found a very spacious valley, well-grown with cottonwoods and alders, through which ran a beautiful river. (1781)
On this day 111 years ago, Rocky Mountain National Park was established by the US Congress, thanks to a man who was a sickly 14-year-old when he first moved near the majestic mountains and lakes and later lobbied for their protection.
Enos Mills wrote many books and articles describing the region and later split his time between the mountains he loved and the cities of the eastern United States, where he fought for legislation to create the park. Mills Lake in 415 square-mile Rocky Mountain National Park is named in his honor. (1915)
And, 37 years ago today, the first weekly meeting in favor of democratic reforms took place in East Germany, with peaceful political protestors gathering in Leipzig at the St. Nicholas Church to demand rights such as the freedom to travel to foreign countries and to elect a democratic government.
After the church’s weekly Monday prayer for peace, a few hundred people gathered, a number that swelled to more than 70,000 (out of the city’s population of 500,000), five days later. The next week, 120,000 demonstrators turned up—all united in peaceful opposition to the USSR-beholden regime and chanting “Wir sind das Volk!” (“We are the people!”).
In one more week, the number more than doubled to 320,000, with East German military units again being deployed on stand-by in the vicinity. This pressure and other key events eventually led to the fall of the Berlin Wall two months later, marking the imminent end of the dictatorial regime. The local Lutheran churches offered sanctuary to alternative political groups, and also offered them financial aid, support from the congregation and a place to communicate. (1989)
Also, Happy wedding anniversary to Kevin Bacon and Kyra Sedgwick, who have stayed married for 38 years, a feat that’s rarely been equaled in Hollywood. They got to know each other during the making of the PBS TV movie Lemon Sky. They had two children together and committed to keeping the marriage a top priority, by always scheduling quality time on date nights. (1988)

title: “Lucha antirracista corresponde a todos”: funcionaria brasileña
content:
Llama a romper pacto de blanquitud
La intersección de raza y género es una barrera en el acceso a oportunidades para las mujeres, denuncia
Domingo 6 de septiembre de 2026, p. 6
Segunda mujer afrodescendiente en ocupar el cargo de ministra de Igualdad Racial de Brasil, la doctora Rachel Barros de Oliveira, afirma que para reconocer plenamente la diversidad y pluriculturalidad de nuestras naciones, es necesario “enfrentar el racismo y las demás estructuras que siguen determinando quién tiene acceso al poder, a los ingresos, a la educación, a la tierra y a los espacios de tomas de decisiones”.
Subraya que un compromiso efectivo en la lucha contra el racismo y toda forma de discriminación pasa por “entender que ésta es una responsabilidad que debe ser compartida no sólo por la población negra, sino por todas las personas”.
Socióloga e investigadora destacada en el estudio de la desigualdad y las políticas públicas para frenarla, enfatiza que la escuela tiene un papel central en la promoción de la igualdad entre toda la población y en la construcción de una cultura antirracista.
“Es en el entorno escolar donde se forman valores, actitudes y referentes que acompañan a niñas, niños y jóvenes a lo largo de la vida. Una escuela que valora la diversidad y promueve el respeto, forma personas mejor preparadas para vivir en sociedad, dialogar con las diferencias y defender los derechos de todos.”
A su paso por México, donde asistió a la convención “A 25 años de Durban” –donde se realizó en 2001 la Conferencia Mundial contra el Racismo, la Discriminación Racial, la Xenofobia y las Formas Conexas de Intolerancia, convocada por Naciones Unidas–, afirma que las personas “no negras” que continúan beneficiándose del racismo estructural, protegidos por el “pacto de blanquitud” en diferentes posiciones de privilegio en los espacios de poder “deben convertirse en aliados de esta lucha contra la discriminación, si se desea formar parte de una sociedad que respete la ciudadanía y la pluralidad.
“Enfrentar estos flagelos que aún prevalecen en el mundo implica la construcción “no sólo del derecho de la población negra a existir, sino también la materialización de las políticas de promoción de la igualdad racial, como un compromiso real y firme con la democracia”.
En entrevista –vía un cuestionario escrito– la ministra brasileña explica que estados pluriculturales como México y Brasil, fueron construidos sobre estructuras coloniales que dividieron a las personas, las culturas y los saberes a partir de criterios raciales.
Diáspora africana
“Los descendientes de la diáspora africana, los pueblos indígenas y otros grupos históricamente marginados tuvieron sus derechos, conocimientos y formas de organización invisibilizados de manera deliberada.
“Nuestro desafío en Brasil ha sido transformar este reconocimiento en políticas públicas permanentes y garantizar que esta parte tan significativa de la población también participe en las decisiones que conciernen a sus vidas”. Por ello, considera que para la realidad de ambas naciones, es necesario formular políticas que sobrevivan a los cambios de administración.
La ministra Barros de Oliveira recalca que ella misma es producto de esas políticas de acción afirmativa implantadas en Brasil a partir de 2003, durante el primer gobierno del presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva; destaca que la creación del Ministerio de Igualdad Racial, así como la expansión del Sistema Nacional de Promoción de la Igualdad Racial y el avance de políticas dirigidas a las comunidades quilombolas (conformadas por afrobrasileños que se rebelaron contra la esclavitud) y a los pueblos de terreiro (aquellos que practican religiones de origen africano), “son ejemplos de cómo hemos buscado incorporar esta agenda a la estructura del Estado”.
A ellas se suman las acciones para promover la valorización de su cultura y sus tradiciones, a partir de planes de acción, legislación estructural y la aplicación de la Ley número 10.639/2003 con la que es obligatoria la enseñanza de la historia y la cultura afrobrasileña en las escuelas primarias y secundarias de Brasil.
Destaca también el programa Caminos Amefricanos, esfuerzo que fue reconocido en el marco de los 25 años de la Convención de Durban, en el que participan estudiantes y docentes de Brasil a quienes se ofrecen intercambios de corta duración en países del Sur global, a fin de valorar la diversidad cultural y racial, es otro ejemplo.
Otro desafío, reconoce, es avanzar en la lucha por la igualdad racial de sectores históricamente olvidados como las mujeres negras e indígenas, quienes se ven afectadas de forma “aún más severa por las desigualdades y las violencias institucionales, ya que la raza y el género se entrecruzan en la manera en que acceden a derechos y oportunidades”.
En Brasil, dijo, este debate también está presente en las políticas para hacer frente a la violencia contra las mujeres. El ministerio que encabeza forma parte del Pacto Nacional de Prevención de los Feminicidios, una estrategia que reúne a diferentes áreas del Estado, involucrando a los tres poderes, y trabaja desde una perspectiva de interseccionalidad, enfatiza.

title: As detetives que combatem deepfakes sexuais na Coreia do Sul
content:
Desde 2018, o governo sul-coreano mantém um centro especializado em rastrear e eliminar conteúdos sexuais ilícitos na internet, com foco em deepfakes, fotos ou vídeos de caráter pornográfico produzidos sem o conhecimento das vítimas. O centro funciona em um pequeno escritório no centro de Seul, decorado com faixas de apoio às vítimas de violência sexual, e é composto exclusivamente por mulheres.
A equipe tem 23 integrantes e atua a pedido das vítimas. Desde a inauguração, o centro já atendeu 53 mil pessoas e removeu mais de 1 milhão de conteúdos sexuais ilícitos da internet. A estrutura conta ainda com 17 filiais regionais, que oferecem apoio psicológico e jurídico.
Como o trabalho é feito
A líder da equipe, Kim Hyojung, descreve o fluxo típico de atendimento: a maioria das vítimas procura o centro depois que um familiar ou conhecido avisa que um vídeo seu está circulando online. A partir daí, um programa de inteligência artificial detecta republicações do mesmo conteúdo, permitindo que a equipe solicite a remoção tanto em redes sociais quanto em sites pornográficos.
Os obstáculos são frequentes. Segundo Kim Hyojung, grande parte dos vídeos está hospedada em sites ilegais cujos provedores não atendem aos pedidos de remoção; nesses casos, a polícia pode intervir para fechar o site. Quando o conteúdo está hospedado no exterior, o problema se repete, mas Kim Hyojung aponta que 80% desses casos envolvem servidores nos Estados Unidos e que as autoridades norte-americanas colaboram com as solicitações de remoção.
Levantamentos da empresa australiana Security Heroes estimam que mais da metade das vítimas de deepfakes pornográficos no mundo são sul-coreanas. O centro registra aumento de casos em todas as faixas etárias.
Impacto psicológico nas profissionais
O trabalho diário de revisar conteúdos pornográficos, às vezes violentos, às vezes envolvendo pornografia infantil, gera consequências para a saúde das integrantes da equipe. Uma das profissionais, identificada apenas como Park, mantém o anonimato como condição para exercer a função.
“Todas nós somos bastante afetadas emocional e psicologicamente por essa atividade. Pela experiência de colegas com quem já trabalhei, algumas desenvolveram insônia, outras começaram a chorar ao ver certas publicações ou perderam o apetite a ponto de pular refeições”, afirmou Park.
Para lidar com esse impacto, o centro implementou acompanhamento psicológico contínuo, com consultas individuais com um psicólogo uma ou duas vezes por mês. Park cita também o retorno das vítimas como fator de motivação: “Quando recebemos mensagens de agradecimento das pessoas afetadas, dizendo que isso as ajudou a retomar sua vida cotidiana, sinto que, mesmo que de forma modesta, pude contribuir para que essas pessoas superassem uma provação tão difícil em suas vidas”.
Beatriz Campos é jornalista formada pela Universidade São Judas Tadeu e jornalista do Olhar Digital.

title: 100-year-old seaside church is Vietnam's first climate change heritage site
content:
The century-old structure, which stands outside the current sea dike, is the Church of the Sacred Heart, which is associated with the birth and development of the former fishing village of Xuong Dien, now part of Hai Tien Commune.
It is known more commonly as Hai Ly church.
Xuong Dien was a coastal settlement in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. As people came to settle in the area, they built dikes and reclaimed land from the sea for agriculture and protecting their homes.
In 1885, the Ngo Ham Dike was built to a length of nearly 12 km, helping protect the reclaimed land.
But the place has been constantly affected by storms, waves, and coastal erosion. In 1925, the dike in Hai Ly Beach was breached for three kilometers. In 1990, around 1.5 km was destroyed and a new one had to be built 150 m inland.
By 2005, a 700 m section of the coastline in Xuong Dien was eroded.
Over the last century or so, the sea has swallowed almost a kilometer of coastal land in the area.
The Xuong Dien shoreline has retreated inland due to the combined effects of waves, currents, winds, and storms, with climate change being a contributing factor.
Managing tourism site
Now, authorities in Hai Tien Commune have been tasked with developing and managing the tourism site.
Associate Professor and Doctor of Science Vu Cao Minh, former deputy director of the Institute of Geological Sciences at the Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology, said the current location of the bell tower provides visible evidence of changes in the shoreline and the process by which people reclaimed and protected coastal land.
"The fact that a structure built about 100 years ago now stands on the beach, outside the dike, provides valuable material for studying the history of shoreline changes. It also shows how people have had to continuously reinforce dikes and protect land and production from the forces of nature."
He said the church is not just a relic but also important for its connection with the shoreline, dike, and history of human settlement.
He called it "a special type of heritage in Vietnam and rare in the world."
Internationally, structures affected by erosion, rising sea levels, and natural disasters are preserved for research, community education, and tourism.
In the U.K., for instance, the twin towers of the St Mary's Church in Kent have been preserved as a navigation landmark, and the surrounding ruins illustrate the effects of centuries of coastal erosion.
Minh said these models show that disaster heritage can become a valuable visual record if it is preserved, documented and appropriately developed.
"The value of a heritage site is not simply about preserving a structure, but about helping people understand why the structure is there, how the shoreline has changed and how people have responded. When this is achieved, the site can provide scientific, educational, and tourism benefits."
The area around the Hai Ly church includes Thinh Long Beach with its distinctive culture, cuisine, and fishing life.
Recognition as a tourism site will enable its development as a heritage site and the protection of the remaining structure, landscape, and records documenting changes to the shoreline.

title: Μείωση 35% των θανάτων από καρκίνο στις ΗΠΑ
content:
Η πιο σημαντική ρουτίνα δεν είναι αυτή που οδηγεί στον ύπνο. Είναι εκείνη που κάνει ένα παιδί να νιώθει ασφαλές.
Μείωση 35% των θανάτων από καρκίνο στις ΗΠΑ


Μείωση 35% των θανάτων από καρκίνο στις ΗΠΑ
Για το σύνολο των καρκίνων, η πενταετής σχετική επιβίωση σε ασθενείς με απομακρυσμένη νόσο έχει υπερδιπλασιαστεί τις τελευταίες τρεις δεκαετίες, από 17% στα μέσα της δεκαετίας του 1990 σε 36% την περίοδο 2016-2022
Η έρευνα για τον καρκίνο εξελίσσεται με ταχύτατους ρυθμούς, μεταμορφώνοντας σταδιακά τον τρόπο με τον οποίο οι επιστήμονες προλαμβάνουν, διαγιγνώσκουν και αντιμετωπίζουν τη νόσο. Έλληνες γιατροί αναφέρουν ότι τα αποτελέσματα δεκαετιών έρευνας είναι πλέον μετρήσιμα και στις ΗΠΑ οι θάνατοι μειώθηκαν.
Την σημαντική πρόοδο αποτυπώνει το Cancer Progress Report 2026 της American Association for Cancer Research (AACR), η 16η ετήσια έκθεση που συγκεντρώνει τα νεότερα δεδομένα για την επίπτωση, τη θνησιμότητα και την επιβίωση από τον καρκίνο και αναδεικνύει τον καθοριστικό ρόλο της βασικής, μεταφραστικής και κλινικής έρευνας στη βελτίωση της φροντίδας των ασθενών. Παράλληλα, παρουσιάζει τις επιστημονικές εξελίξεις που αναμένεται να διαμορφώσουν το μέλλον της ογκολογίας, από την τεχνητή νοημοσύνη και την υγρή βιοψία έως τα αντικαρκινικά εμβόλια και τις νέες θεραπευτικές προσεγγίσεις που βασίζονται στο RNA.

Οι Ιατροί της Θεραπευτικής Κλινικής (Νοσοκομείο Αλεξάνδρα) της Ιατρικής Σχολής του ΕΚΠΑ Θεοδώρα Ψαλτοπούλου (Καθηγήτρια Θεραπευτικής - Επιδημιολογίας - Προληπτικής Ιατρικής, Παθολόγος), Δρ. Μαρία Καπαρέλου (Παθολόγος - Ογκολόγος) και Θάνος Δημόπουλος (Καθηγητής Θεραπευτικής - Ογκολογίας - Αιματολογίας, Διευθυντής Θεραπευτικής Κλινικής, Νοσοκομείο «Αλεξάνδρα», τ. Πρύτανης ΕΚΠΑ) αναφέρουν στο Αθηναϊκό/Μακεδονικό Πρακτορείο Ειδήσεων ότι τα αποτελέσματα δεκαετιών έρευνας είναι πλέον μετρήσιμα. Στις ΗΠΑ, το συνολικό ποσοστό θανάτων από καρκίνο μειώθηκε κατά 35% μεταξύ 1991 και 2024, γεγονός που αντιστοιχεί σε περίπου 4,8 εκατομμύρια λιγότερους θανάτους. Στην εξέλιξη αυτή έχουν συμβάλει η μείωση του καπνίσματος, η πρόοδος στην πρόληψη και την έγκαιρη διάγνωση, καθώς και οι αποτελεσματικότερες θεραπευτικές επιλογές.

Βελτίωση καταγράφεται και στους ασθενείς με προχωρημένη ή μεταστατική νόσο. Για το σύνολο των καρκίνων, η πενταετής σχετική επιβίωση σε ασθενείς με απομακρυσμένη νόσο έχει υπερδιπλασιαστεί τις τελευταίες τρεις δεκαετίες, από 17% στα μέσα της δεκαετίας του 1990 σε 36% την περίοδο 2016-2022.

Χρόνια συντονισμένης προσπάθειας και διεπιστημονικής συνεργασίας έχουν οδηγήσει σε σημαντικές θεραπευτικές εξελίξεις, αναφέρουν οι ειδικοί. Όπως καταγράφει το AACR Cancer Progress Report 2026, από την 1η Ιουλίου 2025 έως τις 30 Ιουνίου 2026 ο FDA ενέκρινε 11 νέες αντικαρκινικές θεραπείες. Ανάμεσά τους περιλαμβάνονται η πρώτη μοριακά στοχευμένη θεραπεία για έναν σπάνιο και επιθετικό όγκο του εγκεφάλου με συγκεκριμένη γενετική αλλοίωση, η πρώτη θεραπεία που βασίζεται στην τεχνολογία proteolysis-targeting chimera για ασθενείς με καρκίνο του μαστού, ο πρώτος αναστολέας σημείου ελέγχου για τον καρκίνο των ωοθηκών και η πρώτη CAR-T κυτταρική θεραπεία για ασθενείς με λέμφωμα οριακής ζώνης. Κατά την ίδια περίοδο, εγκρίθηκαν επίσης νέες ενδείξεις για πέντε ήδη διαθέσιμες αντικαρκινικές θεραπείες, μία μη επεμβατική φορητή συσκευή για τη θεραπεία του καρκίνου του παγκρέατος, ένα τεστ αυτοσυλλογής δείγματος για τον HPV που μπορεί να πραγματοποιείται στο σπίτι, καθώς και αρκετά εργαλεία βασισμένα στην τεχνητή νοημοσύνη με στόχο τη βελτίωση της έγκαιρης ανίχνευσης και διάγνωσης του καρκίνου.
Ιδιαίτερη θέση στην έκθεση καταλαμβάνει η τεχνητή νοημοσύνη. Οι εφαρμογές της επεκτείνονται από τη βασική έρευνα και την ανάπτυξη νέων φαρμάκων έως την απεικόνιση, την ψηφιακή παθολογία και τον σχεδιασμό κλινικών μελετών. Παράλληλα, μπορεί να συμβάλλει στη βελτίωση της έγκαιρης ανίχνευσης και διάγνωσης του καρκίνου, στην πρόβλεψη της έκβασης των ασθενών και στην περαιτέρω εξατομίκευση των θεραπευτικών επιλογών.
Νέα δυναμική αποκτούν και τα προληπτικά και θεραπευτικά αντικαρκινικά εμβόλια. Νέες τεχνολογίες επιτρέπουν καλύτερο σχεδιασμό των εμβολίων, αναγνώριση ειδικών στόχων του όγκου και συνδυασμούς με άλλες θεραπείες. Η έκθεση αναφέρει ενθαρρυντικά πρώιμα αποτελέσματα από εξατομικευμένες προσεγγίσεις στον καρκίνο του παγκρέατος, στο μελάνωμα και στον πρώιμο τριπλά αρνητικό καρκίνο του μαστού, καθώς και από εμβόλιο που μελετάται σε άτομα με σύνδρομο Lynch.
Παρά τις σημαντικές εξελίξεις, το φορτίο της νόσου παραμένει μεγάλο. Για το 2026 εκτιμάται ότι στις ΗΠΑ θα διαγνωστούν περισσότερα από 2,1 εκατομμύρια νέα περιστατικά καρκίνου και περισσότεροι από 626.000 άνθρωποι θα χάσουν τη ζωή τους από τη νόσο. Παράλληλα, ιδιαίτερη ανησυχία προκαλεί η αύξηση των καρκίνων πρώιμης έναρξης, δηλαδή εκείνων που διαγιγνώσκονται σε ηλικίες 18-49 ετών. Παγκοσμίως, η επίπτωσή τους αυξήθηκε κατά σχεδόν 80% μεταξύ 1990 και 2019, με ορισμένους καρκίνους του γαστρεντερικού συστήματος να συμβάλλουν δυσανάλογα σε αυτή την αύξηση.

Η πρόοδος στην πρόληψη και την έγκαιρη διάγνωση, η ανάπτυξη νέων θεραπευτικών προσεγγίσεων και η αξιοποίηση τεχνολογιών αιχμής δημιουργούν νέες δυνατότητες για τους ασθενείς. Η συνέχιση της επένδυσης στην έρευνα και η ταχύτερη μεταφορά των επιστημονικών ανακαλύψεων στην κλινική πράξη αποτελούν βασικές προϋποθέσεις ώστε η πρόοδος αυτή να συνεχιστεί και να μεταφράζεται σε μεγαλύτερη επιβίωση και καλύτερη ποιότητα ζωής για όλο και περισσότερους ανθρώπους με καρκίνο.

Την σημαντική πρόοδο αποτυπώνει το Cancer Progress Report 2026 της American Association for Cancer Research (AACR), η 16η ετήσια έκθεση που συγκεντρώνει τα νεότερα δεδομένα για την επίπτωση, τη θνησιμότητα και την επιβίωση από τον καρκίνο και αναδεικνύει τον καθοριστικό ρόλο της βασικής, μεταφραστικής και κλινικής έρευνας στη βελτίωση της φροντίδας των ασθενών. Οι Ιατροί της Θεραπευτικής Κλινικής (Νοσοκομείο Αλεξάνδρα) της Ιατρικής Σχολής του ΕΚΠΑ Θεοδώρα Ψαλτοπούλου (Καθηγήτρια Θεραπευτικής - Επιδημιολογίας - Προληπτικής Ιατρικής, Παθολόγος), Δρ. Μαρία Καπαρέλου (Παθολόγος - Ογκολόγος) και Θάνος Δημόπουλος (Καθηγητής Θεραπευτικής - Ογκολογίας - Αιματολογίας, Διευθυντής Θεραπευτικής Κλινικής, Νοσοκομείο «Αλεξάνδρα», τ. Πρύτανης ΕΚΠΑ) αναφέρουν στο Αθηναϊκό/Μακεδονικό Πρακτορείο Ειδήσεων ότι τα αποτελέσματα δεκαετιών έρευνας είναι πλέον μετρήσιμα.
