His warning that educational backwardness could become “a monster” especially in the states in northern Nigeria, remains painfully relevant.
This is why Governor Sani’s later formulation of democracy is particularly instructive. As Governor, he has argued that “democracy is not the destination; it is the framework within which a society must pursue human dignity and shared prosperity.” That is a significant departure from the narrow conception of democracy as periodic elections. It places governance under a more demanding obligation: to make political freedom meaningful in people’s everyday lives.
The implication is profound. The ballot box is necessary, but it is not sufficient. A democratic government must educate children, expand economic opportunity, provide healthcare, protect the vulnerable, develop rural communities and create conditions in which young people can imagine a future beyond poverty and exclusion.
The same principle informed Fawehinmi’s later political battles. Following the return to civilian rule, he and his associates, including Uba Sani, challenged restrictions on political participation and the denial of registration to parties outside the initial political arrangement. The legal battle eventually reached the Supreme Court and helped widen Nigeria’s political space.
That history deserves remembrance because political freedom has a tendency to become invisible once it becomes familiar. Many Nigerians who participate in today’s multiparty system may have little knowledge of the struggles that made such participation possible.
As Senator Shehu Sani observed at the Kaduna presentation, “Democracy has a history,” and that history includes sacrifice.
It is this historical consciousness that makes the book timely. Nigeria’s present political class is often accused, with justification, of possessing little institutional memory. Political actors inherit freedoms without remembering their custodians; they occupy democratic institutions without appreciating the battles that secured them; they speak of public office as privilege when it should be understood as responsibility.
The Fawehinmi-Sani story offers a corrective. The most important inheritance from the elder to the younger man was not political machinery. It was an ethic of service. The note was simple: never forget the masses.
The real test, therefore, is whether that instruction survives in governance.
Uba Sani’s stated priorities in Kaduna: education, infrastructure, security, healthcare, agriculture, vocational training, social protection and access to justice, can be understood within that broader philosophy. His administration’s allocation of 25 per cent of the 2026 budget to education, alongside substantial commitments to infrastructure, health and agriculture, reflects an understanding that public expenditure is ultimately a moral document. Budgets reveal what a government considers important.
Likewise, the expansion of vocational education and the graduation of thousands of young people with practical skills speak to a proposition that Fawehinmi understood deeply: empowerment is more enduring than dependency.
The same logic applies to Governor Sani’s administration’s intervention in the criminal-justice system. The release of hundreds of convicts and persons awaiting trial, together with the payment of fines and compensation for beneficiaries, rests on the idea that justice must retain a human face. As Uba Sani put it: “Justice must never be reduced to punishment. It must contain humanity, rehabilitation and the possibility of a second chance.
That is precisely where the mentor’s old counsel meets the responsibilities of contemporary office
Yet the significance of this relationship should not be reduced to the record of one administration. Its larger importance lies in the question it poses to every Nigerian entrusted with authority: whom do you remember when you acquire power? Fawehinmi’s answer was clear. Remember those without power.
Remember the poor. Remember unemployed youths. Remember citizens whose voices are easily drowned by the machinery of the state. Remember that public office derives its legitimacy from service.
The finest tribute to Gani Fawehinmi, therefore, cannot be a ceremony, a memorial or even a book, valuable as all three may be. His true memorial would be a Nigeria in which the law protects the weak as confidently as it restrains the powerful; in which education is treated as national security; in which democratic freedom is matched by social justice; and in which political authority remains answerable to the people. That is the enduring lesson of the relationship between Gani Fawehinmi and Uba Sani
A mentor’s greatest achievement is not to reproduce himself, but to prepare another person to carry a principle beyond his own lifetime. Fawehinmi did precisely that. He planted in a young activist a conception of service that has travelled from the streets of the pro-democracy struggle to the corridors of democratic government.
The note he left was brief. Its implications are not. “Do not ever forget the masses of our people.”
In a country perpetually tempted to confuse power with purpose, those words remain a formidable standard. They remind every occupant of public office that history will judge not merely the battles he fought, the positions he occupied or the honours he accumulated, but the extent to which ordinary citizens found their dignity enlarged by his stewardship
That is the leadership note Gani Fawehinmi bequeathed to Uba Sani. It is also a note Nigeria should never stop reading.
Dr. Salifu, a university teacher, resides in Samaru, Zaria.

title: Africa’s mother tongues are finding new life as youth connect with roots and relatives
content:
A television game show in Nigeria’s commercial hub of Lagos has an unforgiving rule: Speak English and you lose. For a US-born millennial in the audience and a student of her parents’ mother tongue, the high-stakes setting is a perfect classroom.
Meanwhile, a 15-year-old Canadian speaks to a teacher about 13,000km away in Zimbabwe, learning a language her parents feared she would never speak.
“Mhoroi,” Nyashadzashe Machingura says cheerfully with a pronounced Canadian accent while greeting in Zimbabwe’s vernacular Shona.
The scenes capture a new generation of interest and entrepreneurship around African languages once pushed to the margins by decades of colonialism. Often seen as secondary to English, French and Portuguese, they are enjoying a renaissance that is also creating business opportunities.
Between 1,500 and 3,000 languages in Africa
Africa is home to more than 1 billion people speaking roughly a third of the world’s languages, with between 1,500 and 3,000 across 54 countries, according to Unesco.
Experts say the revival in some of them is driven in part by second- and third-generation Africans in the diaspora finding it easier to reconnect with their roots and communicate with older relatives, thanks to social media, online learning, and entertainment.
“There were times I definitely felt left out because my family around me were all speaking Shona. And I just couldn’t understand them,” Nyashadzashe said after a lesson covering traditional greetings, proverbs and ancestral clan symbols. She said she had eaten the food and worn the traditional clothing but still felt left out.
But now her conversations with her grandparents in Zimbabwe are growing longer.
“Being able to connect with them on that level makes me really proud of my heritage,” she said.
African languages were never ‘modernised’
Her Zimbabwe-based tutor, Shungu Chidovi, left her banking career in January to focus full-time on ZimbOriginal, an online platform that teaches Shona through storytelling, book clubs and “buddy pairing” exchanges.
Now she teaches about two dozen learners in Zimbabwe, Canada, Australia, South Africa, Ireland and Scotland, charging $50 a month.
The business, part of a small but growing number of online initiatives teaching African languages, emerged almost by accident. Chidovi began writing a blog about Zimbabwean traditions in 2016. Readers began asking whether she taught Shona.
“I didn’t see it at the time that I was really writing about the Shona language,” Chidovi said.
Like many in Africa, she grew up with the understanding that to get ahead, she had to embrace Western languages rather than her mother tongue. English remains the dominant language for education, business and government affairs in the southern African nation that officially recognises 16 mostly indigenous languages.
“When you talk of Africa, you talk of English, French, Portuguese,” said Believe Mubonderi, a linguistics lecturer at Zimbabwe Open University. His research highlights the importance of ensuring that African languages have a place in the technologies that shape how people communicate, learn and trade.
“In most cases, African languages were sidelined. They were never exposed or modernised to be used in commerce, science and technology,” he said. ”When a language has a very low status, there’s a danger that that language eventually becomes endangered.”
Culture and connection are driving the new interest
Governments and international organisations are trying to reverse that trend.
The African Union’s 2022 decision to adopt Kiswahili, spoken in much of East Africa, as an official working language has raised its international profile. The United Nations declared 2022-32 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.
And the AU continental body and Unesco are supporting efforts to document and revitalise African languages, including the use of artificial intelligence to generate and translate children’s books and teacher guides.
But there’s a steep digital disadvantage. Unesco says only 10 languages worldwide dominate the “internet ecosystem”, while less than 2% of African languages have a meaningful online presence. That leaves many with too little data to train artificial intelligence systems.
Still, momentum for change is growing, with much of it coming from Africans abroad.
“People of African descent have come to realise that we also have our own identity which we need to embrace and be proud of,” Mubonderi said. “You go on Facebook, you go on TikTok, you are seeing many different efforts. Younger diaspora Africans “are trying by all means to revive, to revitalise, to make use of these languages.”
Chindovi said she hears that desire from children and their parents.
“When people are away from home, they long for home more than when they are home,” she said.
Nigerian game show penalises English speakers
That hunger for connection is also reshaping culture.
In Nigeria, a game show called “Masoyinbo”, meaning “Do not speak English”, has turned Yoruba, one of the country’s most widely spoken languages, into prime-time entertainment. Contestants, including diaspora Nigerians, are tested on Yoruba language and culture, with prizes reaching thousands of dollars.
Host Olalekan Fabilola, who started the show in 2024, sees its popularity as part of a wider shift.
“If ‘Masoyinbo’ had started like 10 years ago, it wouldn’t have been what it is now,” he said. “But we are in the age of cultural resurgence. People want to go back to their roots. Everyone wants to know where they are from, and so it’s timely.”
Tomi Adeshokan, a New Jersey resident who is learning to perfect her Yoruba with Fabilola as a tutor, was part of the audience during a recent recording of the show. She said she lost daily exposure to Yoruba after moving out of her father’s home before the Covid-19 pandemic. During the pandemic, she joined Clubhouse (a live, audio-only social media app) just to hear the language and later began taking classes. Now she was back visiting family.
“It’s very important for us to immerse ourselves in our culture and not to fully identify with other cultures, like American or Western culture,” Adeshokan said.
AP

title: From 6 to 194: How Assam Is Bringing the World’s Smallest Pig Back to the Wild
content: Nearly 30 years ago, six tiny pygmy hogs were taken out of the grasslands of Manas in Assam. There was a good reason. The species had come dangerously close to disappearing, and conservationists feared that leaving the few surviving animals in the wild could mean losing them altogether. So, in 1996, six pygmy hogs were captured from the Kuribeel grasslands of Manas National Park to start a breeding programme. This June, their descendants came home. Fifteen captive-bred pygmy hogs, nine females and six males, were released into the same Kuribeel grasslands. No confirmed signs of the species had been recorded there for the past nine years. For conservationists who have spent decades trying to bring the animal back from the brink, the release marked a powerful full-circle moment. Six animals had once been taken from these grasslands to save their species. Today, their descendants are being returned to rebuild a wild population. Six became 194 The June release was carried out under the Pygmy Hog Conservation Programme (PHCP), which has been working to breed pygmy hogs and return them to suitable habitats in Assam. Since 2020, six groups have been released in Manas alone. With the latest 15 animals, the number released in the national park has reached 78. Across Assam, the programme has now bred and reintroduced 194 pygmy hogs. That number carries particular weight for an animal that was once feared extinct. The pygmy hog disappeared from much of its historical range during the 20th century and was thought to have vanished altogether before surviving populations were rediscovered. Captive breeding gave the species a lifeline. The next challenge is much harder: helping these animals live, breed and form self-sustaining populations in the wild. The pygmy hog is endemic to northeast India and was once widespread in the tall, wet grasslands of the Terai from Uttar Pradesh. Photograph: (A. J. T. Johnsingh, WWF-India and NCF) And there are encouraging signs. For the first time since the conservation programme began, wild-born pygmy hogs may now outnumber those living in captivity. That is an important turning point. A species can truly recover when new generations begin surviving and reproducing in the habitat they evolved to live in. The hogs returning to Kuribeel will now have to do exactly that. Why this tiny pig matters A pygmy hog is easy to miss. Porcula salvania, India’s only endemic wild pig, is among the world’s rarest mammals. Its survival is closely tied to one particular landscape: the tall alluvial grasslands of the Himalayan foothills. For the pygmy hog, these grasses are home. They provide places to hide, feed, build nests and raise young. They are also fragile ecosystems. Habitat loss, invasive plants and human disturbance have altered many of these grasslands. As they shrink or change, animals such as the pygmy hog lose the conditions they need to survive. This is what makes the animal valuable far beyond its small size. Conservationists consider the pygmy hog a flagship species for tall grasslands. If these hogs can survive and breed, it is a strong sign that the habitat around them is being protected and restored. Saving the pygmy hog therefore also means protecting the grasslands it depends on. And breeding more animals solves only one part of the puzzle. Each release needs suitable habitat waiting at the other end. Could pygmy hogs return to more parts of India? For now, much of the pygmy hog’s recovery story has centred on Assam. The next chapter could take the species farther across its former range. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has included the pygmy hog in its Species Recovery Programme, with the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) serving as the nodal agency for the conservation project. Over the next five years, the PHCP plans to release around 80 more pygmy hogs in Manas. Photograph: (Udayan Borthakur/Roundglass Sustain) The idea is to strengthen existing populations, improve grassland habitats and study whether pygmy hogs could eventually return to places where they once lived. Potential habitats being considered include Jaldapara in West Bengal and suitable areas in Uttar Pradesh. Before any animals are released, scientists will need to study these landscapes carefully. They must understand whether enough suitable grassland remains, what threats exist and whether a new population could survive there over the long term. The Wildlife Institute of India has already shared information on the species’ present status, captive breeding and conservation work with the government’s Wildlife Committee. The committee has recommended scientific assessments across the pygmy hog’s historical range. In simple terms, the question has moved from “Can we save this species?” to “Can we help it return to more of the places it once called home?” The journey is still unfolding Back in Manas, the work continues. Over the next five years, the PHCP plans to release around 80 more pygmy hogs into the national park. Its longer-term goal is to help build a wild population of around 300 animals by 2040. The effort brings together the Assam Forest Department, Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, the IUCN SSC Wild Pig Specialist Group, Aaranyak and Ecosystems-India. For all the organisations, breeding centres and scientific planning involved, the story ultimately comes down to something remarkably simple. In 1996, conservationists looked at a species with very few animals left and decided there was still time to save it. They began with six. Three decades later, the number of pygmy hogs bred and released has reached 194, and descendants of those first animals are walking through Kuribeel once again. Their future now rests in the grasslands. If those landscapes remain healthy enough for the pygmy hogs to feed, shelter and raise their young, a species once pushed towards extinction may once again become a familiar part of the wild places it came from. Sources: ‘Pygmy hog added to national recovery programme to protect alluvial grasslands’: By Jitendra Choubey, Published on 1 August 2026 ‘Pygmy Hogs Return Home to Manas After 30 Years’: By Hantigiri Narzary, Published on 7 June 2026 ‘Pygmy Hog likely to come under India’s species recovery programme: Environment Ministry’: By Muskan Bhatia, Published on 9 July 2026

title: From shikara to pillars, Ganesh mandal recreates Somnath Temple in Pune
content:
Written by Kalyani Lad
This Ganeshotsav, devotees in Pune don’t need to travel to Gujarat to seek blessings at Somnath Temple. One of the most sacred pilgrimage sites in India, considered to be the first among the 12 jyotirlingas of Lord Shiva, has come to the city.
Somnath Temple dates back to 649 BC but many historians believe it to be older. Now, Hutatma Babu Genu Mandal Trust, popularly known as Navsacha Ganpati, has recreated the historic Somnath Temple in all its grandeur as a Ganeshotsav pandal. Established in 1970, the mandal is celebrating its 53rd year.
The massive set has been crafted by the team of art director Nitin Desai. Led by Hemant and Roshan, a team of 30 to 40 artisans worked through the clock for 25 days to complete the intricate carvings, shikharas and pillars that mirror the original temple. Each of them was aware of the importance of getting every architectural detail right.
“The decoration is not just art; it is an experience where architecture, faith and tradition come together, allowing every devotee to leave with hope that their wish will be fulfilled,” says Kishor Dabare, president.
Visitors to the Somnath Temple have faith in the water bodies of the temple and conduct ceremonies here. The Hutatma Babu Genu pandal has drawn inspiration from the sacred temple tanks of Somnath Temple, where devotees throw a coin to make a wish. They have recreated a north-facing well, where people can make a wish.
“Since the beginning of Ganeshotsav, people across Pune have been coming to make a wish. They have faith in the Ganpati idol. Devotees from Thailand and other countries also visit the mandal to experience the culture and traditions of Ganeshotsav,” says Milap Marne, secretary of the mandal.
Devotees stand before the well, close their eyes, make a wish, and toss a coin into the water. “They believe that the well carries the wish to Bappa,” says Marne. Ketan Pawar, a third generation volunteer at the mandal, says that, over the years, devotees have come to make their desires known to Ganpati by whispering to the ‘Ichha Purti Kalash’. “Many devotees return year after year, saying that their wishes were fulfilled,” says Pawar.
The well is cementing their faith further. Talks are underway with the Pune Municipal Corporation to make the well a permanent feature of the temple. “It has been placed towards the north, a direction associated with progress and prosperity. A fountain and pond have been created around it, so that water offered during prayers flows towards the Kalash and the well,” says Pawar.
(Kalyani Lad is an intern with The Indian Express)

title: Building AI to accelerate science and improve lives
content:
Building AI to accelerate science and improve lives
Today, we reached a significant milestone that stands as a testament to decades of AI research and advancement: Google technologies now support more than 300 languages, spoken by 7 billion people — representing 86% of the global population. To help us understand how these tools are driving real-world opportunity, we also released new interactive insights today with our AI & Economy ATLAS, the most comprehensive look at how real people are using AI globally. This comes on top of a raft of key AI advances in science to benefit people over just the past few weeks:
- We mapped all 9 billion possible single letter genetic changes across the human genome with AlphaGenome Atlas and made it openly available to researchers.
- We introduced WeatherNext 3, our most advanced and accurate global weather model, delivering 50% more accurate precipitation forecasts a day or more ahead — and it’s already in use in our products.
- We brought together data on global health, food security, and socioeconomics into a single Planetary Prediction Engine to forecast planetary crises — this has already been used in the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and in the U.S. in identifying vulnerable communities across 21 CDC health indicators.
- We scaled AI research to help cut the climate impact of aviation — this is already being applied in the U.K. (in collaboration with the government) and in Asia.
What ties all of this work together? It is the belief that advances in AI can accelerate scientific progress in ways that will directly improve people’s lives today and in the future. This is a key element of what motivates our work in AI. We’re focusing our work in key areas that matter most: making disease detectable, treatable, and preventable, predicting natural disasters, expanding learning, and unlocking economic opportunities for more people.
While the possibilities are exciting, the benefits of AI are not guaranteed. Making them real — and mitigating their challenges and risks — demands that society works together. Though there is more still to do, AI’s progress is already making it possible for us to aspire to do bold and ambitious things that can benefit people, and to ask and address questions that were once considered impossible to solve.
We’re making progress in using AI to improve disease detection and diagnosis, and to better understand health conditions:
- Deepening scientific discovery: Our Nobel-Prize winning AlphaFold has predicted all 200 million protein structures known to science, providing a new basis for understanding and researching diseases. It is now used by 4 million researchers in 190 countries in areas from drug discovery to understanding neglected diseases like Chagas disease and leishmaniasis. AlphaMissense is helping researchers predict disease-causing genetic mutations. And now, we’re building on AlphaFold and AlphaMissense with AlphaGenome Atlas, offering scientists predictive insights into how genetic variations alter cellular behavior.
- Earlier detection: Our recent breast cancer study with Imperial College London and the U.K.’s NHS showed AI can detect 25% of interval cancers previously missed in mammograms of 175,000 women. At the same time, we’re making meaningful progress in tools to help detect lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and genetic mutations in tumor cells.
- Global screenings: For tuberculosis — where ~40% of infected people worldwide go undiagnosed — our chest X-ray (used by Nexus Intelligence) has screened over 25,000 x-rays across 40 locations in six nations. We are also using bioacoustic models to detect TB via coughs using Health Acoustic Representations. Meanwhile, our diabetic retinopathy model, developed with partners, has supported more than 1.15 million screenings globally, with plans to expand to 6 million over the next decade to help detect a treatable but growing cause of preventable blindness.
- Expanding access: We’re pioneering the use of everyday smart phones and wearables for early detection of cardiovascular disease, insulin resistance, hypertension, loss of pulse, and passive heart rate monitoring. We’re working with leaders in Arkansas to help develop a blueprint for improving health outcomes in rural areas.
- Tools for scientists and health practitioners: Collaborative AI tools like Co-Scientist are helping researchers accelerate and expand core steps of the scientific method, like generating and validating novel hypotheses (such as identifying new therapeutic applications for existing drugs for acute myeloid leukemia). We have also open-sourced AI tools like DeepConsensus, DeepVariant, and DeepPolisher. Over the last decade, these tools have assisted in completing the human genome, drafting the first pangenome, and enabling ongoing work as part of the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium, better representing human genetic diversity and allowing experts to more accurately diagnose and treat diseases. Through AMIE (Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer), we are continuing to work on prospective evidence in real-world settings, collaborating with academic and medical institutions (e.g., Beth Israel Deaconess Center), and conducting a first-of-its-kind nationwide trial in real-world care settings. AMIE assists those providing care on the frontlines — freeing up doctors to spend more time with their patients.
To protect people’s safety and livelihoods, we need accurate predictions of natural disasters and weather. To make accurate predictions, we must understand the physical earth. Here’s how our technical and scientific progress is already making a difference in crisis prediction and detection:
- Extreme weather and earthquakes: Last year, authorities in Jamaica used WeatherNext to accurately predict Hurricane Melissa’s path, securing early disaster funding and enabling life-saving emergency preparations long before the storm made landfall. Just a few months ago, our Earthquake Alert system alerted millions of people in Venezuela ahead of an earthquake. And we’re making progress in other areas, including cyclones and extreme heat.
- Monsoons and floods: The scale of this work is encouraging. In 2025, our monsoon predictions provided information for 38 million farmers in India. And in just a few years, our forecasts on Flood Hub — now including both riverine floods and flash floods — have grown to cover 2 billion people across more than 150 countries in areas at risk for significant flood events.
- Wildfires: Our AI tools have helped predict wildfire boundaries in the U.S. and 33 other countries. We’re also working with partners toward a FireSat constellation of satellites to detect wildfires previously too small to detect anywhere on earth. In 2025, we generated more than 520 crisis alerts on Google Search that provided timely wildfire information to over 75 million users around the world.
- Next-gen prediction: With WeatherNext 3, we’re combining real-time satellite observations with AI, delivering high-resolution, hourly forecasts without immense supercomputing power — a major step forward for data-sparse regions that have been long underserved by high-resolution forecasting.
- Planetary crisis mapping: We recently introduced the Earth AI Planetary Prediction Engine (PPE), an autonomous AI system that uses simple language instructions to almost instantly predict global crises like disease outbreaks, food shortages, and climate risks, helping humanitarian responders act faster during emergencies. In the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, PPE successfully pinpointed 83% of emerging hotspots ahead of time, beating current forecasting systems. In Nigeria, PPE doubled food security forecasting accuracy at the local district level. And in the U.S., PPE outperformed traditional models in identifying vulnerable communities across 21 CDC health indicators. We’re continuing to expand prediction horizons to make these tools even more useful.
Learning is the bedrock of economic and societal progress. The world has made huge strides in education: 90% of primary school-aged children globally are enrolled in school, and approximately 87% complete their primary education. But 2022 research showed uneven access to education, differences in education quality, and limited content availability across languages, among other issues. Global learning outcomes have declined over the last two decades across 81 countries.
AI offers a profound opportunity to expand access to knowledge and support learners and educators alike:
- For learners: AI can enable personalized learning, remove language barriers, and make complex subjects more accessible through tools like Guided Learning. It can also expand access and support for learners and teachers, for example with free access to student tools in multiple countries.
- For educators: AI can help with research, preparation, and administrative tasks, freeing up time to spend with students.
Tackling challenges and focusing on responsible design: AI presents real challenges for learning, including questions on accuracy, safety, critical thinking, cheating, and learning loss. That’s why we have partnered with ISTE+ASCD to provide AI literacy training to all 6 million educators in the U.S., while conducting ongoing and rigorous research to ensure we design our educational tools with teachers in the lead, and AI as the assistant. We still have much to work through together.
Across the economy, AI can drive innovation and productivity for workers, businesses, and organizations across sectors. Its true value isn’t in what it does on its own, but in how people choose to use it and what they build with it:
- For small businesses: AI can help deliver new products, services, and economic growth. Small businesses are scaling custom marketing campaigns with Pomelli and bringing together complex regional sales data from different product lines with the Gemini Enterprise App.
- The future of work: The economic benefits of AI are neither automatic nor guaranteed. Like other new technologies, we expect AI to reshape work in three major ways: Some jobs are likely to decline, some jobs will grow, and many more jobs will change as AI increasingly assists workers. To understand these shifts, we’ve launched the AI & Economy ATLAS, which provides empirical insights on how people are using AI tools at work and in their daily lives, and translated the data into an interactive, open-access experience.
- Skilling: Training and skill building must be accessible to all regardless of a person's geography, language, or access to capital. To date, Google has provided more than $1 billion globally in training and skilling initiatives, helping over 100 million people gain essential digital and AI skills, from electricians and other skilled tradespeople, to rural healthcare workers, to manufacturing workers. More tailored worker assistance and transition support will likely be needed.
Grounded in our company’s founding mission, we are making important strides in breaking down languages and accessibility barriers with products, research, and models that understand the world’s languages exactly as they are expressed:
- Language tools: AI and machine learning have been part of Google Translate since its launch in 2006. Since then, advances in AI have helped us expand our technologies and products to support nearly 300 languages, spoken by 7 billion people — representing 86% of the world’s population, and helping more than 1 billion people translate around 1 trillion words each month. Our goal is to support the world’s 1,000 most-spoken languages.
- Inclusive speech technology: Access is broader than translation alone. For example, automatic speech recognition uses AI to understand spoken words and convert them into text. To help build inclusive speech technology, we partnered with Makerere University, University of Ghana, and Digital Umuganda to create an open dataset for 27 African languages spoken by over 100 million people. One language alone may have 100 dialects, each with its own nuance, which is why we’ve also partnered with IISC-Banglore and ARTPARK on Project Vaani to open-source speech and image datasets for 109 Indic languages.
- Accessibility: Beyond spoken languages, we've been making our tools more accessible for people with disabilities, including with our recent sign-language-to-text (SL2T) model for sign-to-text dictation.
Bold and responsible, together
We believe that such bold ambitions for the societal benefits of AI must always be accompanied by an equal commitment to responsibility. This is the basis of our bold and responsible approach to AI. Beyond our ongoing work to address the immediate and future risks of AI (detailed in our annual updates), the application of AI and science presents distinct challenges: On the one hand, we need the right detection, reporting, and mitigation tools in place to address risks around chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) mis-use. At the same time, it is important to avoid the risk of missed use — that is, not applying AI in places and communities where it would provide benefit and, in some cases, worsening existing societal challenges and gaps.
We believe advancing scientific discovery and bringing those benefits to communities requires that we collaborate deeply with many other researchers and scientists working to tackle similar issues, including academia, national laboratories, philanthropic foundations, non-governmental organizations, governments, other companies, and local partners. The examples of advances cited above have benefited from such research collaborations and our own Google.org grant-making to accelerate scientific discovery and to address society’s greatest challenges. That’s why as part of our longstanding commitment to supporting science and discovery in academia, Google has given more than $1 billion across 1,700+ research institutions worldwide since 2006.
As Nobel laureate Joel Mokyr noted, new technology drives scientific advances, which in turn drive new technologies, creating "a positive feedback loop that can keep growing with no end in sight.” And it does so in ways that have improved people’s wellbeing and propelled societal progress. AI is the most powerful engine for that loop we have ever built — and we’re just getting started.
Read more about how we’re using AI to help people, improve lives, and benefit society at our website.

title: Robotic sign language interpreter for deaf Māori in development
content:
World's first indigenous language robot interpreter
New robotic interpreters built by experts at the University of Auckland will bring sign language underpinned by a Māori worldview to Turi Māori - Māori who are deaf.
Dr Tauwehe Tamati, who is leading the project alongside Dr Ho Seok Ahn told Morning Report, the signs have been developed in partnership with Turi Māori, whānau, Iwi and Hapū.
"I think that's why I got involved in the project in the first place. That would have been at least five years ago when I was approached by our colleagues.
"I had to think through how to connect the expertise of my colleagues in robotics, megatronics and so on. How do you connect it with a culture, with a people? And particularly with the most vulnerable of our own people."
Tamati is bilingual in Te Reo Māori and English. She used both languages and a whānau-based home sign with her father who was hard of hearing for most of his life, becoming profoundly deaf in his final 20 years.
"Our dad grew up in Te Ao Māori. He knew he was Māori and he was a hard worker at our pā. The cultural, social, and collective life on the marae continually reinforced his identity and sense of belonging.
"Over time, however, he stopped going to the pā and didn't like relatives coming around.
"We'd be making up excuses because he was deaf. We couldn't help him get through that. So when my engineering colleagues approached me about the project, I just thought of him and said, 'I'll do this for dad."'
Researchers used Māori sign-language models who were filmed and photographed, to capture the different elements of communication, including mannerisms and lip movement.
An advanced AI system called a weighted multimodal network was then used to develop the robots ability to interpret the signs.
The University of Auckland says the robots are now built and functioning within its research lab.
Models have been made at both adult and children's sizes.
Work on the project began more than five years ago as part of the Science for Technological Innovation National Science Challenge, with additional financial support coming from the Vision Mātauranga Fund and the Endeavour Fund in 2024.
"I think our project now has reached such a level of success that we do have all the people in the hapū excited and participating.
"They don't need to hear us. They just look around and they know they can feel they are the reason why we're all helping," Tamati said.

title: The Promise of the Kurdish Peace
content:
August brought some truly transformative good news for Turkey, the Kurds, and Turkey’s immediate neighborhood in the Middle East. On Aug. 10, the Turkish Parliament passed a law establishing a legal framework for the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), the Kurdish militant group, and creating a phased pathway for reintegration of its members into society.
For more than four decades, the Kurdish issue has run like an electrified barbed wire through conversations in Turkey. The armed conflict between the PKK and the Turkish government has killed around 40,000 militants, soldiers, and civilians, and cost Turkey losses estimated to be around $2 trillion since 1984. Following peace talks, in July 2025, the PKK held a symbolic weapon-burning ceremony, starting a process of disarmament and moving toward ending the armed conflict.
The law offers legal protections to former PKK militants who have not committed specific crimes and helps suspend prison sentences for some members of the group. Thousands of sympathizers, activists affiliated with the PKK, and Kurdish politicians have been living in exile in Europe and elsewhere to escape legal prosecution. The law opens a path for them to return to Turkey. And the passage of this law in the Turkish parliament with broad support is a transformative step toward lasting peace and the creation of a new social contract between Turkey and the Kurds, domestically and regionally.
How to make peace
In the past decade, Turkey established clear military dominance in the fight against the PKK. Changes in military technology, intelligence, and surveillance systems, especially the rise of Turkish drones, strengthened the country’s counter-insurgency efforts. Yet Turkey’s military capacity to suppress an insurgency was not the sole factor in persuading the PKK to give up arms. Turkey did suppress waves of Kurdish rebellions in the past without creating space for Kurdish aspirations, and each suppression was followed by a more formidable and more violent rebellion.
Turkey’s embrace of a political process—instead of simply pursuing a decisive military path—to end the conflict made it more acceptable to the PKK leadership and the Kurdish movement. Abdullah Ocalan, the leader of the PKK, had to persuade his comrades to dissolve their organization, abandon the armed struggle, and choose political struggle. Unfavorable broader regional trends against armed militancy may have helped convince Ocalan and his comrades to make that consequential choice.
The legitimacy of the political solution, in the eyes of the Kurds, determines its sustainability and transformative impact. The current peace process seeks to end the insurgency and transform the struggle for Kurdish rights and aspirations into a nonviolent political one. It could transform Turkey’s relations with its own Kurdish community and the Kurdish communities in Iraq, Syria, and Iran. Leaders of the Kurdish movement believe that they can achieve more through politics than through armed struggle, and that it isn’t only they who are transforming, but that the state, political, and legal systems in Turkey can also change. The promise of the future, rather than being beholden to the grievances of the past, is the way forward.
The Turks and the Kurds managed it without relying on foreign peacemakers or mediation. The disarmament and demobilization process for the PKK was designed, executed, and monitored domestically, without involving any foreign mediators. The talks were held between Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization, Ocalan, and several other leaders of his group based in the Qandil Mountains in Iraqi Kurdistan and across Europe. The process involved the Turkish parliament and political parties through a Parliamentary Committee, formed in Aug. 2025 to work on legal and political dimensions of the PKK’s dissolution, which helped garner broad support for the peace process across political divides in Turkey.
Turkey and the Kurds have entered a new phase that demands greater buy-in for the peace process from politicians, lawmakers, ordinary people, and from the institutions that will implement the new law. To ensure the peace process has broader societal support, the political class will need to make clear why it matters and what it promises. The stakes of getting that right are high for Turkey and extend beyond its borders.
Seeing like a state
The nation-state in the 20th century largely adopted a conception of nationhood based on a single identity and was intolerant, assimilationist, or exclusionary toward other identities. The effect was to politicize and mobilize the very groups it sought to submerge. This was true of Turkey as well. The Turkish Republic was based on a single identity and an overly centralized state with its own insecurities, largely stemming from the traumatic experience during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.
Today, Turkey needs a new conception of the nation-state that is inclusive of different identity groups, and a new idea of a strong state that is premised on broader societal legitimacy. Centralization coupled with exclusion is a recipe for societal discontent, which weakens, rather than strengthens, the state. Turkey’s real challenge is building an inclusive national identity that recognizes distinct identity groups without losing the thread of what binds them together. The task of the ongoing Kurdish peace process, and the Kurdish politics that will follow it, will be to achieve exactly this: an inclusive notion of national identity capacious enough to accommodate Kurdish identity and aspirations.
The current political mood in the Middle East and elsewhere is not one of militant groups and insurgencies. The broader trend runs toward their integration into state structures or their disarmament and demobilization. How these processes of demobilization and integration are carried out will be highly consequential. If they rely solely on coercion, rather than embracing persuasion and the prospect of mutual transformation, disarmament risks being a prelude to the next cycle of violence, waged under new names and banners.
Demobilization of insurgent groups succeeds when it rests on the prospect of mutual transformation. The armed groups dissolve themselves and remake themselves as political actors, who cease to be adversaries of the state and work as agents of its transformation.
The state and the polity, in turn, must transform alongside them, arriving at a more inclusive conception of national and geopolitical identity. In Turkey, it would mean embracing Kurdishness and honoring Kurdish political, democratic, and cultural rights, and regarding the Kurds outside of Turkey’s borders not as threats but as allies.
The PKK’s demobilization will reshape Turkey’s threat perception, and with it, Turkey’s approach to Kurds in Iraq, Syria, Iran and their countries. Already, in step with the pace of the PKK disarmament, the language used by Turkish officials and Kurdish actors across the region towards each other has improved significantly.
Fruits of peace
Turkey and its neighborhood have already benefited from the peace process and the demobilization of the PKK. That process faced two formidable tests in Syria and Iran and passed both. Turkey treated the PKK’s demobilization at home and the integration of Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF)—led by a Kurdish militia with close ties to the PKK—into the Syrian state as parts of a single process.
After the fall of the Assad regime, reuniting a fractured Syria became one of the most formidable tasks for the new government. The SDF controlled almost a quarter of Syrian territory. Limited fighting and military pressure earlier in the year helped shift the balance, stripping the SDF of a large portion of the land it had held.
What helped make the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state relatively smooth was the peace process already underway in Turkey, given the SDF’s close ties to the PKK. August brought two momentous developments: Turkey’s parliament passed the landmark legislation providing for the disbanding of the PKK, the reintegration of its fighters and the dismissal of charges against thousands of its sympathizers and prisoners; and the SDF announced its own dissolution.
A parallel drama played out during the Iran War. There were fears that the Iranian Kurdish militant group known as the Party for Free Life in Kurdistan, or the PJAK, might join the American war against Iran. Given its close ties to the PKK, such a move could have weakened the PKK’s commitment to disarmament and risked a new phase of conflict among Turkey, the PKK, and the PJAK. Despite pressure from the Trump Administration and Israeli plans to draw them into the conflict, Iranian Kurdish groups stayed out of the war. The peace process in Turkey was a major factor in persuading them to remain on the sidelines.
Together, the Syrian and Iranian cases reveal the power of political imagination and legitimacy in advancing national security. In both instances, Turkey has achieved more through political engagement than through military force. Any national security doctrine devoid of political imagination or legitimacy remains incomplete. The tests posed by Syria and Iran have demonstrated the PKK’s commitment to demobilization, confirmed that its decision is strategic rather than merely tactical, and helped build trust between Turkey and the PKK.
This process will also have considerable implications for Turkey’s relations with major powers. No issue has bedeviled Turkish-American relations more than the Syrian civil war did before the collapse of the Assad regime. At its core, that crisis reflected the conflicting American and Turkish approaches to the Syrian Kurds, specifically the People’s Protection Units (YPG), a PKK affiliate that, with American military advice and support, was later rebranded as the SDF.
By enabling the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state, the PKK’s demobilization has removed the most formidable sticking point in Turkish-American relations, clearing the way for closer cooperation between the two countries in Syria and beyond. Ocalan framed the recently passed Turkish law as the first step of a 1000 kilometer journey. The Turkish model, and the peace it promises, are still a story in the making. Despite the milestones already reached, formidable challenges remain, demanding persistence and commitment.
No two conflicts or two peace processes are alike. Yet the central message is universal: peace is possible and leadership matters. Long-running conflicts around identity are not fates to be endured but political questions to be settled. In a world still defined by war and insecurity, the story of peacemaking is, inherently, a global one.

title: Pearce ready to carve place in AFL history with Freo
content:
Fremantle captain and Tasmanian export Alex Pearce leads team into AFL grand final
In short:
Tasmanian footballer Alex Pearce can create history on Saturday by becoming the Fremantle Football Club's first-ever AFL premiership captain.
Pearce was born and raised on Tasmania's north-west coast, where resilience is bred, and sport reigns supreme.
What's next?
On Saturday, Fremantle face the Brisbane Lions, who are chasing a three-peat, having won the previous two years in a row.
If Fremantle wins the AFL premiership, the year 1995 will not only be known as the year the Dockers entered the AFL.
It'll be known as the birth year of the club's first-ever premiership captain.
Ruth Forrest was not only there on June 9, 1995, at the North West Regional Hospital in Burnie — she was the midwife who delivered Alex Pearce into the world.
"He was a beautiful, big baby," she says.
"And when you hold these babies in your hand after they're born, there's just this unlimited potential in every child."
Thirty-one years later, Pearce stands on the doorstep of football immortality.
Ms Forrest, who Tasmanians know as the independent member for Murchison in the state's upper house, has kept tabs on Pearce since he was a newborn.
"He's just this genuine, inspirational leader. That's what he is," she said.
"To see him grow up into that, it must be huge pride for his family, and I share a tiny bit of that."
Young Alex wanted to play cricket at the MCG
Forrest may have delivered Pearce, but it was parents Scott and Karen who raised him on the coast, in the cradle of Tasmanian sport.
Mum and sister Georgia were star equestrian riders, while Dad was a gun cricketer for Ulverstone.
He still umpires and administers the regional competition, while Uncle Jason remains as president of the Ulverstone Cricket Club.
For young Alex, cricket was the great constant.
"I played my last game of cricket ever with Alex, in a second grade grand final," Scott said.
But footy was in the blood too.
Grandfather Wayne Pearce was a goal machine for the Ulverstone Robins in the 1960s.
"As a kid growing up, his main aim was to play in a Boxing Day Test at the MCG in cricket,"Scott said.
"It's funny how things work out. He's now going to play at the MCG in a grand final as captain of an AFL team, so he got there in the end."
Scott still has to remind himself that his son is indeed on the brink of becoming an AFL premiership captain — a title he never thought Alex would hold.
"Christ, no," he said.
"We knew he had some ability as a junior; he had a growth spurt, played one year with the Tassie Mariners. He didn't play too bad."
"But he wasn't a stand-out player. He was okay," he said.
Out of nowhere, Pearce, who stands 200 centimetres, was drafted to the Dockers at pick 37 in 2013.
From there, he flourished, and the traits that would see him named Dockers captain began to blossom — loyalty, justice and trademark north-west coast resilience that was tested when he fractured his leg twice and didn't play for almost two years.
He forged a connection with a number of Fremantle's First Nations players and began to explore and celebrate his own identity as a Palawa man.
It's a pursuit that his dad is particularly proud of, and that inspired him to delve into his own ancestry.
"It's something I need to do more of, but I'm glad that I've looked into a little bit of it so far," he said.
"As a rule, you didn't look too much into that in years gone by, when I was a kid and in early adulthood.
"But we're very proud of the way he represents the Indigenous people of Tasmania, and it's something he's very proud of as well"
Ulverstone painting the town purple
Then came the confidence, and the individuality.
During COVID, Pearce decided to grow his hair out and pierce his own nose.
Scott said he "doesn't care much about that stuff" — but that he took the news of the piercing "better than his mother did".
Scott's job requires him to be on the road, hopping between Ulverstone, Devonport and Burnie.
His shifts run a little longer, due to locals bailing him up to talk footy, cricket and Alex.
It's indicative of a region where town rivalries are put aside when a coastal son or daughter succeeds.
"We're a footy family and we know Alex personally," Kim Smith, owner of Urban Surf and Co in Ulverstone, said.
"When they won the other night, his mum said to paint the town purple, so we thought why not."
Local real estate agent Jakub Lehman is on board too.
"That's what small communities are there for," he said.
The entire coast is aware of the history that Pearce stands to create if the Dockers defeat Brisbane.
He'd become the third-ever Tasmanian premiership captain, behind the iconic Darrel Baldock and Royce Hart.
And he'd also become the first-ever First Nations-identifying premiership captain.
But to his family, he will still just be Alex — or "Moose".
"That's probably one of the great traits," his dad said.
"He hasn't changed. He hasn't got ahead of himself or anything like that"
"He's just a boy from Ulverstone."

title: «Las lenguas y culturas indígenas están sobreviviendo, y seguirán sobreviviendo»: Entrevista con Kshetrabasi Juanga, escritor en lengua juang
content:
Este artículo es parte de la serie «Spotlight» de Global Voices de agosto de 2026, «Derechos indígenas«. Esta serie ofrece una visión de las vidas y experiencias de los pueblos indígenas con el fin de establecer vínculos entre regiones, destacar las experiencias indígenas y contar historias de líderes, activistas, miembros de la comunidad y otras personas. Puedes apoyar esta cobertura con una donación.
La mayoría de los idiomas del mundo son hablados principalmente, no escritos. Por lo tanto, el conocimiento de las comunidades hablantes es oral, pero Wikipedia y otros proyectos de Wikimedia requieren citas escritas.
OpenSpeaks Archives está desarrollando un proceso para que los wikimedistas puedan citar el conocimiento oral de comunidades indígenas y otras comunidades lingüísticas con pocos recursos, que incluyen casi 20 comunidades lingüísticas de India, Nepal y Sri Lanka. Este proceso incluye documentación audiovisual, creación de recursos tecnológicos y educativos, y fortalecimiento de las capacidades de la comunidad.
Esta serie de entrevistas recoge las historias de algunos de nuestros colaboradores que documentan el conocimiento oral a través de medios audiovisuales. La primera es con Kshetrabasi Juanga, educador, escritor y hablante de la lengua juang, lengua indígena en peligro de extinción con alrededor de 30,000 hablantes del estado de Odisha, al este de India.
Opino Gomango y Subhashish Panigrahi entrevistaron a Kshetrabasi Juanga en nombre de Rising Voices, presencialmente y por teléfono, respectivamente. A continuación presentamos una entrevista en video con Kshetrabasi Juanga realizada por Opino Gomango para OpenSpeaks Archives, que está disponible al público bajo una licencia Creative Commons.
Kshetrabasi Juanga (KJ): Some work has been done. The Odisha government has worked on the language through the MLE program. The Academy of Tribal Language & Culture (ATLC) has published tri-language books. The Eastern Regional Language Centre (ERLC) has published a primer and a grammar book. The Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) conducted a significant research programme on Juang. But our people, society, and culture — our festivals, marriage ceremonies and songs — are rarely documented.
Kshetrabasi Juanga (KJ): Se ha hecho algo al respecto. El Gobierno de Odisha ha trabajado en el idioma a través del programa MLE. La Academia de Lenguas y Culturas Tribales (ATLC) ha publicado libros en tres idiomas. El Centro Regional de Lenguas del Este ha publicado un libro de lectura para principiantes y un libro de gramática. El Instituto Central de Lenguas Indias llevó a cabo un importante programa de investigación sobre el juang. Pero nuestro pueblo, nuestra sociedad y nuestra cultura, nuestras fiestas, ceremonias de matrimonio y canciones rara vez se documentan.
Rising Voices (RV): ¿Qué tan útil es la documentación audiovisual para tu idioma?
KJ: This is helpful and a welcome step. Juang is shifting. But while globalisation is bringing more languages to people through technology, our language and culture risk becoming stagnant. Documentation is essential, and that is why this work matters.
Imagine someone from the next generation doing their PhD on tribal languages and cultures. When they do, they will find a great deal of information waiting for them. It will also be invaluable for young speakers. Today’s children are tomorrow’s young people, and if they one day watch videos in Juang, they will feel that some effort has been made to preserve what is theirs. Those videos will remain on Wikipedia and beyond.Suppose a recording is made today, in 2026. When someone listens to it decades from now, they will be able to understand how the language was gradually changing, how a culture was being challenged, and how it survived. I think of it like a bitumen road. In some places, the surface has cracked, the bitumen risen, and green grass has pushed through. I see our language like that green grass surviving despite countless vehicles crushing it every day. No matter how globalised the world becomes, Indigenous languages and cultures are surviving, and will continue to survive.
KJ: Es útil y representa un paso positivo. El juang está cambiando. Pero aunque la globalización acerca más idiomas a las personas a través de la tecnología, nuestro idioma y nuestra cultura corren el riesgo de estancarse. La documentación es esencial, y por eso este trabajo es importante.
Imagina que alguien de la próxima generación haga su doctorado sobre lenguas y culturas tribales. Al prepararlo, encontrará que lo espera una gran cantidad de información. También será invalorable para los jóvenes hablantes. Los niños de hoy son los jóvenes de mañana, y si algún día ven videos en juang sentirán que se ha hecho un esfuerzo por preservar lo que es suyo. Esos videos permanecerán en Wikipedia y otros sitios.
Supongamos que hoy, en 2026, se hace una grabación. Cuando alguien la escuche dentro de décadas podrá comprender cómo la lengua fue cambiando gradualmente, cómo una cultura se vio amenazada y cómo sobrevivió. Lo veo como una carretera de asfalto. En algunos lugares, la superficie se ha agrietado, el asfalto se ha levantado y la hierba verde ha brotado. Veo nuestra lengua como esa hierba verde que sobrevive a pesar de que innumerables vehículos la aplastan todos los días. No importa cuán globalizado se vuelva el mundo, las lenguas y culturas indígenas están sobreviviendo y seguirán sobreviviendo.
RV: ¿Cómo ayudará la documentación audiovisual a los hablantes de juang?
KJ: It will be very helpful, especially for those interested in our language and culture. It will mean a great deal to young children aged three to twelve. From a child psychology perspective, children in that age range can learn multiple languages and cultures simultaneously. What we are building now will serve them directly.
And how about subtitling/captioning documented audio/video?
Consider two groups of Juang speakers. There are those who have moved away from rural areas due to urbanisation, perhaps one per cent live in cities today. If a Juang person living in a city comes across this documentation, it will feel like history to them. They will find self-respect and feel proud.And then there are those who remain in their communities, holding on to a way of life that carries deep moral value. In the Juang tradition, if four or five people are walking together, holding bows, arrows, and spears, it signals that sad news is coming that someone in a village has passed away. Such traditions carry meaning that cannot easily be written down. Or consider how our mothers collect firewood: They go out, gather dry wood and twigs, stack them, and break branches piece by piece. No one else takes those branches everyone knows someone has kept them there. That trust, that unspoken moral code, is something a society outside our community can learn from. The subtitles help them understand. To me, documenting these traditions will create an invaluable resource for the entire humankind.
KJ: Será de gran ayuda, especialmente para quienes tengan interés en nuestra lengua y cultura. Significará mucho para los niños pequeños de tres a doce años. Desde la perspectiva de la psicología infantil, los niños de ese rango de edad pueden aprender múltiples lenguas y culturas simultáneamente. Lo que estamos construyendo ahora les servirá directamente.
¿Y qué hay de subtitular o añadir leyendas al material de audio y video documentado?
Pensemos en dos grupos de hablantes de juang. Están los que se han alejado de las zonas rurales por la urbanización, quizás el 1% vive hoy en ciudades. Si un juang que vive en una ciudad se encuentra con esta documentación, le parecerá historia. Encontrará autoestima y se sentirá orgullosa.
Y luego están quienes permanecen en sus comunidades, aferrándose a un modo de vida que encierra un profundo valor moral. En la tradición juang, si cuatro o cinco personas caminan juntas y llevan arcos, flechas y lanzas, eso indica que se avecinan malas noticias: que alguien en la aldea ha muerto. Esas tradiciones encierran un significado que no se puede plasmar fácilmente por escrito. O pensemos en cómo nuestras madres recogen leña: salen, juntan madera seca y ramitas, las apilan y rompen las ramas una por una. Nadie más toma esas ramas; todos saben que alguien las ha dejado ahí. Esa confianza, ese código moral tácito, es algo de lo que una sociedad ajena a nuestra comunidad puede aprender. Los subtítulos les ayudan a entender. Para mí, documentar estas tradiciones creará un recurso invaluable para toda la humanidad.
OG: ¿Cómo has contribuido a subsanar las brechas en la documentación de la lengua y la cultura juang?
KJ: I’m documenting our traditional knowledge through my YouTube channel, Majang Studio Vlogger. It has videos on how to ignite a fire with stones and how to take shelter under palm leaves during the rainy season. It’s so hard to record these in books. I couldn’t record as well as expected, but I’m trying. People are moving away from many traditional techniques. I continue to share my identity as an Adivasi through whatever means are available. More documentation needs to be done on a scale.
KJ: Estoy documentando nuestro conocimiento tradicional a través de mi canal de YouTube, Majang Studio Vlogger. Tiene videos sobre cómo encender un fuego con piedras y cómo refugiarse bajo hojas de palma durante la temporada de lluvias. Es muy difícil registrar esto en libros. No pude grabarlo tan bien como esperaba, pero lo estoy intentando. La gente se está alejando de muchas técnicas tradicionales. Sigo difundiendo mi identidad como adivasi a través de cualquier medio disponible. Es necesario hacer más documentación a gran escala.

title: How Indigenous Protected Areas became a vital way to protect nature in Australia
content:
When you think of conservation in Australia, chances are you’ll think of a national park.
But there’s another fast-growing way of conserving land: Indigenous Protected Areas (IPAs). These areas of land or sea Country are voluntarily dedicated by Traditional Owners to protect nature and cultural values and responsibilities.
Once dedicated, an IPA becomes part of Australia’s National Reserve System – our network of protected areas. To protect the area, Indigenous rangers tackle invasive species and undertake cultural burning and many other tasks.
In 2022, the Australian government signed up to an international pledge to protect 30% of lands and waters by 2030. This is one reason why IPAs have grown so rapidly in recent years.
In July, 4.7 million hectares of the Simpson Desert was dedicated as the newest protected area – the Pmere Atherre Antenterreme IPA.
Maintaining the success of Indigenous Protected Areas will require long-term funding, strong Indigenous governance and complementary conservation elsewhere.
How does this work?
While national parks are established and managed by governments, IPAs are Indigenous-led.
After deciding to establish an IPA, Traditional Owners develop a management plan and determine how Country is to be cared for, drawing on Indigenous knowledge and contemporary conservation science.
Caring for Country means looking after plants, animals, water, fire, sacred places and cultural practices as part of an interconnected whole.
Declaring an IPA doesn’t change existing tenure arrangements. For example, an IPA can cover freehold Indigenous land, land granted under land-rights legislation, Indigenous-held leasehold or pastoral land, Crown land and marine areas.
From pilot program to over half of Australia’s reserve system
In 1998, Nantawarrina became Australia’s first Indigenous Protected Area. The former pastoral station in South Australia’s Flinders Ranges was heavily degraded. Over the following decades, the Nipapanha people worked to restore the land and its biodiversity.
There are now 96 IPAs across Australia, spanning 113 million hectares. That’s almost 15% of the continent. Marine IPAs cover a smaller portion of Australian waters – 9.3 million hectares, or about 1.1% of our marine estate.
The growth of IPAs has far outstripped the growth of other types of conservation land. IPAs now make up more than 55% of lands protected in Australia’s National Reserve System.
Across all types of protection – both government and non-government – 25% of Australia’s land is now protected and 24% of seas are highly-protected “no-take” areas where fishing is banned.
The largest IPAs lie in Australia’s deserts, some of the world’s largest uncleared arid ecosystems. They form part of a vast, culturally-connected landscape shaped by Indigenous stewardship over tens of thousands of years.
People who care for Country
At the heart of Indigenous Protected Areas are Indigenous rangers, who combine cultural practice and traditional knowledge with contemporary conservation practices.
Ranger teams began growing in number from 2007, when dedicated federal funding became available. The program is now called the Indigenous Rangers Program.
No two Indigenous ranger programs are alike – each is locally led and grounded in Traditional Owner priorities. The program of work can include burning to prevent large wildfires or maintain cultural practice and care for Country.
Rangers look after cultural sites and culturally important species, and protect threatened species by managing threats, monitoring how populations are faring and undertaking surveys and research to find out more about them.
Rangers and researchers have worked together to combine Indigenous knowledge with new technologies such as drones, satellite imagery and environmental DNA to better understand how Country is changing and inform its care.
Ranger programs also create local jobs, stronger community governance and opportunities for Elders to pass on language, cultural knowledge and practical skills to younger generations. These programs show that caring for Country can deliver environmental, cultural and social benefits.
Many Indigenous Protected Areas welcome visitors, offering cultural and nature-based tourism, walking, camping, fishing and guided experiences. Access rules do vary. Some have restricted access at certain times, or require permission to enter. These arrangements reflect Indigenous ownership and management.
How are these areas funded?
Like many other protected areas, IPAs are publicly funded. The Australian government gives funds to declare and manage new IPAs through protected area and Indigenous ranger programs. Some state governments provide extra support to ranger teams.
However, these funds usually only cover a fraction of the costs of managing Country in this way. IPAs with ranger programs receive just over A$1 per hectare from government funding. By comparison, national park funding varies from around $16 per hectare in Queensland to $58 per hectare in NSW. State governments largely fund national parks.
Many Indigenous organisations try to augment funding with income from carbon projects, philanthropic grants, research partnerships and environmental management contracts. This financial uncertainty creates a large administrative workload.
Can we make these areas even stronger?
As this approach to conservation matures, our growing reliance on IPAs as a key conservation approach should be matched by increased funding and capability support.
It also makes sense to invest more in monitoring and reporting to track environmental, cultural and social benefits, and to pinpoint any areas to strengthen. Better data will also help policymakers know how Australia is tracking towards our commitments to the Global Biodiversity Framework.
Indigenous Protected Areas are working well. But they’re not the answer to every conservation challenge. They complement but do not replace other protected areas. The complex land tenures of the more heavily cleared and densely populated areas on Australia’s east coast makes it more challenging to declare new IPAs here, for instance.
As Australia works towards its conservation goals, it will rely more and more on Indigenous Protected Areas. But we believe the success of these areas speaks to something much deeper – the fact that Australia’s oldest systems of caring for Country is still one of the most effective ways to conserve nature.

title: Exhibition Centre comes alive with tradition, talent and flavour of Guyana’s First Peoples
content:
Arts, craft and Indigenous cuisine are taking centre stage at the Amerindian Heritage Month exhibition at the Exhibition Centre Sophia, providing all Guyanese with an opportunity to experience and celebrate the rich traditions of the country’s First Peoples.
The exhibition is among a number of activities being held throughout September as Guyana observes Amerindian Heritage Month, creating a platform for Indigenous artisans, entrepreneurs and producers to showcase their talents, products and culture.
Among the exhibitors is Danesh Camacho of Hummingbird Products, who is offering a variety of locally produced sauces and other products, along with Indigenous-inspired cuisine.
Camacho said the celebrations provide an important opportunity for persons, particularly those living in Georgetown and other coastal communities, to gain a deeper understanding and appreciation of Indigenous heritage.
“When September comes around, a lot of the Georgetown population would have an opportunity to partake in Indigenous cuisines, buy the crafts and partake in Indigenous culture that they wouldn’t normally get access to,” he explained.
He noted that the exhibition also helps to stimulate Indigenous economies by creating markets for entrepreneurs and opening opportunities for business partnerships.
Meanwhile, Indigenous craftswoman Morna Ferreira is displaying a variety of handcrafted items made from tibisiri, including jewellery boxes, placemats and fruit bowls.
Ferreira, has been participating in exhibitions for about twenty years, she explained that her craft has played an important role in supporting her family.
As a single parent of five children, she said the income earned from producing and selling her crafts helped her to raise her children and provide for their needs.
She encouraged Guyanese to support Indigenous artisans and use the exhibition as an opportunity to learn more about Amerindian culture.
“Come out, you could see different things, you could learn from it as well,” Ferreira encouraged.
The exhibition is also providing opportunities for other Indigenous artisans to display their creativity.
Cheryl, an exhibitor from the Mouraikubai community, is showcasing a range of handmade items, including headdresses, earrings, outfits and other craft pieces.
She said she was happy to be part of the Heritage Month celebrations and encouraged Guyanese to support the exhibitors throughout the observance.
Another exhibitor, Don Calbert, is using the occasion to showcase traditional Indigenous items, including fish traps, baskets, jewellery and other handcrafted pieces.
He said the exhibition gives Indigenous peoples an opportunity to proudly display their culture and traditions while interacting with fellow Guyanese and members of Indigenous communities.
The Heritage Month activities are not only helping to preserve and promote Guyana’s Indigenous traditions but are also creating valuable economic opportunities for artisans, entrepreneurs and producers.
Through initiatives such as the exhibition, Guyanese are being encouraged to experience the country’s rich cultural diversity while supporting Indigenous businesses and the preservation of traditional knowledge and skills.
Amerindian Heritage Month celebrations will continue until September 30, with several activities planned, including an Amerindian Heritage Dinner, school tours and an Amerindian Heritage Safari.
The month-long observance continues to provide a platform for Guyana’s First Peoples to celebrate, preserve and showcase their unique culture, traditions, talents and significant contributions to national development.

title: South Africa: Thousands of Zulu women gather for reed dance ceremony
content:
Tradition
Bright outfits and dancing filled the streets of Ingwavuma, in South Africa's southeastern KwaZulu-Natal province on Saturday, as thousands of young zulu women gethered to take part in the annual Reed Dance ceremony.
Every September, young women, locally known as "maidens", head to the royal palace to present a long reed to Zulu King Misuzulu kaZwelithini.
For participant Sno’thando, the event is a way of preserving tradition.
"We are here to be taught how to respect ourselves, our bodies, and remember our culture and preserve it for the coming generations," she says.
For the participants, the reed is a symbolic gesture implying their commitment to maintaining a tradition passed down through generations.
Participants aso view it as a way of looking after themselves. Cebisa Ntshangeni says "it's important because this continues to encourage us to look after ourselves, we love it and most of the time it's in your heart that when you are a maiden you must look after yourself until its time to get married."
The event is also attended by members of the royal family, traditional Zulu regiments and instructors who accompany the participants. Among those who gathered for the ceremont on Saturday is 71-year-old Mam’Mahlinsa, who came with girls from her region.
"My name is Mom Mahlinza, and I am responsible for the girls from Elangeni here in Ngwavuma. Today we are here accompanying the girls [ed. maidens], in this celebration of the reeds, here in Ngwavuma, whereby the young ones, the ‘pure’ girls who have looked after themselves as maidens, come here to the royal house to bring “Ngangezwelakhe” [ed. the King] the reeds , showing that they are still looking after themselves as maidens, and remain like that," she says.
Singing and dancing took place throughout the ceremony. The yearly gathering remains an important expression of Zulu cultural identity, bringing together generations and preserving a tradition that has been ongoing for centuries.

title: Scotland's first 'fire dog' is honoured with statue in Glasgow Central
content:
Scotland's first 'fire dog' is honoured with statue in Glasgow Central
- Published
For several years he was a familiar sight on the streets of Glasgow, racing towards blazes just ahead of the city's firemen.
Now Scotland's first ever "fire dog" - a setter-collie called Wallace - has been honoured in the city with a statue, 104 years after he died.
Wallace was taken in by firemen at the Central Fire Station in 1894 after he followed a horse-drawn engine taking part in a lifeboat demonstration, and became well-known around the city.
The new statue is at Glasgow Central railway station, following several years of campaigning by Possilpark woman Jean Dallas.
Wallace was most famous for running about 20 or 30 yards in front of horse-drawn fire appliances as they made their way to emergencies, taking direction from a coachman.
He would then sit next to the tethered horses, guarding them until the men returned.
The bond he had with the firemen was such that they paid to have him embalmed after his death in 1902.
Legend states that his heroic reputation grew to such an extent that he was once gifted a set of rubber boots to protect his paws by an elderly woman who saw him limping due to stone sets in the road.
Allegedly he only wore them once, as he promptly lost two of the four boots on the way back from a call-out.
After being embalmed and encased, he sat "on guard" in the foyer of the North Glasgow fire service headquarters at Cowcaddens and then at the Strathclyde Fire Brigade headquarters in Hamilton, before moving to a fire service museum in Greenock.
The boots form part of the new sculpture at Central Station, which Jean Dallas hopes will help introduce his story to a new generation.
She first became aware of the fire-fighting pooch in 2017, following a trip to the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service Heritage Centre and Museum in Greenock - where Wallace remains encased and on display.
Jean, 81, told BBC Scotland News: "I just fell in love with the story and thought we needed to get him back home to Glasgow.
"I did a lot of fundraising, everything from making tablet to doing arts and crafts, and the money went towards this (the statue).
"He had a lot of courage, he helped people and was brave. It's a great story."
Jean even raised money while abroad, after telling other holidaymakers about the story of Wallace.
A variety of groups came together to work on the sculpture, with Jean fundraising for a plinth.
People in custody at HM Prison Barlinnie stepped forward to sculpt the artwork, which eventually found a home at Central Station after Network Rail heard the story of Wallace.
The tune I Belong To Glasgow was played on bagpipes as Wallace's statue was unveiled on Tuesday.
City of Glasgow Group Commander Craig Campbell represented the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service at the unveiling.
He said: "Wallace is a local and fire service legend, and this is a fitting celebration of his life and another reminder of the proud history the service shares with Glasgow."
Mick Stoney, the governor of HMP Barlinnie, added the prisoners involved in the meeting had taken great pride "in bringing an important piece of Glasgow's history to life" through the statue.
Support for the new statue also came from other sources, including the social landlord ng Homes.
