title: Beyond the screen: The untold stories of India’s revolutionaries
content:
Beyond the screen: The untold stories of India’s revolutionaries
The descendants of the revolutionaries portrayed in the recently released Amazon Prime series reveal the personal sacrifices, family struggles and transnational networks that sustained India’s armed freedom struggle.
Written by Shriya Dasgupta and Oyeshi Ganguly
On September 11, Amazon Prime released The Revolutionaries, a web series based on economist and historian Sanjeev Sanyal’s 2023 bestseller, Revolutionaries: The Other Story of How India Won Its Freedom. The series explores lesser-known episodes of India’s militant nationalist movement, including the Delhi Conspiracy Case of 1912, the transnational Indo-German Conspiracy (1914-1917), the Battle of Buribalam (1915) and the Rodda Company arms heist (1914), bringing some of the forgotten revolutionaries and episodes back into public conversation.
Although these events unfolded in different parts of the country, they were connected by a broader network of revolutionaries spread across cities including Lahore, Amritsar, Ambala, Delhi, Dehradun, Benaras, Calcutta, Chandernagore and Balasore.
In an interview with the oral history project Agnijug Archive, Sanyal spoke about how both sides of his family had been involved in the freedom struggle, and how his book was, in part, an effort to document his family’s lesser-known history.
“On my father’s side of the family, many of them were involved in revolutionary activities with the Anushilan Samiti, Ghadar movement, and were acquaintances of Rash Behari Bose,” he says.
Sanyal’s is one of more than 70 family stories Agnijug Archive has recorded since its inception in July 2022.
Tragic, brave but always humane, these stories put a human face to the names and events that have gathered dust in archives. Here are some of the personal stories shared by the families of the real-life revolutionaries portrayed in The Revolutionaries.
The birth of Bengal’s Revolutionary Movement
The advent of the revolutionary political movement in India can be traced to 1902, with the creation of the secret society Anushilan Samiti in Calcutta. What began as physical education and gymnasium clubs soon became a hub of anti-British revolutionary activities.
After Sri Aurobindo and his younger brother Barin Ghosh returned to Calcutta from Baroda following the Partition of Bengal in 1905, the Maniktala Secret Society was founded under Barin’s leadership. Unlike Sri Aurobindo, who advocated building the capacity to organise a violent armed uprising against the Empire, Barin believed in targeted assassinations.
The first phase of the revolutionary uprising, which began in 1906, saw several attempts to assassinate British officials and the first use of bombs. It reached a climax with the Alipore Bomb Trials (1908-09). The first phase of armed resistance in Bengal subsequently waned as many nationalist leaders were arrested and imprisoned in connection with the case.
Rash Behari Bose, the master of disguise
Rash Behari Bose, introduced in The Revolutionaries as a ‘beheroopiya’ (master of disguise), was a man who lived many lives. Growing up in the French colony of Chandernagore in the Hooghly district of the erstwhile Bengal Presidency, Bose was initiated into revolutionary politics at Dupleix College by its principal, Charu Chandra Roy, during 1903-04.
He was known for masterminding the 1912 Delhi-Lahore Conspiracy to assassinate Viceroy Lord Hardinge, and for his involvement in the 1915 Ghadar Conspiracy.
Speaking to Agnijug Archive, Indrani Basu, Bose’s niece, shares an anecdote about the aftermath of the Delhi Conspiracy of 1912, spearheaded by Bose. At the time, Bose was working as a head clerk at the Forest Research Institute in Dehradun. To avoid suspicion, he quickly slipped back to the institute, taking the night train from Delhi on the evening of the attack.
Indrani recounted how, on reaching the institute, Bose spearheaded a meeting condemning the attack on the Viceroy. “Further, when Lord Hardinge had moved to Dehradun for his recovery, Bose had even greeted the Viceroy with a bouquet, wished him get-well-soon messages, and prayed for his speedy recovery,” she said.
In 1915, Bose and Jatindranath Mukherjee, a founding member of Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar, secret societies that promoted armed revolution in Bengal, organised the Ghadar Mutiny, aimed at inciting a pan-India mutiny in the British Indian Army. During this period, several other secret societies emerged, including the Bengal Volunteers.
There was another anecdote from Bose’s years on the run. During a police raid on his hideout between 1914 and 1915, a servant opened the door and politely asked the officers to wait while he fetched the master of the house. After waiting in vain, the police stormed inside, only to find an empty home. The ‘servant’ who had casually greeted them was Bose himself, already long gone.
Bose later left for Japan in 1915, where he spent the rest of his life in exile. He played an instrumental role in the formation of the Indian National Army in Japan during the early 1940s.
Basanta Biswas and a fatal homecoming
Basanta Biswas was Bose’s comrade-in-arms and the revolutionary who threw the bomb at Lord Hardinge in 1912. Bose and Biswas were acquaintances, and the latter had been handpicked and trained by Bose for the attack on Viceroy Lord Hardinge. The two had also been together on the day of the attack in Delhi.
Tarun Biswas, a descendant of Basanta Biswas, challenges a detail entrenched in popular retellings of the 1912 attempt on the Viceroy, including its depiction in The Revolutionaries. The show depicts Basanta throwing the bomb at Hardinge from a Chandni Chowk rooftop while disguised as a woman. According to the family’s account, however, Bose changed the plan at the last moment.
Basanta had been trained to throw the bomb upwards, from a lower to a higher position. While the original plan required him to disguise himself as a woman to enter the courtyard reserved for women, Bose ultimately instructed him to change back into male clothing and throw the bomb from below.
Tarun also speaks of a betrayal that altered the course of his family’s history.
After nearly two years in hiding, 19-year-old Basanta secretly returned to his family home in Nadia on February 5, 1914, after learning of his father’s death. His return would lead to his arrest and, ultimately, his execution by hanging.
“Basanta had come home to perform his father’s last rites, and had travelled to his uncle’s house nearby to buy some materials required for the sraddha. There, his uncle’s relative, a certain Promothonath Biswas, a government servant eyeing a lucrative promotion, spotted Basanta and quietly reported his presence to the local police station.
“Basanta’s cousin and fellow revolutionary Manmatha Biswas, on getting a whiff of the impending police arrival, tried to warn Basanta and aid his escape, but it was too late. He was arrested two days before he could perform his father’s sraddha”, says Tarun.
Basanta was hanged at Ambala on May 11, 1915, aged 20. Despite repeated requests, his body was never returned to his family for the last rites.
Waiting for Jatin
When the First World War broke out, revolutionaries of the Jugantar group sought to procure arms from Europe and use them to overthrow British rule in India. The plan, known as the Indo-German Conspiracy, was developed with the support of the Berlin Committee in Germany and revolutionaries operating in India.
Jatindranath Mukherjee was one of Bose’s co-conspirators in the plot. The two also worked closely within the wider revolutionary network, with Bose coordinating efforts with secret societies across North India.
The Indo-German Conspiracy ultimately failed after some conspirators acted as police informers and revealed the plan to the British authorities. The ammunition the revolutionaries were expecting never reached them. Jatindranath was killed in a frontal battle with the police in Balasore, Odisha, during the Battle of Buribalam in September 1915, and Jugantar lost one of its most prominent leaders.
Despite this setback, revolutionaries continued trying to arrange weapons through the eastern Indian route via China and Assam under the leadership of Jadugopal Mukherjee, Jatindranath’s erstwhile foreign secretary and the man in charge of the group’s transnational dealings.
While the world remembers the bravado of Jatindranath, his granddaughter Manjusha Chatterjee remembers the price his family paid for it. When he died, he left behind a young widow and three children, aged two-and-a-half, five, and seven. But the sacrifices at home had begun long before his death.
“My Dadu (grandfather) would give away all of his monthly salary to the revolutionaries for nationalist activities,” Manjusha recalls. “So much so that, most months, my grandma Indubala had barely enough money to buy food for the family.
“Slowly, his fellow revolutionaries learnt of this precarious situation at home and decided to take matters into their own hands. On a particular payday, a friend approached Jatin and cried to him about a family member’s illness, saying he urgently needed money. Jatin gave away his entire salary, keeping only the money needed for the tram ride home. When he returned home empty-handed, the friend was already there. He smiled and said he had given the salary directly to Indubala, reprimanding Jatin that his generosity was becoming a cause for his family’s starvation.”
Manjusha recalls how Jatindranath’s death in 1915 left Indubala suspended between grief and hope. On hearing the news, she refused to believe that her husband was dead. Their family guru, Bholananda Giri, comforted her with the assurance that Jatindranath was alive and would one day return.
Indubala held on to those words for the rest of her life. Until her death in 1937, she continued to dress as a married woman, wearing sindoor and the sankha-pola (conch-shell bangles), as though Jatin had never left.
The inheritance of revolution
Sachindranath Sanyal was another prominent revolutionary of the period. Born in Varanasi into a Bengali family, he founded a branch of the revolutionary Anushilan Samiti in Patna in 1913 and took part in the Delhi Conspiracy against Viceroy Hardinge. He later played a role in planning the 1915 Ghadar Mutiny.
After Bose fled to Japan, Sachindranath emerged as one of the movement’s senior figures, mentoring younger revolutionaries including Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh.
The mutiny formed part of the broader Indo-German Conspiracy, which saw members of the Ghadar Party return from North America to Punjab to foment an anti-British uprising. The revolutionaries sought to coordinate a pan-Indian mutiny within the British-Indian Army in February 1915. Sachindranath played a key role in connecting revolutionary networks in eastern India with those in the north.
In 1924, he co-founded the Hindustan Republican Association (later HSRA) to pursue armed resistance against British rule. Convicted in the Banaras Conspiracy case (1917) and Kakori Conspiracy case (1925), Sachindranath was one of the few revolutionaries to be transported twice to the Cellular Jail in the Andamans, where he wrote his memoir, Bandi Jeevan. He died of tuberculosis in Gorakhpur jail in 1942.
Recalling Sachindranath’s role in the freedom struggle, his nephew Surajit Sanyal says their family home in Madanpura, Uttar Pradesh, was often frequented by revolutionaries like Sri Aurobindo even in the early years of armed struggle.
Sachindranath travelled to Calcutta to hand over money looted during the Kakori Robbery to barrister-politician and freedom fighter Chittaranjan Das, to support the then-young Subhas Chandra Bose’s dream of raising an army against the British.
Emphasising how the networks of secret societies operated across generations and regions, Surajit says Sachindranath not only inspired his brothers, all of whom became revolutionaries, but also helped raise Bhagat Singh as his political protégé.
Humanising the heroes
More than a century later, the stories of these revolutionaries reveal a dimension of India’s freedom struggle that is often overshadowed by better-known narratives of the nationalist movement.
Their lives demonstrate that the revolutionary struggle was not limited to isolated acts of violence or individual heroism. It was sustained by extensive networks of families, friends, sympathisers and ordinary people who took enormous personal risks.
As The Revolutionaries brings some of these forgotten figures back into public conversation, their descendants offer another way of understanding that history: through ordinary people who transcended extraordinary obstacles, and through the families who continued to live with the personal costs of the struggle for India’s freedom.
The writers are co-founders of the Agnijug Archive.

title: Western Arrernte man's journey of healing after problems with alcohol
content:
Western Arrernte man Tim McNamara yarns about alcohol problems, encouraging others to change
Hermannsburg/Ntaria traditional owner Tim Tjupurrula McNamara describes himself as "a leader, a cultural man and storyteller".
The proud Western Arrernte man is a mentor to boys and men in his community.
He passes on traditional knowledge and builds relationships through activities such as making spears and boomerangs, working with the Hidden Valley Camp Community Centre, the Tangentyere Men's Behaviour Change Program and other groups.
"I am the good leader of the community, good leader of my families," he said.
But Mr McNamara says he has been on a journey to become the man he is.
"Before, I was just nothing. I was just nobody," he said.
Taking ownership
About 10 years ago, Mr McNamara was ordered by a court to attend the Central Australian Aboriginal Alcohol Programs Unit (CAAAPU), a drug and alcohol support service in Alice Springs.
"I was really struggling with my life," he said.
"I got into trouble so many times, drink and drive, domestic violence, and all sorts of things that were related to alcohol."
Mr McNamara completed his mandated program and returned to his community, but says friends and family again tempted him back down the "wrong roads", so he decided to return to the rehabilitation program, this time of his own volition.
"It was my choice to change," he said.
"CAAAPU was the place we was healed from the things that we do … I learned more about what I need in my life."
Sharing the message
Since then, Mr McNamara said he had been on a journey towards accountability and ownership of his own life, describing it as "freedom".
"Freedom means that you are men in charge for everything that you needed not to take the wrong choice," he said.
"I have more freedom and more space and more sharing, stories, connection about countries, the knowledge that you use and pass it on to others, especially the little people, for my grandchildren.
"We need to continue to do these things, as a man, as an Aboriginal man."
Mr McNamara returned to CAAAPU to share his story with other men and show them change is possible.
"My journey takes me quite a while, but it's more to learn and more to teach others to be men, to understand each other, what is our responsibility," he said.
Positive examples 'a catalyst for change'
CAAAPU chief executive Demian Coates said it was "wonderful" to see Mr McNamara sharing his story.
He said while there was a lot of focus on issues such as substance abuse, domestic violence, crime and health gaps in Indigenous communities, there were "literally thousands" of examples of people overcoming and tackling these challenges.
"It's good to hear the other side, where people have been at rock bottom, and they've changed their whole life," he said.
"It's an inspiration. It's a catalyst for change."

title: American doctor visited Kainchi Dham; Neem Karoli Baba changed his life
content:
In the early 1970s, American physician Dr. Larry Brilliant travelled to India and spent time at Neem Karoli Baba’s ashram at Kainchi Dham, seeking spiritual guidance during a period of personal uncertainty. Baba reportedly began calling him “Doctor America”. In an interview with Tricycle: The Buddhist Review, he said the spiritual guru later urged him to go to Delhi and work for the United Nations to help eradicate smallpox.
Brilliant eventually joined the World Health Organization’s smallpox eradication programme in India. His journey to the ashram and his work against the disease became closely connected in his later recollections. For Brilliant, the journey was deeply connected to his encounter with Neem Karoli Baba, whom he credited with giving his life a new direction.
When he recalled his conversation with Neem Karoli Baba
Brilliant recalled that the spiritual teacher had called him “Dr. America”.
In an interview published by Tricycle: The Buddhist Review in 2023, Dr. Larry Brilliant spoke about his time with Neem Karoli Baba and the teacher’s instruction to help eradicate smallpox. He said, “One day in July 1973, Neem Karoli Baba told me to go to Delhi immediately to work for the United Nations and help eradicate smallpox.”
Brilliant recalled that the spiritual teacher had called him “Dr. America”.
In the interview, he also spoke about the money he had with him and in America. “He (Neem Karoli Baba) said to me, Dr. America, because that was the name he had given me, Dr. America, how much money do you have? And that, you know, there's a whole other channel down which that goes. And I said, I have $500. He said, $500. You're lying. How much money do you have back in America?”
Brilliant then thought about the time he had worked as an emergency room doctor. “And I said, I have $500 in America too.” The conversation soon turned into a joke, as Brilliant remembered it. “And then he started to chant. You have to understand that everything was funny. Everything was a comedian. Everything was a joke. He turned every single moment into something funnier than you ever thought anything could ever be.”
Brilliant recalled Baba chanting about the money he had in India and the money he had in America. “And he started to chant $500 here, $500 there. You are no doctor, which is exactly what my mother had said to me. You can't make any money. You're not a real doctor.”
He recalled that Baba continued repeating the words, first in Hindi and then in English. “$500 here, $500 there. You are no doctor. U-N-O doctor.” It was then that the conversation took a turn Brilliant would remember for the rest of his life.
“United Nations organization. Dr. America is going to become a United Nations doctor. And you're going to work to help eradicate smallpox.” According to Brilliant’s recollection, Baba then spoke about the disease and its future. “Because this horrible disease is going to be lifted off of the back of humanity by God, who has a gift to humanity, will conquer this one form of suffering.”
From Kainchi Dham to the fight against smallpox
Brilliant’s account of his encounter with Neem Karoli Baba is closely connected to his later work in public health. He eventually joined the World Health Organization’s smallpox eradication programme in India. The WHO campaign became one of the most significant achievements in global public health.
In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated worldwide. It was the first human disease to be officially declared eradicated. For Brilliant, the memory of Kainchi Dham remained connected to his professional journey. In his recollections, Neem Karoli Baba’s words gave him a new direction and encouraged him to use his medical skills in the fight against smallpox.

title: Who is responsible for protecting and preserving Indigenous cultures?
content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights.” This series offers insight into the lives and experiences of Indigenous peoples to build connections across regions, center Indigenous experiences, and share the stories of leaders, activists, community members, and more. You can support this coverage by donating here.
There are 476 million Indigenous people in the world, about 6.2 percent of the global population. Though only 25 percent of the Earth’s landmass is left to be stewarded by these original inhabitants, they have long protected global biodiversity — often better than any official government programs and efforts. For hundreds of years, Indigenous groups have weathered colonization, violent settler occupation, oppression, and forced assimilation. Yet despite this dark past — which continues today in the 21st century — Indigenous people continue to fight for their fundamental rights and their own lands and resources.
As I read through the pieces Global Voices’ authors contributed to the August 2026 Spotlight series, “Indigenous Rights,” one common question stands out for me: Who gets to decide? We are past the question of whether Indigenous peoples deserve recognition, land, cultural, and political representation. The key is to ask who holds the power to grant or withhold, and who gets to decide on Indigenous identity, land, culture, safety, and profit.
Not all Indigenous peoples can claim their Indigenous identities because the state sometimes denies this right.
A genocide by the Ottoman Empire wiped out nearly 75 percent of the Assyrian people, and the Iraqi army led another genocide in 1933. Yet, not a single constitution of the region recognizes the Assyrians as an Indigenous people.
It took 30 years for Taiwan’s Siraya people to be officially recognized as Indigenous, but Japan’s Ryūkyūan people have only seen denials by the state. The Ryūkyūan were once removed from their own lands by the U.S. military during World War II. Decades later, the U.S. military continues to hoard Okinawan land through its military bases and destroy natural resources through unchecked pollution.
In Europe, “autochthonous,” perceived descendants of the original inhabitants, has become a discursive tool to promote nationalism and build hate against the “guests,” the immigrants. Ironically, depictions of Native American “heroes” in European popular culture have fuelled this.
While recognition as an Indigenous people is a critical first step for any Indigenous community, it does not always translate to decision-making. When Indigenous leaders in Nueva Vizcaya, the Philippines, organized an anti-mining rally, they were arrested and charged, with over 30 criminal cases filed against them. Brazil’s case was even scarier — 258 Indigenous people were murdered in 2025 for defending their land rights, according to Cimi (the Missionary Indigenist Council). In Thailand, mining activities are polluting the Kok River. Hundreds of villagers, Indigenous leaders, monks, and civil and environmental rights activists carried out a “peace walk” to defend their Indigenous cultural identity and a vital source of drinking water, irrigation, fisheries, and transportation.
Almost always, when the state goes against its Indigenous peoples, it is to extract the latter’s lands, waters, other natural resources, or community products. Lack of Indigenous recognition also translates to significant state control over lands and land-related decisions. China’s new cotton law mechanized cotton production, making the cotton supply chain state-traceable, state-inspectable, and state-governable through data. Concurrently, this policy coerced over seven million Uyghur, Tibetan, and other Indigenous farmers to use their own lands under significant government supervision. In northern Tanzania, the Indigenous Maasai lands are taken by the state in the name of environmental protection only to use them for tourism, hunting, and private investments.
All of these stories raise the original question — who gets to decide. When Indigenous communities control decisions, they are able to protect and nurture their lands, resources, languages, and cultures. For example, 14 members of the Kam community in Nigeria created 307 audiovisual recordings in the Kam language, which has 8,000–11,000 speakers, after receiving training from a linguist, buffering against the threat of language endangerment. In India, Kshetrabasi Juanga, an Indigenous educator, goes from village to village, documenting the endangered Juang language. Far away in Russia, the Buryat fashion designer Oksana Alkhunsaeva has created an occupation for herself that both employs and supports her whole family, and keeps the Buryat textile heritage alive.
The question of who gets to decide also shapes the impact of modernization on Indigenous communities. As Nepal’s Rana Tharu language is threatened due to the prioritization of English and Nepali, women often become the last line of defense, preventing the loss of local languages. Dambe, a martial art form of Nigeria’s Hausa tribe, sees the new safety measures, regulations, and modernization through organized tournaments as a welcome step. But YouTube contests that attract external participation and viewership are erasing the Hausa cultural heritage long associated with it.
There is a strong case for the protection of Indigenous knowledge, and even state support, when its economic value flows into the community. Ghana’s traditional medicine sector serves 60 to 70 percent of the population, as the profit-driven Western medicine market fails to make medicines affordable. The cassava, millet, and sorghum market is expanding across Africa, as these Indigenous crops are a better alternative to imported wheat- economical and gluten-free- opening potential for leading an international market. Indigenous knowledge and data are a core part of AI policies. As Chadian environmental activist Hindou Oumarou Ibrahim rightly puts it, “Indigenous peoples must be recognized as rights holders and decision-makers — especially when newfangled technology has implications for their lands or intellectual heritage.”
The state’s control over Indigenous bodies goes hand-in-hand with state surveillance. In Australia, Indigenous children are 23 times more likely to be under supervision and 28 times more likely to be in detention.
What really stands out for me is what Genner Llanes-Ortiz, a Mexican Mayan researcher, argues — most modern state structures have categorically failed to understand the Indigenous communities. These societies once lived on the lands that provide homes to the descendants of settler-colonists as well as those who arrived in other ways.
One important human aspect we may forget when discussing these issues is that the onus of protecting and preserving Indigenous cultures falls on individuals like Kshetrabasi Juang or Oksana Alkhunsaeva. There is an urgent need for resources — for more Indigenous individuals to collaborate before the few individual leaders burn out.

title: Indígenas waraos de Benítez presentaron ponencia y exposición sobre su cultura en el Ateneo de Carúpano
content:
El gobernador indígena warao, Venancio García, presentó en la sala de conferencias del Ateneo Luis Mariano Rivera de Carúpano, una ponencia para dar a conocer la cultura y la vida de esta etnia, asentada en el municipio Benítez.
El líder indígena estuvo acompañado por nativos waraos, quienes presentaron una exposición de artesanías y vestimentas de esa cultura.
García dijo que la intención es dar a conocer las creaciones de los indígenas, la medicina tradicional, sus bailes y en general, todo lo que los caracteriza desde lo sociocultural. La ponencia recogió todo lo relativo al territorio warao y sus vivencias.
En el territorio indígena habitan unos 2,500 miembros de la etnia, y conviven 7.500 personas (se incluyen personas de otras razas), en distintos poblados.
Señaló que el papel del gobernador aborigen es acompañar a los pobladores en todas sus necesidades y problemas.
”Debo estar presente con ellos y darles ánimos para seguir avanzando”, dijo.
Sucre/ Yumelys Díaz

title: Mary Goretti Kariaga: The Kenyan scientist who pioneered mushroom farming in Kenya
content:
Mary Goretti Kariaga: The Kenyan scientist who pioneered mushroom farming in Kenya
What you need to know:
- From plant pathology and sugarcane research to pioneering commercial mushroom production, Mary Goretti Kariaga built a remarkable career in Kenyan science and agriculture.
- Her journey took her from the University of Nairobi to Zimbabwe and back to Kenya, where she pioneered mushroom farming and trained aspiring growers.
On August 1, 1982, Mary Goretti Kariaga was in her third trimester of pregnancy with her first child when intense anxiety took hold of her. She was in her rented house in Arina, Kisumu, listening to KBC news of an emerging coup. She grew more worried as she wondered whether hospitals would be operational in time for her delivery.
Mary's father, John Joseph Odera, a successful entrepreneur, valued academic advancement. He funded her O-Levels at Loreto Girls in Limuru and her A-Levels at Kenya High School, instilling in her a strong drive for intellectual achievement. She enrolled at the University of Nairobi in 1975 and graduated four years later with a Bachelor of Education (Science).
She was recruited as an Agricultural Research Officer at the Kenya Agricultural Research Institute in Kibos, Kisumu. After the attempted coup, Mary safely delivered her first child, Patricia, on the night of August 17, 1982, at Kisumu's Victoria Hospital. She later travelled to Port Louis to spend three months at the Mauritius Sugar Industry Institute, studying the agronomy of sugarcane cultivation.
In 1986, she began her master's degree in plant pathology at the University of Nairobi, focusing on fungal, bacterial and nematode diseases. Her thesis centred on parasitic nematodes of sugar cane, and she later authored an academic manual titled Plant Parasitic Nematodes Associated with Sugar Cane at the Nyanza Sugar Belt. She also looked into the challenges of communal sugarcane farming and completed her studies in 1988, a year before giving birth to her son, Stephen.
She became a member of African Women in Science and Engineering, an associate of the International Network of Women Engineers and Scientists, and a founding scholar of the Kenya Professional Association of Women in Agriculture and Environment. Her expertise led to her appointment at the Lake Basin Development Authority's Fibre Research Station in Kibos.
In 1995, she began lecturing at Maseno University before moving with her family to Harare, Zimbabwe, on January 5, 1999, after her husband, Billy, was employed by the University of Zimbabwe. Her deep interest in fungi led her to start a botanical programme to study mushroom cultivation. She began culturing and bulking spawn (mushroom seeds), and in 2000, she started producing Agaricus bisporus (button mushrooms) at the secondary entrance to her home, at the back of the University of Zimbabwe campus.
Also read: Kabete's queen of mushroom farming
Mary held weekend mushroom training sessions for interested participants at her house and went on to study the production of other edible mushrooms, including Ganoderma lucidum, shiitake and Pleurotus ostreatus (oyster mushrooms).
In September 2001, she walked into Standard Chartered Bank on Bond Street at the Mount Pleasant Shopping Centre, within walking distance of the university. Suddenly, five armed men carrying AK-47 rifles rushed into the bank and ordered the crowd in Shona, "Vese rarai pasi! (Everybody lie down!).”
Because of the similarities between Shona and Swahili, both Bantu languages, Mary understood the order and lay face-down along with the other clients. An overweight white client appeared stunned and confused by the Shona commands until a rifle was pointed directly at his face. Because of his large belly, he ended up lying on his back instead of his stomach, while a terrified woman lying next to Mary began sobbing as the robbers collected money from the tellers.
In her book, The Woman Who Pioneered Mushroom Production in Kenya, Mary writes that minutes after the gunmen left with their loot, everyone remained frozen on the floor in fear. When a person walked in and whispered, “They've gone,” Mary was the first to get up and run out of the bank.
In 2002, she relocated to Kisumu, applied for a position at Maseno's Faculty of Botany, and began pursuing her long-term goal of fighting protein deficiency and raising income levels through mushroom production.
At the time, there were no individual commercial mushroom producers in Kenya. Mary set out to introduce mushroom farming to empower smallholder farmers using oyster mushrooms, which were highly resistant to infection, in high demand and had significant medicinal value.
Because of the uniqueness of her work in mushroom cultivation, Maseno called on her on July 29, 2004, to deliver the keynote presentation to President Mwai Kibaki at the annual Kisumu Agricultural Show. That morning, Kibaki, First Lady Lucy and their security detail listened in astonishment as Mary gave a compelling address on the potential of mushroom production.
Her passion caught the attention of KTN reporter David Ohito, who arranged an interview with Mary and filed a story with his colleague, sparking demand for mushrooms across Kenya. Mary began receiving calls from entrepreneurs requesting mushroom training, as interest in mushroom cultivation grew. She registered her company, Mount Pleasant Mushroom Consultants, named after her former residential suburb in Zimbabwe, and used it to partner different organisations.
She was later elected treasurer of the Universities' Academic Staff Union and negotiated a 50 per cent salary increment for lecturers during the 2007 nationwide strike, the highest lecturers' salary increment in Kenya's history.
In late 2007, Mary's research in sugarcane diseases caught the interest of the Faculty of Agriculture, Veterinary Science and Technology at Masinde Muliro University in Kakamega. She joined the institution and completed her PhD dissertation on Rice Blast, identifying a sequence of four races of the same pathogen, which were later registered at the National Centre for Biotechnology Information. Shortly after being promoted to senior lecturer at Masinde Muliro, she narrowly survived a harrowing carjacking at gunpoint at the entrance of her home.
The writer is a novelist, Big Brother Africa 2 Kenyan representative and founder of Jeff's Fitness Centre (@jeffbigbrother).

title: Participatory budgeting behind bars: Durham, North Carolina, gives incarcerated residents a say
content:
Since Durham, North Carolina, implemented participatory budgeting in 2018, its organizers say they have been intentional about inviting as many residents as possible to take part in the citywide initiative. The process gives anyone who lives or goes to school in Durham and is at least 13 years old a direct say in how the city spends a portion of its budget.
People incarcerated in the Durham County Detention Facility have been allowed to vote on spending decisions from the beginning, but they couldn’t participate in idea generation, proposal development and deliberation, according to staffers with PB Durham, which oversees participatory budgeting in the city. Program leaders saw a missed opportunity.
“One of the really important things for participatory budgeting is to elevate all of the Durham resident voices,” Carmen Ortiz, Durham’s assistant director of community partnerships and engagement, told Smart Cities Dive. “We have residents who are incarcerated who have really tight, strong connections to the community. So, for us, it was really important to engage them in the process.”
The city redesigned its PB program so it could run idea-collection sessions inside the jail and worked with the Durham County Sheriff’s Office to identify incarcerated residents who could serve as budget delegates. The expanded program received a 2026 Smart Cities Dive Community Project Award.
The detention facility residents evaluated budget proposals, meeting biweekly over an eight-week period and working one on one with PB Durham staff. They used iPads to access data from the Durham Neighborhood Compass, a public data platform, and Google Maps’ street view to evaluate projects and inspect sites from inside the jail.
“The iPads were really helpful,” said Durham Innovation Manager Lyndsay Gavin. “We would [look at] a street view of a park, and then some of the participants would be like, ‘Oh, yeah, I do know that park. And I know that it doesn’t have enough play equipment,’ or something like that. It was much more engaging than if we had just printed things and brought them to them.”
“High expectations for our guys”
Before PB Durham could get greater participation from residents who are incarcerated, it had to enlist the cooperation of the county sheriff’s office. It was an easy sell.
“When they gave me the spiel, it really made sense,” said Durham County Sheriff Clarence Birkhead. Residents who are incarcerated “haven’t lost their right to vote and engage in conversations, so why not allow them to be part of the participatory budgeting process as well? It aligned with the things we’re doing inside the Durham County Detention Center.”
The sheriff’s office partners with education institutions for inmates who want to finish high school or get a GED and participates in programs including You Can Vote, which helps people who are incarcerated access absentee ballots, and Welcome Home, a city program that provides support to people returning to Durham after incarceration, Birkhead said.
“We have very high expectations for our guys,” said Justin Ellerbe, chief of detention services for the sheriff’s office, about those incarcerated at the detention center. “We want to raise their ceiling and their expectations.”
Ellerbe says he tells those who are incarcerated that while an event may have put them in the detention center, it does not define them. “The direction that we’re taking our facility is letting all of our detainees know you still have a voice, you still are productive,” Ellerbe said. “Let’s find your values, find your power and get it out there.”
Logistics of participation
In the most recent round of participatory budgeting, 10 residents from the men’s detention center participated in proposal development, 110 participated in idea collection and 230 voted, Ortiz said. (PB Durham hopes to open the program to women who are incarcerated next year, she said.)
The detention center staff screens and approves residents before they’re selected and treats the meetings like an attorney visit in terms of the search and security procedures, Birkhead said. PB Durham sent two to three staff members to each session.
The biggest hurdle the PB Durham team encountered was the residents’ fluctuating availability, the staff members said. Developing proposals takes many months, and inmates can end their terms, get transferred to another facility or lose their privileges, making them unable to participate, Ortiz said. Only three of the 10 residents stayed involved throughout the entire proposal-development phase, she said. “We didn’t anticipate that so many would drop out during the process for different reasons.”
The PB Durham staff members “met our residents where they were,” Birkhead said. “They didn’t talk down to them. They had conversations with them.” For her part, Ortiz said “the sheriff’s team was incredibly supportive.”
“This is, as far as we're aware, a first-of-its-kind approach [to] treating incarcerated residents not as passive recipients of a ballot, but as decision-makers with real authority in a public budgeting process,” Gavin stated in nominating the project. “This was an intentional structural redesign of who gets to hold power in a civic process typically closed to this population.”
“I’m going to see what my voice did”
The incarcerated residents overwhelmingly gravitated toward supporting youth-oriented programs and projects such as basketball courts and playgrounds, Ortiz said. “It’s almost like they’re looking at where they are and they’re like, ‘We want to make sure that our kids don’t end up here.’ There’s just so much power in that.”
Several participants said the experience increased their trust in government, gave them a stronger sense of connection and inspired them to vote or engage with the City Council after their release, according to Gavin. One participant said it offered him a chance to retain “some type of humanity in my situation,” she said. (Smart Cities Dive was unable to get comments directly from detention center residents who participated in the process by the time this article was published.)
The detention center participants took pride and a sense of ownership in being a part of the process, Birkhead said.
They learned that their voice and their ideas mean something, according to Ellerbe. “They had an opportunity to give back to the community and be part of something that’s bigger than they are,” he said.
Some of the participants had to leave the county facility to serve terms in other facilities, Ellerbe added. “They were excited to say, ‘Hey, when I come back home, I’m going to see what my voice did.”

title: “It’s Not the Whole Story”: Aral School Participants Rethink Karakalpakstan
content:
A proverb about seasonal food caught the attention of Australian researcher, multimedia artist, and producer Jess Nikitina-Li while she was at the Aral School in Nukus.
“I’m interested in language, art and storytelling, and I didn’t really know what I would be working on during the program, but I became obsessed with this proverbial wisdom that kept coming up when we started asking questions about food systems in Karakalpakstan,” she told The Times of Central Asia. One proverb in particular became important to her work: “Three months of pumpkin, three months fish, three months melon, three months milk. All four seasons of the year the people are well fed and a lot of sweet fruit we have in our lands.”
“This really grounded my thinking because it reflects my belief that people are not inherently depleted,” she said. “People become depleted through extraction. Seasonal abundance has always been in this land, and people know how to work with the seasons; people are adaptive.”
The school is an initiative of the Uzbekistan Art and Culture Development Foundation (ACDF). Its first cohort studied food and water at a household level. Applications for the second cohort, which will explore the theme of “Climate and Landscape” from January to June 2027, are open until October 25.
TCA spoke with participants about their work in Karakalpakstan.
Nikitina-Li became particularly interested in the role of women within households, including kelin, a term referring to a young bride or daughter-in-law. “One of the key projects I worked on was a project called Tabak,” she said. “Tabak is a specifically resonant symbol in Karakalpakstan. It is the iron plate that everyone traditionally eats from.”
Her work with women eventually led to the creation of a cooking collective called “The Wild Kelin,” through which participants explored traditional recipes, nutrition, seasonality, and the knowledge passed between generations.
“I wanted to see what was important to them, what was relevant to their households, because that to me is the test of what is relevant to this region,” she said.
“We did a lot of community programming, textbook research, field research, field recordings and filmmaking, but the most important thing for me was done in close collaboration with our local colleagues,” she told TCA. “This was really a priority for me. It was why I came here, to have this strong intercultural exchange and to make solidarities with the land and with the people who understand the land the best.”
“We didn’t do this through this lens of people as victims, but through a lens of empowerment and understanding people as having agency – that they have an inherent capability of keeping themselves, and each other, alive,” Nikitina-Li said. “Something unique to this program was understanding how to create a community – a community of thinkers and makers who are grounded in the same principles, values and ethos, but who work so differently.”
“My biggest takeaway from the first cohort is wow – this was very well curated in terms of people. You have engineers and ecologists, and you have chefs, and then someone like me in art and anthropology. It encourages these different fields, but also the in-betweens, to really come through and collectivize. We all work so differently, but essentially we worked from the same starting point of caring for this place and understanding that people here already know so much.”
“There is conflict that happens, but this was an important part of community building. This is something I will take away with me, the understanding that through tension and difficulty a community can be built. I learnt so much about cultural resilience that wouldn’t have been possible sitting behind a computer or being at home.”
“I’ve learnt so much from being able to visit people’s families,” she said. “I’ve learnt about how a household functions, how a neighborhood functions, how a community functions, how people sustain each other through generations. This region can be painted through a lens of disaster and collapse and crisis, but people here are so joyous. This is what I mean when I talk about learning about what cultural and community resilience means.”
Bekmurat Abdikairov, a researcher from Karakalpakstan, specializes in geographic information systems (GIS) and remote sensing. His research uses geospatial analysis to examine changes in agricultural land, with Chimbay district serving as a case study.
“Participating in the Aral School was a very valuable experience for me, both professionally and personally,” he said. “As a young researcher from Karakalpakstan working on environmental issues, I had the opportunity to meet researchers, experts, and young professionals from different countries and to exchange perspectives on the challenges facing the Aral region.”
“One of the main things I gained was a broader understanding of the Aral crisis,” he told TCA. “Before the School, I was mostly looking at the region through the perspective of scientific research, particularly soil salinity, land degradation, remote sensing, and GIS. The School helped me see that these environmental problems cannot be considered separately from water management, agriculture, climate change, public health, livelihoods, and the social dimensions of the region.”
“What particularly impressed me was the diversity of perspectives,” Abdikairov said. “People from different disciplines and countries may look at the same problem differently, and bringing these perspectives together can lead to new ideas and more comprehensive solutions.”
Abdikairov’s work draws on satellite imagery and machine-learning approaches to monitor soil salinity and land conditions.
“The School reminded me that technological approaches should be connected with field observations and local knowledge,” he said. “Satellite data can show where changes are occurring, but understanding why those changes are happening requires cooperation between scientists, local communities, institutions, and policymakers.”
Islam Nurmukhamedov, a geophysicist born in Nukus and educated in Tashkent, is a PhD researcher focusing on ecology at the Karakalpak Scientific Research Institute of Natural Sciences.
“As a geophysicist and ecology researcher in Karakalpakstan, I believe that groundwater is still poorly studied, particularly its levels, composition, and available volume,” he told TCA. “This issue is becoming even more important as global warming and climate change continue to affect the region.”
“First, there is a language barrier and cultural differences between local communities and the international community. Another important issue is the low level of trust that local communities sometimes have toward external organizations and researchers. Aral School provides a valuable platform for breaking down these barriers and building cooperation between local and international communities,” Nurmukhamedov said. “It creates an opportunity to exchange knowledge, understand different perspectives, and develop projects together.”
A discussion with an international participant turned to construction. “I realized that local materials can be very well adapted to our dry and harsh climate,” he said. “They can also be more environmentally friendly and affordable. I think combining local knowledge with modern scientific approaches can lead to more sustainable solutions for our region.”
Sarthak Chakraborty, an interactive media artist and photogrammetrist based in India, works with indigenous knowledge systems and 3D technologies.
“I had a perspective and a knowledge of this place before coming,” he said. “I had consumed all the media through the internet, and I was told a story of scarcity, and that is what was fed. What I discovered when I came was very different. I expected it to be worse here based on the narrative I got online. But then after coming here, I feel like it’s a story of scarcity that has been sold, and that should not be the case. There’s so much life, there’s so much energy; there is so much wildlife: the plants, the animals, the people.”
“I found this book in the Aral School library called Deserts are Not Empty that talks about living as a state of mind,” he told TCA. “There are so many microorganisms; there are so many fungi. There are people still living in that space; they’re also embodying the region. They’re surviving. And when you visit Moynaq, you feel that scarcity, the emptiness; you feel like time has stopped in that place, but it’s not the whole story.”

title: Nearly forgotten languages are finding new words for Colombia’s dragonflies
content:
Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries.
When researchers began cataloging dragonflies in Guainía, a remote region in eastern Colombia, the scientific record contained only about 10 species. By working with Indigenous communities, they’ve found nearly 120.
“When we started, very little was known,” Yiselle Cano, biodiversity leader of the Dragones Guainía project, told contributor Manuel Fonseca for Mongabay.
“I think we must be close to 120 species by now,” Cano said. “It’s a hugely diverse group, because it includes dragonflies native to the Orinoco, Amazonas, and dragonflies that are endemic to the Guiana Shield.”
The diversity makes Guainía a hotspot for dragonflies and damselflies. It may also provide insights on what is happening to the region’s water. These insects depend on healthy freshwater ecosystems, and their aquatic habitats are coming under growing pressure from mining, deforestation, poorly managed waste, and rapidly expanding tourism.
Cataloging the insects was only part of the work. Once the researchers had begun filling gaps in the scientific record, they held workshops to share their findings with local communities. There they encountered another gap: the language of biology meant little to people whose understanding of the landscape had been formed outside scientific taxonomies. Some participants didn’t speak Spanish at all.
Community leaders invited everyone, from young children to elders who retained ancestral knowledge. As researchers displayed the dragonflies found around puddles, streams, and rivers, participants tried to identify them in their own languages.
“This is something that sometimes leaves us speechless,” Delio Suárez, a Tucano Indigenous leader of the multiethnic community La Ceiba, told Mongabay. “This leaves us with the task of recovering their names, of looking back and asking the last remaining wisdom keepers that we have.”
Sometimes the words could be recovered. Sometimes they had to be invented. In the community of Remanso, members of the Puinave tribe created names in an ancestral language that is itself at risk of disappearing. Tucano and Curripaco communities have also begun naming the insects while working to recover their languages.
Communities are now developing their own means of monitoring dragonflies and, through them, the condition of the water on which they depend.
Read the full story by Manuel Fonseca here.
Banner image: Guainía, also known as the land of many waters, is a remote biodiversity hotspot at the meeting point of the Amazon Rainforest, the Orinoco River Basin, and the Guyana Shield. Image courtesy of Jenilee Montes.
